d: A list of about 3,000 core academic lemmas derived from the academic portion of the Corpus of Contemporary American English. Unlike the AWL, it uses lemmas rather than word families and does not exclude high-frequency general words outright, selecting items that are notably more frequent in academic than non-academic texts.
e: research, analysis, and data are on the AVL; because it counts lemmas, a noun and a verb with the same spelling are counted as different items rather than as one family.
p: Developed by Dee Gardner and Mark Davies (2014).
s: Gardner, D., & Davies, M. (2014). A new academic vocabulary list. Applied Linguistics, 35(3), 305–327.

d: A list of 570 word families that occur frequently and across many disciplines in academic texts but are not among the 2,000 GSL words. It is divided into ten sublists by frequency and is widely used in English for Academic Purposes; critics note it is based on word families and was later challenged by lemma-based lists such as the AVL.
e: analyze, concept, data, significant, and hypothesis are AWL headwords.
p: Developed by Averil Coxhead (2000) from a corpus of about 3.5 million running words of academic texts.
s: Coxhead, A. (2000). A new academic word list. TESOL Quarterly, 34(2), 213–238.

d: The features of pronunciation that identify where a speaker is from, which social group they belong to, or which language they learned first. Unlike a dialect, an accent concerns pronunciation only; every speaker has an accent, including speakers of standard varieties.
e: A speaker of General American usually pronounces car with a final [ɹ], while many speakers in southern England say [kɑː] without it.

d: A debate within generative SLA about whether adult L2 learners still have access to the innate linguistic principles (Universal Grammar) thought to guide child L1 acquisition. Positions range from full access, through partial access via the L1, to no access, in which adults rely on general learning mechanisms.
e: Researchers test whether English learners of Japanese show knowledge of subtle constraints on Japanese sentences that are not taught and not found in English; such knowledge is taken as evidence of UG access.

d: A model proposing that the degree to which learners acquire an L2 depends on their social and psychological distance from the target-language community: the more learners integrate socially and feel psychologically close, the further they are predicted to progress. It grew out of a study of six learners in which one adult (“Alberto”) made very little progress, and it has been criticized for treating social distance as easy to measure.
e: An immigrant who lives, works, and socializes only within his home-language community, with little contact with English speakers, would be predicted to make limited progress in English.
p: Proposed by John Schumann (1978).
s: Schumann, J. H. (1978). The pidginization process: A model for second language acquisition. Newbury House.

d: A test that measures how much of the content or skills of a specific course or syllabus learners have learned.
e: An end-of-unit quiz on the vocabulary and grammar from Chapter 5 of the course book is an achievement test.
a: Progress test (when given during a course)

d: Language planning aimed at increasing the number of people who know and use a language, mainly through education, teaching materials, and learning opportunities.
e: Wales funds Welsh-medium schools so that children from English-speaking homes can become fluent in Welsh.
p: Added as a third type of planning by Robert L. Cooper (1989).
s: Cooper, R. L. (1989). Language planning and social change. Cambridge University Press.

d: The claim that there are two separate ways of developing an L2: acquisition, a subconscious process driven by meaningful communication, and learning, a conscious process of studying rules. In its strong form it holds that consciously learned knowledge cannot turn into acquired knowledge; many researchers dispute this and argue that the two kinds of knowledge interact.
e: A learner who “just knows” that She go sounds wrong without being able to explain why is said to rely on acquired knowledge; a learner who recalls the rule “add -s for third person singular” is using learned knowledge.
p: Proposed by Stephen Krashen as part of his Monitor Model (late 1970s–early 1980s).
s: Krashen, S. D. (1982). Principles and practice in second language acquisition. Pergamon.

d: A word formed from the initial letters (or parts) of a phrase and pronounced as an ordinary word. Some writers use "acronym" more broadly to include initialisms, which are pronounced letter by letter.
e: NASA (National Aeronautics and Space Administration), laser (light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation).

d: Descriptions by the American Council on the Teaching of Foreign Languages (ACTFL) of what language users can do at different levels of functional ability in speaking, writing, listening, and reading. The major levels are Novice, Intermediate, Advanced, Superior, and Distinguished; Novice, Intermediate, and Advanced are each divided into Low, Mid, and High sublevels.
e: A learner rated Intermediate Mid can handle simple everyday conversations by creating with the language but has difficulty narrating in the past.
r: Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR)
p: First published by ACTFL in 1986 as an academic adaptation of the U.S. government's Interagency Language Roundtable (ILR) scale, and revised in 1999/2001, 2012, and 2024 (the current, fourth edition).
s: ACTFL. (2024). ACTFL proficiency guidelines 2024. ACTFL.

d: A situation in which a person learns a second language while continuing to develop and value their first language, so that the new language is added to their repertoire. It is generally associated with positive cognitive and educational outcomes and is common when the L1 has high social status or institutional support.
e: An English-speaking child in Canada attends French immersion school while continuing to use English at home and in the community.
p: Terms commonly attributed to Wallace Lambert (1975).

d: A sequence of two related turns produced by different speakers, where the first part (such as a question or invitation) makes a particular type of second part (such as an answer or acceptance/refusal) expected next. If the expected second part does not come, its absence is noticeable.
e: A: Hi! B: Hi! (greeting–greeting); A: Want to join us? B: Sure! (invitation–acceptance).
p: Described by Emanuel Schegloff and Harvey Sacks (1973), drawing on Sacks's earlier lectures.
s: Schegloff, E. A., & Sacks, H. (1973). Opening up closings. Semiotica, 8(4).

d: A word class whose members typically describe properties of entities and modify nouns or serve as complements after linking verbs. Many English adjectives can be graded (taller, most useful) and modified by very.
e: a quiet room (attributive use); The room is quiet (predicative use).

d: An optional element that adds information (such as time, place, manner, or reason) to a phrase or clause without being required by the head. Adjuncts can usually be omitted or stacked without making the sentence ungrammatical.
e: In She read the book in the library yesterday, in the library and yesterday are adjuncts.

d: A word class whose members typically modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs, or whole clauses, expressing manner, degree, time, frequency, or the speaker's stance. It is a mixed category in traditional grammar, and many linguists divide it into subclasses.
e: She spoke quietly (manner); very cold (degree); Fortunately, we arrived (stance).

d: A grammatical function, usually optional, that gives information about circumstances such as time, place, manner, frequency, or reason. Adverbials can be adverbs, prepositional phrases, noun phrases, or clauses.
e: In Last week we met at a café because it was raining, last week, at a café, and because it was raining are adverbials.

d: The claim that emotional factors such as anxiety, low motivation, and low self-confidence act like a filter that blocks input from being used for acquisition. The idea is intuitively appealing, but the filter itself has been criticized as vague and hard to measure directly.
e: A student who is afraid of being laughed at may understand a classroom conversation but, according to the hypothesis, acquire less from it than a relaxed classmate.
p: Developed by Stephen Krashen as part of the Monitor Model, drawing on an earlier proposal by Heidi Dulay and Marina Burt (1977).
s: Krashen, S. D. (1982). Principles and practice in second language acquisition. Pergamon.

d: A bound morpheme that attaches to a root, stem, or base to form a new word or a new form of a word. Affixes are classified by their position relative to the base.
e: dis- in dislike and -ness in kindness are affixes.

d: A consonant that begins as a stop and is released as a fricative at the same or a nearby place of articulation, functioning as a single sound unit.
e: /tʃ/ in church and /dʒ/ in judge are English affricates; German /pf/ in Pferd 'horse' is another.

d: A systematic, rule-governed variety of English spoken by many African Americans, with its own patterns of grammar, pronunciation, vocabulary, and discourse; it is not slang or a collection of errors. Its origins are debated (some scholars stress links to earlier British dialects, others to creole languages or African substrate influence), and it has been central to discussions of linguistic discrimination in education.
e: She be working means 'she usually works' (habitual be), whereas She working means 'she is working right now.'
s: Green, L. J. (2002). African American English: A linguistic introduction. Cambridge University Press.

d: The ways in which the age at which a person starts learning an L2 (age of onset) relates to the rate and outcome of learning. Research generally finds that older beginners progress faster at first, while earlier starters in immersion settings more often reach higher long-term levels; how to explain these patterns remains debated.
e: Teenagers who move to a new country often outperform younger siblings in grammar tests during the first year, but after ten years the younger siblings are more likely to sound native-like.
p: A widely cited study of age of arrival and grammatical attainment is Jacqueline Johnson and Elissa Newport (1989).
s: Johnson, J. S., & Newport, E. L. (1989). Critical period effects in second language learning: The influence of maturational state on the acquisition of English as a second language. Cognitive Psychology, 21(1).

d: The thematic role of the participant who deliberately carries out or causes the action described by the verb.
e: In The chef chopped the onions, the chef is the agent.

d: A language in which words are typically built by stringing together several morphemes, each with a clear boundary and usually expressing one meaning.
e: Turkish evlerimde ‘in my houses’ = ev ‘house’ + -ler (plural) + -im ‘my’ + -de ‘in’.

d: A relationship in which the form of one word changes to match grammatical features, such as person, number, or gender, of another word it is related to. English shows limited subject–verb agreement, while languages such as Spanish or Swahili show much richer agreement.
e: The dog barks / The dogs bark; Spanish la casa blanca 'the white house', where the article and adjective agree with the feminine noun.

d: One of two or more different forms (morphs) that express the same morpheme, with the choice usually depending on the phonological or lexical context.
e: The English regular plural has three allomorphs: /s/ in cats, /z/ in dogs, and /ɪz/ in horses.

d: One of the actual pronunciations (phonetic variants) of a single phoneme. Using one allophone instead of another does not change a word's meaning, and which allophone appears is often predictable from the neighboring sounds or position in the word.
e: English /t/ is aspirated [tʰ] in top, unaspirated [t] in stop, and often a tap [ɾ] in American English water.

d: Describing a consonant produced with the tongue tip or blade against or near the alveolar ridge, the bony ridge just behind the upper front teeth.
e: English /t/, /d/, /n/, /s/, /z/ and /l/ are alveolar, as in ten, den, net, sue, zoo and let.

d: A type of semantic change in which a word acquires a more positive or more prestigious meaning over time.
e: Old English cniht meant 'boy' or 'servant'; its descendant knight came to mean a man of honorable military rank.

d: A scoring method in which raters judge several separate aspects of a performance and give a score for each. It gives more detailed diagnostic information than holistic scoring but takes longer.
e: An essay receives 4/5 for content, 3/5 for organization, 2/5 for grammar, and 4/5 for vocabulary.

d: The addition of interpretive linguistic information to a corpus, such as word classes, lemmas, syntactic structure, or learner errors. Annotation can be done automatically, manually, or with automatic tagging followed by manual correction.
e: In the annotated line She_PRP reads_VBZ books_NNS, each word carries a part-of-speech tag from the Penn Treebank tagset.

d: The relation between words with opposite meanings. Linguists distinguish several types, mainly gradable antonyms, complementary antonyms and converses, which behave differently in logic and grammar. Some authors reserve the term "antonym" for gradable pairs only.
e: Hot/cold, alive/dead and buy/sell are all opposites, but each pair is a different type.
s: Lyons, J. (1977). Semantics (Vols. 1–2). Cambridge University Press.

d: An acquired language disorder caused by brain damage, often from stroke, that affects the ability to produce or understand language, including reading and writing. It is distinguished from problems caused by hearing loss, motor weakness, or general cognitive decline.
e: After a left-hemisphere stroke, a patient may understand questions well but struggle to find and produce the words for answers.

d: A three-level distinction for describing language teaching. An approach is a set of beliefs about language and learning; a method is an overall plan for teaching built on an approach; and a technique is a specific classroom activity. Richards and Rodgers later reworked the model into approach, design, and procedure.
e: Believing that language is learned through meaningful communication (approach) can lead to communicative language teaching (method), which may use an information-gap activity in class (technique).
p: Proposed by Edward M. Anthony (1963).
s: Anthony, E. M. (1963). Approach, method and technique. English Language Teaching, 17(2), 63–67.

d: A consonant produced with the articulators close together but not close enough to create turbulent airflow, so the sound is smooth rather than noisy.
e: English /w/ wet, /j/ yet, /ɹ/ red and the lateral approximant /l/ led are approximants.

d: An expression required by the meaning of a predicate, such as the participants in the event a verb describes. Arguments are distinguished from adjuncts, which add optional information; the boundary between the two is sometimes debated.
e: In Kim put the keys on the table, Kim, the keys, and on the table are all arguments of put.

d: A grammatical category that expresses how a situation unfolds in time, such as whether it is viewed as complete, ongoing, habitual, or having current relevance, rather than when it happens. English marks progressive and perfect aspect with auxiliaries.
e: Progressive: She is writing. Perfect: She has written. Both are present tense but differ in aspect.

d: A short burst of breath, heard as a delay before voicing begins, after the release of a voiceless stop. In English it is predictable (allophonic), but in languages such as Hindi, Thai and Korean it distinguishes phonemes.
e: English pin is [pʰɪn] with aspiration, but spin is [spɪn] without it; in Hindi, /kʰaːl/ 'skin' and /kaːl/ 'time' are different words.

d: The process of gathering and interpreting information about what learners know and can do. It is broader than testing: it includes tests, but also observation, portfolios, self-assessment, and informal classroom checks.
e: A teacher assesses speaking by combining a recorded interview, notes from class discussions, and students' self-ratings.

d: A process in which a sound becomes more like a neighboring sound in some property, such as place of articulation, voicing or manner. It is called regressive (anticipatory) when a sound is influenced by a following sound and progressive when it is influenced by a preceding one.
e: ten bikes is often pronounced [tɛm baɪks], with /n/ taking the bilabial place of the following /b/ (regressive); the plural ending is [s] after voiceless /t/ in cats [kæts] (progressive).

d: The idea that speakers shift style mainly in response to their audience, including the people directly addressed and others who may be listening. It offers an alternative to explaining style through attention paid to speech.
e: In New Zealand, the same newsreaders voiced the /t/ in words like better more often when reading for a station with a broader local audience than for a more prestigious national station.
p: Proposed by Allan Bell (1984).
s: Bell, A. (1984). Language style as audience design. Language in Society, 13(2), 145–204.

d: A method popular in the United States in the 1950s and 1960s, based on structural linguistics and behaviorist psychology. It treats language learning as habit formation through repetition, memorized dialogues, and pattern drills, and it tries to prevent errors rather than correct them.
e: In a substitution drill, the teacher says I go to school every day, gives the cue work, and the class responds I go to work every day.

d: In language testing, the degree to which test tasks correspond to the ways language is used in the real-world situations the test is meant to predict. In teaching, the term is also used for materials produced for real communication rather than for language learners.
e: A test for future nurses that asks candidates to complete a patient handover based on a recorded nurse–patient conversation has higher authenticity than one that asks them to fill blanks in unrelated sentences.

d: A verb that combines with a main verb to express grammatical meanings such as tense, aspect, voice, or modality. In English, auxiliaries (be, have, do, and the modals) invert with the subject in questions and take not directly.
e: She has finished. Has she finished? She hasn't finished.

d: A learner’s tendency to underuse or steer around an L2 structure or word that they find difficult, often because it differs from their L1. Avoidance matters for research because counting only errors can hide difficulty: a learner who avoids a structure makes few errors with it.
e: Schachter (1974) found that Chinese and Japanese learners, whose L1s place relative clauses before the noun, produced fewer English relative clauses (the man who I met) than other learners, and therefore fewer relative-clause errors.
p: Brought to prominence by Jacquelyn Schachter (1974), who showed that error counts alone can be misleading.
s: Schachter, J. (1974). An error in error analysis. Language Learning, 24(2).

d: A stage of infant vocal development in which babies produce syllable-like sequences of consonants and vowels without meaning. Canonical babbling, with well-formed syllables, usually begins around 6 to 10 months, often as repeated syllables, and its sounds gradually come to reflect the ambient language.
e: An eight-month-old repeating [bababa] or [dadada] is producing canonical (reduplicated) babbling.

d: A word formation process in which a new, shorter word is created by removing what speakers take to be an affix from an existing word, even though the longer word was not historically derived from the shorter one.
e: edit from editor, burgle from burglar, babysit from babysitter.
p: The term was introduced by James Murray in 1889, in the New English Dictionary (later the Oxford English Dictionary), in his entry for burgle.

d: A curriculum planning process that starts from the desired learning results, then decides what evidence (assessment) will show those results, and only then plans learning activities.
e: A teacher first decides that students should be able to write a persuasive letter to a city council, designs a rubric for that letter, and then plans lessons on argument structure and formal register.
p: Popularized by Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe (1998).
s: Wiggins, G., & McTighe, J. (1998). Understanding by design. ASCD.

d: Any form, simple or complex, to which an affix or other morphological process is applied at a given step of word formation. The term is broader than root and is often used for derivation as well as inflection.
e: happy is the base for unhappy, and unhappy is in turn the base for unhappiness.

d: The language skills needed for everyday, face-to-face social interaction, which is usually supported by context such as gestures and shared situations. The framework holds that such skills often develop within about two years of exposure; it has been criticized for oversimplifying and for being misread as a deficit label.
e: A newly arrived student can chat fluently with classmates about weekend plans and video games in English after about a year.
p: Distinction introduced by Jim Cummins (1979; developed further in the early 1980s).
s: Cummins, J. (1979). Cognitive/academic language proficiency, linguistic interdependence, the optimum age question and some other matters. Working Papers on Bilingualism, 19, 121–129.

d: The level in a category hierarchy that people find most natural and use most often, lying between more general (superordinate) and more specific (subordinate) levels. Basic-level terms tend to be short, learned early by children, and associated with a typical shape and way of interacting with the object.
e: Chair is basic level, between superordinate furniture and subordinate armchair.
p: Proposed by Eleanor Rosch and colleagues (1976).
s: Rosch, E., Mervis, C. B., Gray, W. D., Johnson, D. M., & Boyes-Braem, P. (1976). Basic objects in natural categories. Cognitive Psychology, 8(3), 382–439.

d: Describing a consonant produced by bringing both lips together or close to each other.
e: The first sounds of pie, buy and my, /p/, /b/ and /m/, are bilabial.

d: The hypothesis that regularly managing two languages strengthens general executive functions such as inhibitory control and task switching, giving bilinguals an edge on nonverbal cognitive tasks. It is strongly debated: early studies, notably by Ellen Bialystok and colleagues, reported advantages, but many larger studies and meta-analyses find small or no reliable differences once factors such as socioeconomic status are controlled, and some point to publication bias.
e: A study compares bilingual and monolingual children on a Simon task, where they must respond to a color while ignoring its location on the screen.
s: Paap, K. R., & Greenberg, Z. I. (2013). There is no coherent evidence for a bilingual advantage in executive processing. Cognitive Psychology, 66(2).

d: The use of two languages by an individual or within a society. Definitions range from native-like control of both languages to the ability to function in some way in a second language; many researchers now argue that a bilingual is not simply two monolinguals in one person, since each language is used for different purposes and people.
e: A child in Montreal who speaks French at school and with friends and English with her grandparents.

d: A word formation process in which parts of two (or more) words are fused into one new word, typically combining the beginning of one with the end of another. The result is called a blend.
e: brunch (breakfast + lunch), smog (smoke + fog), motel (motor + hotel).

d: The tendency for an established word to prevent the formation of a regularly derived or inflected word with the same meaning.
e: went blocks *goed in adult English (ungrammatical); glory blocks *gloriosity (unattested, marked with *).
p: Most closely associated with Mark Aronoff's (1976) analysis of English word formation, though the idea of a more specific form preempting a general rule goes back to Pāṇini.
s: Aronoff, M. (1976). Word formation in generative grammar. MIT Press.

d: The adoption of a linguistic feature, most often a word, from another language, usually as a result of contact between speakers. A borrowed word is called a loanword and is often adapted to the sound system and grammar of the receiving language (the term 'borrowing' is a metaphor: nothing is given back).
e: English took beef and pork from Norman French, sky and they from Old Norse, and tsunami from Japanese.

d: A morpheme that cannot occur on its own and must be attached to another morpheme. Most affixes are bound, and some roots are bound as well.
e: The plural -s in cats, the prefix re- in redo, and the bound root -ceive in receive and perceive.

d: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more general, so that it covers a wider range of referents than before.
e: Holiday originally meant 'holy day' (a religious festival) but now refers to any day or period off from work or school.

d: A type of aphasia marked by slow, effortful, non-fluent speech in which function words and inflections are often omitted, while comprehension of everyday conversation is relatively preserved. It is classically linked to damage in and around Broca's area, but the match is not exact: lasting Broca's aphasia usually involves damage extending beyond that area, and damage to Broca's area alone may cause only milder, temporary problems.
e: Asked about a weekend trip, a patient might say Walk… park… dog… sun… good.

d: A region in the inferior frontal gyrus, usually in the left hemisphere, traditionally associated with speech production. Current research links it to a wider set of functions, including aspects of syntax and working memory, and it is seen as part of a larger language network rather than a single "speech center."
e: Broca's patient Leborgne could produce little except the syllable tan; after his death Broca found a lesion on the surface of the left frontal lobe, and modern scans of the preserved brain show the damage extended deeper and more widely than the area named after Broca.
p: Named after the French physician Paul Broca, who reported the case of his patient Leborgne in 1861.

d: In generative syntax, a structural relation in a tree: a node A c-commands node B if neither dominates the other and the first branching node above A also dominates B. It is used to state conditions on phenomena such as the interpretation of reflexive pronouns.
e: In John's brother admires himself, himself can refer only to John's brother, not to John, because John's brother c-commands the reflexive but John (embedded inside that noun phrase) does not.
p: The term and its standard definition were introduced by Tanya Reinhart in her 1976 MIT dissertation, building on earlier notions of "command" (e.g., Langacker, 1969).
s: Reinhart, T. (1976). The syntactic domain of anaphora [Doctoral dissertation, Massachusetts Institute of Technology].

d: A type of borrowing in which an expression from another language is translated part by part, instead of being taken over in its original form.
e: English skyscraper was rendered in French as gratte-ciel (literally 'scrape-sky') and in German as Wolkenkratzer ('cloud-scraper', with 'clouds' in place of 'sky').

d: A description of a language task a learner is able to perform at a given level, written in positive, practical terms. Can-do statements are used for goal setting, self-assessment, and reporting proficiency, notably in the CEFR and in NCSSFL-ACTFL materials.
e: I can write a short email to a friend inviting them to a party.
r: Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR)

d: A set of reference vowel qualities, defined by extreme tongue positions, that phoneticians use as fixed points for describing the vowels of any language. They are not the vowels of a particular language.
e: Cardinal vowel 1 is [i], the highest and most front vowel possible; the English vowel in see can be described by how close it is to this reference point.
p: Devised by Daniel Jones, who defined the eight primary cardinal vowels in 1917; similar reference systems had been proposed earlier by A. J. Ellis and A. M. Bell.

d: A grammatical category marking the function of a noun phrase in a clause, such as subject or object, usually through inflection on nouns, pronouns, or determiners. In generative syntax, "abstract Case" is also assumed in languages with little visible case marking.
e: English pronouns show case: she (nominative) versus her (accusative); German der Mann (nominative) versus den Mann (accusative).

d: The tendency to perceive gradually varying stimuli as belonging to distinct categories, so that differences across a category boundary are easier to detect than equally large differences within a category. Its strength varies, being clearer for many consonants than for vowels.
e: When voice onset time is varied in small steps from [ba] to [pa], English listeners hear a sudden switch from /b/ to /p/ rather than a gradual change.
p: Demonstrated by Alvin Liberman and colleagues at Haskins Laboratories (Liberman, Harris, Hoffman, & Griffith, 1957).
s: Liberman, A. M., Harris, K. S., Hoffman, H. S., & Griffith, B. C. (1957). The discrimination of speech sounds within and across phoneme boundaries. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 54.

d: The special way many caregivers talk to young children, often with higher and more varied pitch, slower rate, simpler sentences, repetition, and a focus on the here and now. Its role in acquisition is debated, and its form varies considerably across cultures.
e: A parent says Look! A doggie! See the doggie? Big doggie! in a sing-song voice.

d: An affix made of two parts, one placed before and one after the base, which together express a single meaning or function. Some linguists prefer to analyze such cases as a prefix and suffix that must co-occur.
e: German past participle ge-…-t: spielen ‘to play’ → gespielt ‘played’.

d: Corrective feedback in which the teacher signals that the learner's utterance was not understood or was ill-formed and asks the learner to say it again, without giving the correct form.
e: Student: I want practice speak. Teacher: Sorry? Can you say that again?
p: One of the six feedback types in Roy Lyster and Leila Ranta's (1997) classification, based on teacher–student interaction in primary-level French immersion classrooms in Montreal.

d: A grammatical unit that typically contains a subject and a predicate. A sentence may consist of a single clause or of several clauses linked by coordination or subordination.
e: When the bell rang, the students left contains two clauses: when the bell rang and the students left.

d: A construction that divides a simple clause into two parts in order to highlight one constituent as the focus. English it-clefts and wh-clefts (pseudo-clefts) are the main types, and clefting is also used as a test for constituency.
e: Anna broke the vase → It was Anna who broke the vase (it-cleft) or What Anna broke was the vase (wh-cleft).

d: A word formation process that shortens a longer word by cutting off one or more syllables, usually without changing its meaning, although the clipped form is often more informal.
e: laboratory → lab, influenza → flu, examination → exam.

d: A morpheme that behaves syntactically like a word but is phonologically dependent on a neighboring word, sitting between a free word and an affix. Unlike most affixes, clitics can attach to words of many different classes or to whole phrases.
e: English possessive 's attaches to whole phrases: [the king of Spain]'s daughter; also 'll in she'll.

d: The overlap of articulatory movements for neighboring sounds, so that each sound is produced differently depending on its context. Coarticulation is usually seen as gradient and automatic, while assimilation is a more categorical change, although the boundary between them is debated.
e: The lips are already rounded during /k/ in coo, anticipating the rounded vowel, but not in key; the vowel in man is nasalized, [mæ̃n], because of the surrounding nasals.

d: The consonant or consonants that follow the nucleus within a syllable. Syllables with a coda are called closed, and those without one are called open; many languages restrict which consonants can appear in codas.
e: The coda of lamp is /mp/; Japanese allows very few coda consonants, so Japanese-speaking learners may add a vowel after English final consonants.

d: The combining of elements from two languages, especially within a single sentence or phrase. Some researchers use it as a synonym for code-switching, while others reserve it for switching inside a sentence and use code-switching for switching between sentences.
e: In Hindi-English (“Hinglish”): Main kal office jaaunga 'I will go to the office tomorrow.'

d: Alternating between two or more languages or varieties within a conversation, either between sentences or within a single sentence. Research shows that it follows grammatical patterns and serves social functions such as marking identity, quoting, or changing topic, and it is not evidence of weak proficiency. In popular usage the term is also used for shifting to a standard variety in certain settings.
e: Sometimes I'll start a sentence in Spanish y termino en español ('and I finish in Spanish'), a switch recorded in a Puerto Rican community in New York.
p: Key early work includes Shana Poplack's (1980) study of Spanish-English switching.
s: Poplack, S. (1980). Sometimes I'll start a sentence in Spanish y termino en español: Toward a typology of code-switching. Linguistics, 18(7–8), 581–618.

d: A word that shares a common origin with a word in a related language because both descend from the same ancestral form. In historical linguistics, cognates need not look alike or mean exactly the same thing, and look-alikes due to chance or borrowing do not count; in language teaching, the term is often used more loosely for any similar-looking words with similar meanings.
e: English two, German zwei, Latin duo, and Greek dúo are cognates; English much and Spanish mucho look alike but are not cognates (they come from different roots).

d: The finding that bilinguals typically process cognates (words that share form and meaning across their languages) faster or more accurately than non-cognate words. It is often cited as evidence that both languages are active at once, even when only one is being used.
e: A Spanish–English bilingual recognizes English hospital (Spanish hospital) faster than English window (Spanish ventana).

d: The language ability needed to understand and produce the abstract, decontextualized language of school subjects, such as academic vocabulary and complex sentence structures. The framework claims that CALP typically takes much longer to develop than conversational skills (Cummins’ Toronto data suggested about five to seven years), which has implications for assessing multilingual students.
e: The same student who chats easily with friends struggles to explain in writing how photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy in a science report.
p: Distinction introduced by Jim Cummins (1979; developed further in the early 1980s).
s: Cummins, J. (1979). Cognitive/academic language proficiency, linguistic interdependence, the optimum age question and some other matters. Working Papers on Bilingualism, 19, 121–129.

d: An approach within cognitive linguistics that sees meaning as conceptualization grounded in bodily and cultural experience, rather than as truth conditions alone. It emphasizes prototypes, metaphor, metonymy, frames and construal.
e: Cognitive semantics explains why English speakers say prices rose by appealing to the conceptual link between MORE and UP.
p: Closely associated with George Lakoff, Ronald Langacker, Leonard Talmy and Charles Fillmore, from the late 1970s onward.
s: Lakoff, G. (1987). Women, fire, and dangerous things: What categories reveal about the mind. University of Chicago Press.

d: The quality of a text or conversation making sense as a connected whole, based on logical relations between ideas and the reader's or listener's background knowledge. Coherence is built by the interpreter as much as by the text, so a text can be coherent with few cohesive devices or incoherent despite many.
e: A: That's the phone. B: I'm in the bath. A: OK. There are no cohesive links, but the exchange is coherent (A asks B to answer; B explains why not).

d: The visible linguistic links that connect sentences and parts of a text, such as pronouns, conjunctions, substitution, ellipsis, and repeated or related words. Cohesion helps create, but does not by itself guarantee, coherence.
e: My sister bought a bike. She rides it every day. However, … (pronoun reference and a linking adverb).
p: Classic framework by M. A. K. Halliday and Ruqaiya Hasan (1976), who identified reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction, and lexical cohesion.
s: Halliday, M. A. K., & Hasan, R. (1976). Cohesion in English. Longman.

d: The creation of an entirely new word that is not built from existing morphemes in a regular way, often for a product, brand, or new concept. Coined words such as trade names sometimes become general words.
e: Kodak was invented as a brand name; Kleenex is now widely used for any tissue.

d: The tendency of a word to occur with particular grammatical categories or structures, rather than with specific words. Where collocation describes word-to-word attraction, colligation in this modern sense describes word-to-grammar attraction; J. R. Firth, who introduced the term, originally used it for relations between grammatical categories, and later corpus linguists such as John Sinclair and Michael Hoey gave it its word-centered meaning.
e: The verb avoid typically colligates with a following -ing form (avoid making mistakes), not a to-infinitive (*avoid to make mistakes, ungrammatical).

d: The tendency of particular words to occur near each other more often than chance would predict, or a specific word combination that shows this tendency. Researchers differ in whether they identify collocations mainly by statistical co-occurrence in corpora (the frequency-based view) or by how fixed and semantically restricted the combination is (the phraseological view).
e: English speakers say strong tea and heavy rain; powerful tea and strong rain are grammatical but sound unnatural.
p: Most closely associated with J. R. Firth, who used collocation as a technical term and whose 1957 remark “You shall know a word by the company it keeps” became a guiding principle of corpus linguistics.
s: Firth, J. R. (1957). A synopsis of linguistic theory, 1930–1955. In Studies in linguistic analysis. Blackwell.
a: Collocate (a word that co-occurs with the search word)

t: Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR)
d: A framework published by the Council of Europe that describes language ability on six main levels (A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, C2) using can-do descriptors; the 2020 Companion Volume added a Pre-A1 band and fuller descriptions of “plus” levels (such as B1+). It is widely used to align curricula, textbooks, and tests, although some researchers caution that its levels are not a validated model of acquisition order.
e: A university requires B2 English, meaning applicants can, for example, understand the main ideas of complex texts on familiar and some abstract topics and take part in conversations with reasonable fluency and spontaneity.
p: First published by the Council of Europe in 2001; the Companion Volume (2020) updated it and added new descriptor scales, for example for mediation, plurilingual and pluricultural competence, and sign languages.
s: Council of Europe. (2001). Common European framework of reference for languages: Learning, teaching, assessment. Cambridge University Press.

d: A theory explaining how speakers adjust their speech to the people they talk to: they converge (become more similar) to show approval or reduce social distance, or diverge (become more different) to emphasize distinctiveness. Accommodation can also misfire, as in overaccommodation.
e: A nurse speaks more slowly and simply to an elderly patient (convergence, which may become overaccommodation), while a speaker deliberately broadens a regional accent when talking to someone they dislike (divergence).
p: Developed by Howard Giles and colleagues from the early 1970s (e.g., Giles, Taylor, & Bourhis, 1973), first as speech accommodation theory and later broadened as communication accommodation theory.
s: Giles, H., Coupland, J., & Coupland, N. (Eds.). (1991). Contexts of accommodation: Developments in applied sociolinguistics. Cambridge University Press.

d: The knowledge and ability needed to use language appropriately and effectively in real social situations, not only to form grammatical sentences. Influential models divide it into components such as grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse, and strategic competence.
e: A learner who can form perfect sentences but greets a professor with Hey dude, what’s up? shows grammatical knowledge but limited sociolinguistic competence.
p: Term introduced by the sociolinguist Dell Hymes (published 1972) in response to Chomsky’s narrower notion of competence; adapted for L2 teaching and testing by Michael Canale and Merrill Swain (1980).
s: Canale, M., & Swain, M. (1980). Theoretical bases of communicative approaches to second language teaching and testing. Applied Linguistics, 1(1).

d: An approach, developed from the 1970s onward, that treats the ability to communicate meaningfully and appropriately (communicative competence) as the goal of language teaching. Lessons emphasize real communication, interaction, and fluency, though versions differ in how much explicit grammar teaching they allow.
e: Pairs of students plan a weekend trip together, negotiating dates, budget, and activities in the target language while the teacher monitors and notes problems for later feedback.

d: A group of people who come together around a shared activity and, through doing things together, develop shared practices, including ways of talking. Sociolinguists use the concept to study how variation and identity are produced in local groups rather than in broad categories such as class or gender.
e: Members of a university robotics club develop their own jargon, in-jokes, and ways of greeting each other.
p: Concept from Jean Lave and Etienne Wenger (1991); brought into language and gender research by Penelope Eckert and Sally McConnell-Ginet (1992).
s: Eckert, P., & McConnell-Ginet, S. (1992). Think practically and look locally: Language and gender as community-based practice. Annual Review of Anthropology, 21, 461–490.

d: The central technique of historical linguistics for demonstrating that languages are related and for reconstructing their common ancestor. Linguists gather probable cognates, identify regular sound correspondences among them, and infer the ancestral forms and sound changes that best account for those correspondences.
e: Comparing Italian otto, Spanish ocho, Portuguese oito, and French huit 'eight' points to an ancestral form close to the attested Latin octō, which lets linguists check the method against real records.

d: An element that a head requires or selects to complete its meaning and structure; complements are usually closely bound to the head. The term is also used in traditional and pedagogical grammar for subject and object complements (e.g., after linking verbs), a sense slightly different from its use in generative syntax.
e: In She devoured the cake, the cake is the complement of devoured; *She devoured is ungrammatical without it.

d: Pairs of opposites that divide a domain into two with no middle ground, so denying one asserts the other. They do not normally allow degree modification in their basic sense.
e: Alive/dead: if an animal is not alive, it is dead, and it cannot be neither. In their literal sense these words resist degree modification, which is why very dead sounds odd (it is acceptable only as a joke or exaggeration).
s: Lyons, J. (1977). Semantics (Vols. 1–2). Cambridge University Press.

d: A relationship between two sounds in which each occurs only in environments where the other never occurs. Sounds in complementary distribution that are also phonetically similar are usually analyzed as allophones of one phoneme.
e: English [pʰ] occurs at the start of a stressed syllable (pin) and [p] after /s/ (spin), never the reverse. English [h] and [ŋ] are also in complementary distribution but are treated as separate phonemes because they are so different phonetically.

d: A word that introduces a subordinate clause, especially a complement clause, and marks it as embedded. In generative syntax it heads the complementizer phrase (CP).
e: that in I think that she left; whether and if in I wonder whether she left.

d: An approach that views language and language development as complex systems in which many interacting factors (learner, context, languages) change over time in non-linear and sometimes unpredictable ways. It emphasizes variability, individual developmental paths, and change, rather than fixed end states.
e: A learner’s accuracy with past tense rises, drops, and rises again across a year of weekly writing samples; a CDST researcher treats this variability as meaningful data rather than noise.
p: Introduced into SLA by Diane Larsen-Freeman (1997).
s: Larsen-Freeman, D. (1997). Chaos/complexity science and second language acquisition. Applied Linguistics, 18(2).

d: A sentence containing a main clause and at least one subordinate clause. Traditional grammar contrasts it with the simple sentence (one clause) and the compound sentence (two or more coordinated main clauses).
e: Although it was raining, we went for a walk is a complex sentence.

d: Three dimensions commonly used to describe and measure L2 performance and proficiency: complexity (how elaborate and varied the language is), accuracy (how free it is from errors), and fluency (how smoothly and quickly it is produced). Researchers note that the dimensions can trade off against one another and that each can be measured in many ways.
e: In a storytelling task, a researcher counts clauses per unit (complexity), the percentage of error-free clauses (accuracy), and words spoken per minute and pauses (fluency).
s: Housen, A., & Kuiken, F. (2009). Complexity, accuracy, and fluency in second language acquisition. Applied Linguistics, 30(4).

d: An approach that breaks word meanings down into smaller, more basic meaning components (semantic features) to show how words in a field are related and how they contrast. Critics argue that many words cannot be fully defined this way and that category membership is often graded.
e: Man = [+HUMAN, +ADULT, +MALE]; girl = [+HUMAN, −ADULT, −MALE].
p: Brought into generative grammar by Jerrold Katz and Jerry Fodor (1963); the method has earlier roots in structuralist semantics and in anthropological analyses of kinship terms (e.g., Goodenough and Lounsbury, 1956).
s: Katz, J. J., & Fodor, J. A. (1963). The structure of a semantic theory. Language, 39(2), 170–210.

d: The principle that the meaning of a complex expression is determined by the meanings of its parts and the way they are combined. It helps explain how speakers understand sentences they have never heard; idioms and context-dependent meanings are often discussed as challenges to it.
e: We understand purple giraffe on first hearing by combining the meanings of purple and giraffe.
p: Usually traced to Gottlob Frege, although whether Frege himself stated or held the principle is debated.

d: A word formation process that combines two or more lexemes (or roots) into a single new word. English compounds may be written as one word, with a hyphen, or as separate words, and they are often identified by stress on the first element.
e: blackboard, toothbrush, mother-in-law, ice cream.

d: Language that learners hear or read and can understand, often with help from context, visuals, gestures, or simplification. Most SLA researchers accept that it is necessary for acquisition, while disagreeing about whether it is sufficient.
e: A science teacher says The water evaporates — it turns into gas and goes up into the air while pointing to a diagram, making the new word evaporates understandable.
p: Term popularized by Stephen Krashen in his Input Hypothesis (late 1970s–1980s).

d: A systematic way of understanding one conceptual domain (the target, usually abstract) in terms of another (the source, usually more concrete). Conceptual Metaphor Theory argues that such mappings shape thought, not just language, a claim some researchers consider too strong.
e: ARGUMENT IS WAR underlies expressions like She attacked my position and He defended his claims.
p: Conceptual Metaphor Theory was introduced by George Lakoff and Mark Johnson (1980).
s: Lakoff, G., & Johnson, M. (1980). Metaphors we live by. University of Chicago Press.

d: A list showing every occurrence of a chosen word or phrase in a corpus, each displayed with a portion of its surrounding text. Concordances let analysts see recurring patterns of meaning and grammar that are hard to notice in a single text.
e: A concordance for cause shows lines such as “…the fire caused serious damage…” and “…smoking can cause cancer…”, revealing that its objects are usually unpleasant.

d: A software tool that searches a corpus and produces concordances, usually along with word lists, collocation statistics, and keyword lists. Concordancers can sort results alphabetically to the left or right of the search term so that patterns become visible.
e: AntConc, Sketch Engine, and #LancsBox are widely used concordancers in applied linguistics research and data-driven learning.

d: A closed-class word that links words, phrases, or clauses. Coordinating conjunctions join elements of equal status, while subordinating conjunctions introduce subordinate clauses.
e: Coordinating: and, but, or. Subordinating: because, although, if, when.

d: Speech as it is produced in continuous utterances rather than as isolated words, where neighboring words affect each other through processes such as assimilation, elision, linking and weak forms. Awareness of these processes is important in teaching listening and pronunciation.
e: In casual American English, Did you eat yet? can sound like [dʒiːt jɛt].

d: The additional associations, feelings or evaluations a word carries beyond its core literal meaning. Words with the same denotation can differ in connotation, and connotations may vary across speakers, communities and cultures.
e: Slim, skinny and scrawny describe similar body types, but slim is usually positive and scrawny negative.

d: Teaching activities that help learners become aware of a feature of the target language, often by asking them to discover a rule from examples, without requiring them to produce the feature immediately. Grammar consciousness-raising tasks combine this with communicative discussion of the data.
e: Students compare sentences with since and for (since 2019, for five years) and work out in groups when each word is used.
p: Discussed as a teaching option by Michael Sharwood Smith (1981) and William Rutherford; grammar consciousness-raising tasks were developed by Sandra Fotos and Rod Ellis (1991).
s: Fotos, S., & Ellis, R. (1991). Communicating about grammar: A task-based approach. TESOL Quarterly, 25, 605–628.

d: A speech sound produced with a closure or a noticeable narrowing somewhere in the vocal tract. Phonologically, consonants usually occupy the edges of syllables rather than the center; some sounds, such as /w/ and /j/, are vowel-like phonetically but behave as consonants.
e: The first sounds of pat /p/, sat /s/ and mat /m/ are consonants.

d: A sequence of two or more consonants with no vowel between them, most often within one syllable. Languages differ greatly in how many consonants a cluster may contain and which combinations are permitted.
e: split begins with the cluster /spl/, and texts ends with /ksts/.

d: A word or group of words that functions as a single unit within the hierarchical structure of a sentence. Constituents are identified by tests such as substitution with a pronoun, movement, coordination, and use as a fragment answer.
e: In The old man saw the boat, the old man is a constituent because it can be replaced by he; man saw is not a constituent.

d: The extent to which a test actually measures the theoretical ability or trait (the construct) it claims to measure, and not something irrelevant. In unified validity theory it is the overarching concept that other kinds of validity evidence support.
e: A listening test whose questions require long written answers may partly measure writing ability, which threatens its construct validity as a listening measure.

d: A family of theories in which grammar consists of constructions, learned pairings of form and meaning at every level from words and idioms to abstract sentence patterns. It rejects a strict division between lexicon and syntax, and many versions are associated with usage-based approaches to acquisition.
e: The caused-motion construction gives She sneezed the napkin off the table its meaning, even though sneeze is normally intransitive.
p: Developed by Charles Fillmore, Paul Kay, and colleagues (e.g., Fillmore, Kay & O'Connor, 1988) and extended to argument structure by Adele Goldberg (1995).
s: Goldberg, A. E. (1995). Constructions: A construction grammar approach to argument structure. University of Chicago Press.

d: An educational approach, especially common in Europe, in which a school subject is taught through an additional language with planned goals for both content and language. It is closely related to content-based instruction, and scholars debate whether the two are meaningfully different.
e: In a Spanish secondary school, students take their biology class in English, with the teacher planning both science learning outcomes and the vocabulary and structures needed to describe processes.
p: The term was coined by David Marsh (University of Jyväskylä, Finland) in 1994.

d: The extent to which a test's tasks adequately represent the content or skills it is meant to cover, usually judged by comparing the test with a syllabus or specification.
e: A final exam for a course on academic writing that includes only grammar items, and no writing tasks, has poor content validity.

d: An approach that teaches language through academic or thematic subject matter, so learners develop language while learning content. Programs range from content-driven models (for example, a history course taught in a second language) to language-driven models that use themes mainly as a vehicle for language.
e: An intermediate ESL course is organized around units on climate science, in which students read articles, watch lectures, and write summaries on that topic.

d: A sentence that cannot be true in any situation because of its meaning, or a relation between two sentences that cannot both be true at the same time.
e: My brother is an only child is a contradiction; The light is on and The light is off contradict each other.

d: The proposal that L2 difficulty can be predicted by systematically comparing the learner’s L1 with the target language: similar features will be easy and different features hard. The strong (predictive) version lost support when research showed that many predicted errors did not occur and many errors could not be traced to the L1; a weaker version uses comparison to explain errors after they appear.
e: Contrastive analysis predicts that Arabic speakers will find the English contrast between /p/ and /b/ difficult because Arabic lacks a /p/ phoneme.
p: Most closely associated with Robert Lado (1957), building on Charles Fries.
s: Lado, R. (1957). Linguistics across cultures: Applied linguistics for language teachers. University of Michigan Press.

d: An implied meaning that comes from the conventional meaning of a particular word rather than from context or conversational reasoning, and that does not affect whether the sentence is true. Whether conventional implicature is a real separate category is debated; some scholars treat these meanings as semantic.
e: She is poor but honest suggests a contrast between being poor and being honest because of but, although the sentence is true as long as she is both.
p: Introduced by H. Paul Grice (1975).
s: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and conversation. In P. Cole & J. L. Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and semantics: Vol. 3. Speech acts. Academic Press.

d: An approach to studying social interaction that examines recordings and detailed transcripts of naturally occurring talk to discover how participants organize it turn by turn. It focuses on what participants themselves display in their talk rather than on researchers' assumptions about intentions.
e: Analyzing a recorded phone call to show how the callers jointly move from greetings into the reason for the call.
p: Developed in the 1960s–1970s by Harvey Sacks, Emanuel Schegloff, and Gail Jefferson, growing out of ethnomethodology.
s: Sacks, H., Schegloff, E. A., & Jefferson, G. (1974). A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation. Language, 50(4).

d: An implied meaning that the listener works out from the context together with the assumption that the speaker is following the cooperative principle and maxims. Unlike logical entailments, conversational implicatures can be canceled without contradiction. Grice distinguished generalized ones, which arise in most contexts, from particularized ones, which depend on a specific context.
e: Some students passed implicates 'not all students passed', but the speaker can cancel it: Some students passed; in fact, all of them did.
p: Introduced by H. Paul Grice (1975).
s: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and conversation. In P. Cole & J. L. Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and semantics: Vol. 3. Speech acts. Academic Press.

d: Pairs of words that describe the same relation or event from opposite points of view, so that one sentence can be restated with the other word by swapping the participants.
e: Maria sold the car to Ken means the same as Ken bought the car from Maria; similar pairs are parent/child and above/below.
s: Lyons, J. (1977). Semantics (Vols. 1–2). Cambridge University Press.

d: A word formation process in which a word changes its word class without any change in form. Some analysts treat it as derivation with a zero affix ("zero derivation"), while others reject positing an invisible affix.
e: email (noun) → to email (verb); a run (noun) from to run (verb).

d: The assumption that participants in a conversation generally try to make their contributions fit the shared purpose of the exchange. Listeners rely on this assumption to infer meanings that are not stated directly. It is a description of how interpretation works, not a rule that people are always cooperative.
e: A: Is there a gas station near here? B: There's one around the corner. A assumes B is cooperating and therefore that the station is probably open.
p: Proposed by H. Paul Grice in his 1967 William James Lectures, published as 'Logic and conversation' (1975).
s: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and conversation. In P. Cole & J. L. Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and semantics: Vol. 3. Speech acts. Academic Press.

d: The joining of two or more elements of equal grammatical status, usually with a coordinating conjunction such as and, or, or but. Coordinated clauses form a compound sentence, and the ability to be coordinated is a common test for constituents.
e: Sam cooked and Lee washed the dishes coordinates two clauses; tea or coffee coordinates two noun phrases.

d: A verb, in English mainly be, that links a subject to a complement describing or identifying it rather than expressing an action. Many languages omit the copula in some contexts, such as the present tense.
e: In The soup is hot, is is the copula and hot is the subject complement.

d: A large, principled collection of authentic spoken or written texts stored electronically so that it can be searched and analyzed by computer. Texts are chosen according to explicit design criteria (for example genre, time period, or speaker group) so that the corpus can represent a particular variety of language.
e: The British National Corpus (BNC) contains about 100 million words of late-20th-century British English, roughly 90% written and 10% spoken.

d: An approach to studying language that analyzes patterns of real use in large electronic text collections, typically combining frequency counts with close reading of examples. Scholars debate whether it is mainly a methodology usable within any theory or a distinct approach to theory-building in its own right, a debate related to the distinction between corpus-based and corpus-driven research.
e: A researcher compares how often big and large occur with different nouns in a corpus and finds that large is far more common with amount and number.

d: Language planning that changes the form of a language itself, for example by creating or reforming a writing system, standardizing grammar and spelling, or developing new vocabulary for modern domains.
e: Quebec's language office has promoted courriel as a French word for 'email.'
p: The distinction between status and corpus planning is credited to Heinz Kloss (1969).
s: Kloss, H. (1969). Research possibilities on group bilingualism: A report. International Center for Research on Bilingualism.

d: A teacher's or peer's response showing that a learner's language contains an error. Feedback can be oral or written, explicit or implicit, and can either give the correct form or push the learner to correct themselves. Researchers continue to debate which types work best for which learners and structures.
e: Student: I have 20 years. Teacher: You mean you are 20 years old.
p: A widely used classification of six oral feedback types was proposed by Roy Lyster and Leila Ranta (1997).
s: Lyster, R., & Ranta, L. (1997). Corrective feedback and learner uptake: Negotiation of form in communicative classrooms. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 19(1), 37–66.

d: Hidden positive value attached to nonstandard forms, which can signal local loyalty, toughness, solidarity, or authenticity even though speakers may publicly call these forms “incorrect.” It helps explain why nonstandard varieties persist and why some changes spread from nonstandard speech.
e: In Norwich, England, many men reported using more nonstandard local pronunciations than they actually used in recorded speech, suggesting that they valued these forms.
p: Influentially studied by Peter Trudgill (1972) in Norwich.
s: Trudgill, P. (1972). Sex, covert prestige and linguistic change in the urban British English of Norwich. Language in Society, 1(2), 179–195.

d: A bound morpheme that occurs in only one word (or a very few) and has no clear meaning of its own in the present-day language. It is still treated as a morpheme because the rest of the word is clearly identifiable.
e: cran- in cranberry and huckle- in huckleberry.

d: A language that has developed from contact between languages, often from a pidgin, and has become the first language of a community, with a full grammar and vocabulary. How creoles form is debated, with theories emphasizing the influence of the source languages, universal tendencies, or both.
e: Haitian Creole (Kreyòl), the first language of most people in Haiti, has vocabulary largely derived from French, as in mwen 'I, me.'

d: A test that interprets a person's score in relation to a defined standard or set of skills, rather than in comparison with other test takers.
e: A speaking test in which a learner passes if she can successfully order a meal, ask for directions, and make a phone booking, regardless of how others perform.
p: The distinction between criterion-referenced and norm-referenced measurement was introduced by Robert Glaser (1963).
s: Glaser, R. (1963). Instructional technology and the measurement of learning outcomes: Some questions. American Psychologist, 18, 519–521.

d: An approach to discourse analysis that studies how language use reflects, reproduces, and sometimes resists social power, inequality, and ideology. It is explicitly committed to social critique, which supporters see as a strength and critics argue can lead to selective or biased interpretation.
e: Analyzing how newspaper headlines describe immigrants (for example, with words like flood or wave) and what attitudes these choices promote.
p: Associated especially with Norman Fairclough (1989), Teun van Dijk, and Ruth Wodak, among others.
s: Fairclough, N. (1989). Language and power. Longman.

d: The hypothesis that there is a limited window in development, often said to end around puberty, during which language can be acquired fully and naturally, and after which native-like attainment becomes difficult or impossible. Its application to L2 learning is strongly debated: researchers disagree about whether there is a sharp cut-off, a gradual decline, or mainly differences in input and circumstances.
e: Researchers compare immigrants who arrived in a country at age 5 versus age 25 and find that the earlier arrivals more often sound native-like, then debate whether this reflects biology or experience.
p: Most closely associated with Eric Lenneberg (1967), following earlier proposals by Wilder Penfield and Lamar Roberts (1959).
s: Lenneberg, E. H. (1967). Biological foundations of language. Wiley.

d: The comparative study of how speakers from different languages and cultures perform and interpret communicative acts such as requests, apologies, and compliments. It examines both similarities and differences in norms and strategies.
e: Comparing how directly speakers of Hebrew, German, and Australian English phrase requests in similar situations.
p: A landmark study was the Cross-Cultural Speech Act Realization Project (CCSARP), reported by Shoshana Blum-Kulka, Juliane House, and Gabriele Kasper (1989).
s: Blum-Kulka, S., House, J., & Kasper, G. (Eds.). (1989). Cross-cultural pragmatics: Requests and apologies. Ablex.

d: A broad, theory-neutral term for any way in which a person’s languages affect one another, including L1-to-L2 transfer, L2-to-L1 influence, influence between additional languages, and avoidance. It is often preferred to “transfer” because it covers effects in all directions.
e: A long-term English user whose Polish starts to show English-like word order (L2 influencing L1) shows cross-linguistic influence in the reverse direction.

d: Teaching that uses students' cultural knowledge, prior experiences, and ways of communicating as resources, so learning is more relevant and effective for students from diverse backgrounds. It is related to, but not identical with, Ladson-Billings's culturally relevant pedagogy and Paris's culturally sustaining pedagogy.
e: A writing teacher asks students to analyze storytelling traditions from their own communities before studying narrative essay structure in English.
p: Developed by Geneva Gay (2000).
s: Gay, G. (2000). Culturally responsive teaching: Theory, research, and practice. Teachers College Press.

d: In earlier transformational grammar, an underlying level of syntactic representation from which the surface form of a sentence is derived by transformations; it was meant to capture basic grammatical relations relevant to meaning. Later generative models abandoned this level in its original form.
e: Active The cat chased the mouse and passive The mouse was chased by the cat were analyzed as sharing similar underlying relations.
p: Introduced in this form by Noam Chomsky in Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (1965).
s: Chomsky, N. (1965). Aspects of the theory of syntax. MIT Press.
a: D-structure (later term in Government and Binding theory)

d: The use of words whose reference depends on the context of utterance, such as who is speaking, where, and when. Deictic expressions ('pointing' words) cannot be fully interpreted without knowing that context. The main types are person, place, time, social, and discourse deixis.
e: I'll meet you here tomorrow: who I and you are, where here is, and when tomorrow is all depend on the situation.
s: Levinson, S. C. (1983). Pragmatics. Cambridge University Press.

d: The relation between a word and the class of things in the world it can be correctly applied to; also, that class itself. Denotation is the stable, literal side of meaning, contrasted with connotation. Some authors use it almost interchangeably with extension or reference, while others separate these.
e: The denotation of dog is the set of all dogs.
p: The modern denotation/connotation distinction in logic is associated with John Stuart Mill's A System of Logic (1843), although linguists now use "connotation" differently from Mill.

d: Describing a consonant produced with the tongue tip or blade against or between the upper front teeth. Sounds made with the tongue between the teeth are sometimes called interdental.
e: English /θ/ in think and /ð/ in this are dental fricatives, and many learners replace them with [t]/[s] or [d]/[z]; Spanish and French /t/ are also dental, transcribed [t̪].

d: Modality concerned with obligation, permission and prohibition, typically imposed by a person, rule or social norm.
e: You must wear a helmet (obligation), You may leave early (permission). Note that must and may can also be epistemic.
s: Palmer, F. R. (2001). Mood and modality (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.

d: A family of grammatical theories that describes sentence structure as a network of directed relations between individual words (heads and their dependents), rather than as nested phrases. It is widely used in computational linguistics and treebanks such as Universal Dependencies.
e: In Students read books, read is the root, with students (subject) and books (object) as its dependents.
p: Modern dependency grammar is traced to Lucien Tesnière's Éléments de syntaxe structurale (published posthumously in 1959).
s: Tesnière, L. (1959). Éléments de syntaxe structurale. Klincksieck.

d: The formation of a new lexeme from an existing one, usually by affixation, often changing the word's meaning and frequently its word class.
e: teach (verb) → teacher (noun); happy → unhappy (meaning change, same class).

d: An account of how speakers of a language actually use it, based on observation of real speech and writing. It contrasts with prescriptive grammar, which sets out rules for how people should speak or write, usually based on a standard variety or tradition. Most modern linguistic research takes a descriptive approach.
e: A prescriptive rule says never to end a sentence with a preposition, but a descriptive grammar records that Who are you talking to? is normal, grammatical English.
s: Huddleston, R., & Pullum, G. K. (2002). The Cambridge grammar of the English language. Cambridge University Press.

d: A closed-class word that comes at the start of a noun phrase and specifies features such as definiteness, quantity, or possession. Articles, demonstratives, possessive determiners, and quantifiers are common types.
e: the, a, this, my, every, and some in the book, my book, every book.

d: A series of ordered stages that learners pass through when acquiring a particular structure, such as negation or question formation. Similar sequences have been reported for learners with different L1s and have been argued to be largely resistant to instruction, though learners vary in speed and in how they move between stages.
e: Learners of English negation typically move from *No go, to *He no like it, to negatives with auxiliaries and modals (I can’t play), and finally to tense-marked She didn’t go (the starred forms are ungrammatical).

d: A test designed to identify learners' specific strengths and weaknesses so that teaching can target them.
e: At the start of a writing course, students write a short essay that the teacher analyzes for problems with articles, verb tenses, and paragraph organization.

d: A variety of a language associated with a particular region or social group and differing from other varieties in vocabulary, grammar, and pronunciation. In linguistics everyone speaks a dialect, and no dialect is inherently better than another; whether two varieties count as “dialects” of one language or as separate languages is often decided by political and historical factors rather than by linguistic criteria alone.
e: Many speakers in the southern United States use y'all as a plural “you,” while many speakers in Pittsburgh use yinz.

d: Teaching that adjusts content, process, products, or learning environment to respond to the different readiness levels, interests, and learning needs of students in the same class.
e: In one reading lesson, some students read an adapted text with a glossary, others read the original article, and all groups answer the same central discussion question.
p: Most closely associated with Carol Ann Tomlinson (1999 and later works).
s: Tomlinson, C. A. (1999). The differentiated classroom: Responding to the needs of all learners. ASCD.

d: A stable situation in which two varieties of one language are used in a community for different functions: a “High” variety for formal, written, and official purposes and a “Low” variety for everyday conversation. The term was later extended by other scholars, notably Joshua Fishman, to cases involving two unrelated languages.
e: In many Arabic-speaking countries, Modern Standard Arabic (High) is used in news broadcasts and formal writing, while local colloquial Arabic (Low) is used at home and with friends.
p: The term (from Greek, via French diglossie) was used earlier by writers on Greek and Arabic; Charles Ferguson's 1959 article introduced it into English-language sociolinguistics, and Joshua Fishman (1967) extended it to unrelated languages.
s: Ferguson, C. A. (1959). Diglossia. Word, 15(2), 325–340.

d: A vowel whose quality changes noticeably within a single syllable, gliding from one vowel position toward another.
e: English my /aɪ/, how /aʊ/ and boy /ɔɪ/ contain diphthongs.

d: A method that developed in the late nineteenth century as a reaction against grammar-translation. Teaching takes place only in the target language, meaning is conveyed through objects, pictures, and demonstration rather than translation, and grammar is learned inductively from examples.
e: A French teacher holds up an apple and says C'est une pomme, then asks Qu'est-ce que c'est ?, never translating into English.

d: A speech act in which the grammatical form of the sentence matches its function: a declarative makes a statement, an interrogative asks a question, and an imperative gives an order or request.
e: Using the imperative Close the window to request that someone close the window.

d: A term with several meanings: (1) language beyond the level of the sentence, (2) language in use in its social context, and (3) in critical and social theory, ways of talking and thinking that represent the world from a particular perspective (sometimes written 'Discourse' or used in the plural, 'discourses'). Which sense is meant depends on the research tradition.
e: Sense 1: a whole conversation or essay; sense 3: a 'discourse of deficit' that presents multilingual students only in terms of what they lack.

d: A broad family of approaches to studying language in use, from the structure of texts and conversations to how language constructs identities, relationships, and social meanings. Approaches range from descriptive linguistic analysis to critical and social-theoretical work.
e: Examining how teachers and students in a classroom use questions and feedback to structure lessons.
p: The term came into general use after Zellig Harris's 1952 paper, which proposed it as a method for analyzing connected speech and writing beyond the sentence.
s: Harris, Z. S. (1952). Discourse analysis. Language, 28(1).

d: Words or short phrases that signal how an utterance relates to the surrounding talk or text, or to the speaker's attitude, rather than adding to its propositional content. Researchers disagree about exactly which items belong in the category.
e: well, so, oh, anyway, you know, I mean: So, anyway, where was I?
p: Classic study by Deborah Schiffrin (1987), who analyzed markers such as oh, well, so, and y’know in conversation.
s: Schiffrin, D. (1987). Discourse markers. Cambridge University Press.

d: One of the smallest phonetic properties, such as [±voice] or [±nasal], that can distinguish one phoneme from another; in this view phonemes are bundles of features. Several competing feature systems exist, and whether all features are binary is debated.
e: /p/ and /b/ differ only in the feature [±voice]; /b/ and /m/ differ only in [±nasal].
p: Developed by Roman Jakobson with Gunnar Fant and Morris Halle in Preliminaries to Speech Analysis (early 1950s), building on earlier Prague School work, and substantially revised by Noam Chomsky and Morris Halle (1968).
s: Chomsky, N., & Halle, M. (1968). The sound pattern of English. Harper & Row.

d: A cluster of social situations, such as home, school, work, religion, or government, that is typically associated with the use of a particular language or variety in a multilingual community. Analyzing domains helps show how languages divide up social functions.
e: A Turkish-German family uses Turkish at home and at the mosque but German at school and at work.

d: Assessment, based on Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, in which the assessor gives graded mediation (hints, prompts, explanations) during the test and records how much help the learner needs. It aims to reveal abilities that are still developing as well as those already achieved.
e: When a learner makes a tense error while retelling a story, the assessor first pauses, then asks Is there a problem with that verb?, then names the tense, noting which level of help led to self-correction.
p: Rooted in Vygotsky's sociocultural theory; brought into second language research mainly through the work of James P. Lantolf and Matthew E. Poehner (e.g., 2004).
s: Lantolf, J. P., & Poehner, M. E. (2004). Dynamic assessment of L2 development: Bringing the past into the future. Journal of Applied Linguistics, 1(1), 49–72.

d: The stage of English from about 1500 to 1700, the language of Shakespeare and the King James Bible. Much of the Great Vowel Shift took place in this period, printing encouraged more standardized spelling, and forms such as thou/thee were still in use alongside you.
e: Juliet's line Wherefore art thou Romeo? means 'Why are you Romeo?', not 'Where are you?'

d: Corrective feedback in which the teacher prompts the learner to produce the correct form, for example by pausing so the learner can complete the sentence, asking a question, or asking the learner to reformulate.
e: Student: The book is in the table. Teacher: The book is…? (pauses for the student to supply on the table)
p: One of the six feedback types in Roy Lyster and Leila Ranta's (1997) classification, based on teacher–student interaction in primary-level French immersion classrooms in Montreal.

d: The omission of a sound that would be present in a careful or citation pronunciation, common in fast or casual connected speech.
e: next day is often pronounced [nɛks deɪ], without the /t/, and camera as [ˈkæmrə], without the middle vowel.
