d: The omission of words that can be recovered from the linguistic context, leaving the meaning understood. Common English types include verb phrase ellipsis, gapping, and sluicing.
e: Verb phrase ellipsis: Mia can swim, and Leo can __ too (= swim).

d: A language at risk of no longer being spoken, usually because children are not learning it at home as speakers shift to a more dominant language. Vitality scales (e.g., UNESCO's framework or the EGIDS) grade the degree of risk, and many linguists estimate that a large share of the world's roughly 7,000 languages could fall silent within this century.
e: Ainu, the Indigenous language of northern Japan, now has very few remaining first-language speakers.
p: Michael Krauss's (1992) article was an influential warning that urged linguists to prioritize endangered languages.
s: Krauss, M. (1992). The world's languages in crisis. Language, 68(1), 4–10.
a: Moribund language (for the most severe cases)

d: A compound that has a head inside it: the whole compound denotes a kind of whatever the head denotes. In English the head is usually the rightmost element.
e: A bookcase is a kind of case; a greenhouse is a kind of house.

d: English taught where it is not a main language of the surrounding community, so learners mostly meet it in the classroom and through media. The ESL/EFL split is a simplification, since global media and English-medium education blur the boundary in many countries.
e: A secondary student in Japan who studies English four hours a week at school but rarely uses it outside class is an EFL learner.

d: The use of English as a shared language among speakers who have different first languages, often with no native English speakers present. ELF research focuses on mutual intelligibility and accommodation rather than conformity to native-speaker norms; scholars debate whether ELF is a variety or a way of using English.
e: A Brazilian engineer and a Korean engineer negotiate a contract in English, each adjusting their speech to be understood.
p: Associated especially with Jennifer Jenkins (2000) and Barbara Seidlhofer (2011).
s: Seidlhofer, B. (2011). Understanding English as a lingua franca. Oxford University Press.

d: English taught to learners who live where English is a dominant language of daily life, school, and work, so they meet it constantly outside class. Some scholars criticize the label because English may be a learner's third or fourth language, and many institutions now prefer terms such as multilingual learner.
e: A refugee from Afghanistan attending English classes at a community center in Boston, where she also uses English at the pharmacy and at her children's school, is an ESL learner.

d: The teaching of the English needed for study and research in higher education, such as reading academic texts, listening to lectures, participating in seminars, and writing in academic genres. It is usually treated as a branch of English for specific purposes.
e: An international graduate student takes an EAP course on writing literature reviews and paraphrasing sources before starting her dissertation.

d: Language teaching designed around the communicative needs of a particular group of learners, such as nurses, engineers, pilots, or lawyers. Course content is normally based on a needs analysis of the tasks, texts, and situations learners will meet.
e: An aviation English course trains air-traffic controllers in standard radio phraseology and in plain English for unexpected situations.

d: The process by which a set of linguistic features becomes socially recognized as a distinct way of speaking linked to a type of person or social value. It often happens through commentary, media, and products that name and display the features.
e: T-shirts and mugs printed with words such as yinz and n'at help to make “Pittsburghese” recognizable as a dialect.
p: Concept developed by Asif Agha (2003, 2007).
s: Agha, A. (2007). Language and social relations. Cambridge University Press.

d: A relation between sentences in which the truth of one guarantees the truth of the other: if A entails B, it is impossible for A to be true and B false. Unlike implicature, an entailment cannot be canceled without contradiction.
e: Sam killed the spider entails The spider died; saying Sam killed the spider, but it didn't die is contradictory.
s: Lyons, J. (1977). Semantics (Vols. 1–2). Cambridge University Press.

d: The insertion of a sound, either a vowel or a consonant, into a word, often to break up a sequence that the language's phonotactics do not allow. It is a frequent feature of learners' pronunciation and of loanword adaptation.
e: Spanish-speaking learners may say school as [esˈkul]; English strike became Japanese sutoraiku; many English speakers insert [p] in hamster, as in American [ˈhæmpstɚ].

d: Modality concerned with the speaker's judgment about how likely or certain it is that a proposition is true, based on knowledge or evidence.
e: She must be home by now (a confident inference), He may be ill (a possibility).
s: Palmer, F. R. (2001). Mood and modality (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.

d: A research method that collects, identifies, classifies, and explains the errors in learner language in order to understand the learner’s developing system. Developed partly in response to contrastive analysis, it showed that many errors come from general learning processes rather than the L1, though it was later criticized for ignoring what learners do correctly and what they avoid.
e: An analyst finds that a learner writes *goed, *buyed, and *teached (all ungrammatical) and classifies them as overgeneralization of the regular past tense, not L1 transfer.
p: Associated especially with S. Pit Corder, whose 1967 article helped establish it as an approach in SLA.
s: Corder, S. P. (1967). The significance of learner’s errors. International Review of Applied Linguistics in Language Teaching, 5, 161–170.

d: A distinction between errors, which reflect gaps in a learner’s current knowledge and occur systematically, and mistakes, which are occasional slips in performance (due to tiredness, haste, or distraction) that the learner can usually self-correct. In practice the line can be hard to draw from a single utterance.
e: A learner who always writes *She don’t know (ungrammatical) is making an error; a learner who usually writes She doesn’t know but once types *She don’t know in a rushed email and fixes it when rereading has made a mistake.
p: Distinction drawn by S. Pit Corder (1967).
s: Corder, S. P. (1967). The significance of learner’s errors. International Review of Applied Linguistics in Language Teaching, 5, 161–170.

d: A variety of a language associated with speakers of a particular ethnic background, often emerging where a group's heritage language has been in contact with the majority language. Some researchers criticize the term for implying that every member of an ethnic group speaks the same way, and prefer to describe ethnolectal features that speakers may use selectively.
e: Chicano English in the southwestern United States, or Multicultural London English, which developed among young people of many backgrounds and is sometimes called a multiethnolect.

d: The degree to which a language group is likely to survive and act as a distinct collective group, based on its status (social, economic, and political standing), demography (size and concentration), and institutional support (use in schools, media, government, and religion).
e: French in Quebec has high vitality because it has many speakers, official status, and its own schools, universities, and media.
p: Proposed by Howard Giles, Richard Bourhis, and Donald Taylor (1977).
s: Giles, H., Bourhis, R. Y., & Taylor, D. M. (1977). Towards a theory of language in ethnic group relations. In H. Giles (Ed.), Language, ethnicity and intergroup relations (pp. 307–348). Academic Press.

d: The origin and historical development of a word, and the field that studies such histories. Reliable etymologies depend on documented earlier forms and regular sound correspondences, not on surface resemblance; 'folk etymology' is the popular reinterpretation of a word based on a mistaken idea of its origin.
e: Hamburger comes from the city name Hamburg, but speakers reanalyzed it as ham + burger, which gave rise to new words such as cheeseburger.

d: A compound whose meaning is not a kind of either of its parts, so it lacks a semantic head inside the word. Such compounds often name a person or thing by a characteristic feature.
e: A redhead is a person, not a kind of head; a pickpocket is a thief, not a kind of pocket.

d: The thematic role of the participant who perceives something or undergoes a mental or emotional state, rather than acting deliberately.
e: In Luis heard a noise and The film frightened Mia, Luis and Mia are experiencers.

d: A word with no meaning of its own that fills a grammatical position, typically the subject position, because the structure requires one. English uses it and there this way; languages that allow null subjects (e.g., Spanish) usually do not need expletives.
e: It is raining and There are three books on the desk; compare Spanish Llueve 'rains'.

d: Corrective feedback in which the teacher clearly shows that the learner's utterance was wrong and provides the correct form.
e: Student: She don't like coffee. Teacher: No, not don't. You should say she doesn't like coffee.
p: One of the six feedback types in Roy Lyster and Leila Ranta's (1997) classification, based on teacher–student interaction in primary-level French immersion classrooms in Montreal.

d: Conscious knowledge about language that a learner can reflect on and often describe, such as a grammar rule. It is typically accessed slowly and is most useful when the learner has time to plan or edit.
e: A learner explains: “Use the present perfect, have lived, when the action started in the past and continues now.”
s: Ellis, R. (2005). Measuring implicit and explicit knowledge of a second language: A psychometric study. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 27(2).

d: The set of actual things (or situations) that an expression applies to. Two expressions can share an extension while differing in intension.
e: In our world, creature with a heart and creature with kidneys are often said to have the same extension, even though their meanings differ.
p: Developed in modern semantics by Rudolf Carnap (1947).

d: An approach in which learners read large amounts of easy, enjoyable material, usually of their own choice, with a focus on overall meaning rather than detailed study. It contrasts with intensive reading, which analyzes short texts closely.
e: Students choose graded readers from a class library and read one or two books a week for pleasure, writing only a short response afterward.
s: Day, R. R., & Bamford, J. (1998). Extensive reading in the second language classroom. Cambridge University Press.

d: A research method that records where and for how long a person's eyes fixate, used to study reading and spoken-language comprehension in real time. Measures such as fixation duration and regressions (looking back) indicate processing difficulty.
e: When reading The horse raced past the barn fell, readers often fixate longer on fell and make regressions to earlier words.

d: The public self-image that a person claims and wants others to recognize in interaction. Brown and Levinson split it into positive face (the wish to be liked and approved of) and negative face (the wish to be free from imposition); scholars working on East Asian and other contexts have argued that face is more collective and relational than this model suggests.
e: Correcting a colleague in front of others may cause them to 'lose face'.
p: The modern sociological concept comes from Erving Goffman (1955), who drew on the Chinese notion of face; it was adapted for linguistic politeness by Brown and Levinson (1978, 1987).
s: Goffman, E. (1955). On face-work: An analysis of ritual elements in social interaction. Psychiatry, 18(3).

d: In Brown and Levinson's politeness theory, any act that by its nature threatens the positive or negative face of the speaker or the hearer. Requests, criticisms, disagreements, and apologies are typical examples, and speakers choose strategies to soften them depending on social distance, power, and the size of the imposition.
e: Asking a professor Could I possibly get an extension on the paper? is a request (a face-threatening act) softened by indirectness.
p: Term from Penelope Brown and Stephen Levinson (1978, 1987).
s: Brown, P., & Levinson, S. C. (1987). Politeness: Some universals in language usage. Cambridge University Press.

d: The conditions that must be met for a speech act to be performed successfully or appropriately, such as the speaker having the right authority, being sincere, and the circumstances being suitable. If they are not met, the act is 'infelicitous' rather than false.
e: I now pronounce you married only works if said by an authorized official during a proper ceremony; said by a guest, it fails.
p: Builds on J. L. Austin's (1962) account of how performatives can be 'happy' or 'unhappy' (infelicitous); John Searle (1969) reformulated the conditions as preparatory, sincerity, propositional content, and essential conditions.
s: Searle, J. R. (1969). Speech acts: An essay in the philosophy of language. Cambridge University Press.

d: The distinction between clauses or verb forms that are marked for tense (and often agreement), called finite, and those that are not, called nonfinite (infinitives, participles, gerunds). In English, main clauses are normally finite.
e: She leaves contains a finite verb (marked for present tense and agreement); in I want to leave, to leave is a nonfinite infinitival clause.

d: A language a person acquires from birth or early childhood, usually through family and community interaction. A person can have more than one L1, and some scholars avoid the term “native language” because it can imply a fixed ranking of a speaker’s languages.
e: A child raised by Spanish-speaking parents in Mexico City has Spanish as her L1; a child raised with Bengali at home and English at daycare from infancy may have two L1s.

d: The process by which young children acquire their native language or languages, typically without formal instruction. Accounts differ on how much depends on innate, language-specific knowledge (nativist views) versus general learning from rich input and social interaction (usage-based and interactionist views).
e: Most children move from babbling around 6–10 months, to single words around their first birthday, to two-word combinations like more juice by about age two.

d: Openly and deliberately failing to follow a Gricean maxim so that the listener notices and looks for a hidden meaning. Flouting differs from violating a maxim, which is done quietly, for example when lying.
e: A reference letter that says only Mr. X has excellent handwriting flouts the maxim of quantity and implies that he is not a strong candidate.
p: Described by H. Paul Grice (1975).
s: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and conversation. In P. Cole & J. L. Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and semantics: Vol. 3. Speech acts. Academic Press.

d: An activity focused on communicating meaning smoothly and naturally, in which errors are tolerated as long as communication succeeds. It contrasts with an accuracy activity, which focuses on producing correct forms, and many courses deliberately balance the two.
e: In a 4-3-2 activity, a student tells the same story to three partners in four, then three, then two minutes (fluency). Earlier, the class completed sentences with the correct past-tense verb (accuracy).

d: Instruction in which learners' attention is drawn briefly to grammar, vocabulary, or pronunciation while their main focus is on communicating meaning. Long's original definition refers to incidental attention that arises from communication; later writers also include planned, pre-selected forms.
e: During a group discussion, a student says Yesterday she go, and the teacher quickly replies She went? before the discussion continues.
p: Proposed by Michael H. Long (1991).
s: Long, M. H. (1991). Focus on form: A design feature in language teaching methodology. In K. de Bot, R. B. Ginsberg, & C. Kramsch (Eds.), Foreign language research in cross-cultural perspective (pp. 39–52). John Benjamins.

d: Instruction in which language forms are the main content of lessons, usually taught one at a time in a predetermined sequence and practiced outside a communicative context. Grammar-translation, audiolingual drills, and many PPP lessons are typical examples.
e: A syllabus unit called Comparatives and Superlatives explains the rules, then gives twenty sentence-completion exercises.
p: Contrasted with focus on form by Michael H. Long (1991) and further elaborated by Long and Peter Robinson (1998).

d: Instruction that concentrates on understanding and conveying messages and gives little or no explicit attention to language forms, on the assumption that forms will be acquired from exposure to meaningful input. Immersion programs and some versions of the natural approach are examples.
e: Students learn geography entirely through the target language and teachers never correct or explain grammar.

d: A specific type of anxiety linked to learning or using a second or foreign language, involving worry about speaking, being evaluated, or making mistakes in front of others. It is usually found to correlate negatively with performance, though the direction of cause is debated: anxiety may lower performance, and poor performance may raise anxiety.
e: A student who knows the answer freezes, blushes, and forgets simple words when called on to speak French in class.
p: Defined as a distinct construct by Elaine Horwitz, Michael Horwitz, and Joann Cope (1986), who also introduced the Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale (FLCAS).
s: Horwitz, E. K., Horwitz, M. B., & Cope, J. (1986). Foreign language classroom anxiety. The Modern Language Journal, 70(2).

d: A resonance frequency of the vocal tract, visible as a dark band of energy on a spectrogram. The first two formants identify vowel quality: F1 is higher for lower (more open) vowels, and F2 is higher for more front vowels.
e: /i/ in heed has a low F1 and a high F2, whereas /ɑ/ in father has a high F1 and a low F2.
p: The source–filter theory explaining how formants arise was given its classic formulation by Gunnar Fant (1960), building on earlier work by Tsutomu Chiba and Masato Kajiyama.
s: Fant, G. (1960). Acoustic theory of speech production. Mouton.

d: Assessment carried out during learning to give feedback that helps both students and teachers adjust what happens next. The key feature is how the information is used, not the format of the task.
e: After a draft of an essay, students receive comments on organization and evidence and use them to revise before final grading.
s: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (1998). Assessment and classroom learning. Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy & Practice, 5(1), 7–74.

d: Multiword strings that appear to be stored and retrieved as whole units rather than built word by word from grammar rules. It is an umbrella term covering idioms, collocations, lexical bundles, and routine expressions; researchers disagree about how to identify it and whether frequency, fixedness, or psychological storage should be the defining criterion.
e: How are you doing?, by the way, and it goes without saying are typical formulaic sequences that speakers produce fluently as wholes.
p: Alison Wray (2002) offered an influential definition of the “formulaic sequence” as a string that appears to be prefabricated and retrieved whole from memory.
s: Wray, A. (2002). Formulaic language and the lexicon. Cambridge University Press.

d: The apparent permanent stopping of development in some part of a learner’s interlanguage, so that certain non-target forms persist despite continued exposure and instruction. Because it is hard to prove that development has stopped forever, many researchers prefer the more cautious term “stabilization.”
e: An adult who has used English daily for 20 years but still says *I am here since 2005 (ungrammatical; target: I have been here since 2005) may show fossilization of that structure.
p: Introduced by Larry Selinker (1972) as part of the interlanguage framework.
s: Selinker, L. (1972). Interlanguage. International Review of Applied Linguistics in Language Teaching, 10(1–4).

d: An approach holding that word meanings can only be understood against a background structure of knowledge (a frame) about a type of situation, its participants and their relations. Words evoke frames and highlight particular parts of them.
e: Buy, sell, pay and cost all evoke a commercial transaction frame with a buyer, seller, goods and money.
p: Developed by Charles Fillmore from the 1970s; the basis of the FrameNet project.
s: Fillmore, C. J. (1982). Frame semantics. In The Linguistic Society of Korea (Ed.), Linguistics in the morning calm (pp. 111–137). Hanshin Publishing.

d: A morpheme that can stand alone as an independent word without any other morpheme attached to it.
e: book, run, and the are free morphemes; book can also combine with bound morphemes, as in books.

d: A situation in which two or more sounds can occur in the same position without changing the meaning of a word. Sociolinguistic research shows that such variation is often not truly “free” but is influenced by speaking style, social factors or speech rate.
e: The final /p/ of cup can be released [kʌpʰ] or unreleased [kʌp̚] with no change in meaning.

d: How often a word or other linguistic feature occurs in a corpus, reported either as a raw count or as a normalized rate (for example, per million words) so that corpora of different sizes can be compared. Frequency is a central guide for deciding which vocabulary learners should meet first.
e: A word that occurs 250 times in a 5-million-word corpus has a normalized frequency of 50 per million words.

d: A consonant produced by forcing air through a narrow gap between two articulators, which creates turbulent, hissing noise.
e: English fricatives include /f/ fine, /v/ vine, /θ/ thin, /ð/ then, /s/ sue, /z/ zoo, /ʃ/ shoe, /ʒ/ vision and /h/ who.

d: A language in which a single affix often expresses several grammatical meanings at once, and morpheme boundaries may be blurred by sound changes.
e: Spanish habló ‘(s)he spoke’: the ending -ó signals third person, singular, past, and indicative all at once.

d: A grammatical sentence that leads readers or listeners to build an initial interpretation that turns out to be wrong, forcing them to go back and reanalyze it. Such sentences are used as evidence that people interpret sentences word by word rather than waiting until the end.
e: The horse raced past the barn fell. Readers first take raced as the main verb, but the sentence means 'The horse that was raced past the barn fell.'
p: The classic example sentence is from Thomas G. Bever (1970).
s: Bever, T. G. (1970). The cognitive basis for linguistic structures. In J. R. Hayes (Ed.), Cognition and the development of language. Wiley.

d: A list of about 2,000 high-frequency English headwords selected as the most useful general vocabulary for learners, based on frequency and on criteria of usefulness. Though dated, it long served as the standard definition of “high-frequency” words; newer lists such as the New General Service List (2013) were built from modern corpora.
e: Words such as accept, bring, and common are on the GSL, so the Academic Word List deliberately excludes them.
p: Compiled by Michael West (1953), building on earlier vocabulary-selection work of the 1930s.
s: West, M. (1953). A general service list of English words. Longmans, Green.

d: An approach to linguistics that aims to build an explicit set of rules or principles capable of producing all and only the grammatical sentences of a language, modeling speakers' unconscious knowledge. The term covers a family of theories, most prominently those developed by Noam Chomsky and his colleagues.
e: A generative grammar of English should generate Who did you see? but not *Who did you see Mary? (ungrammatical).
p: Associated with Noam Chomsky, beginning with Syntactic Structures (1957).
s: Chomsky, N. (1957). Syntactic structures. Mouton.

d: A recognizable type of text or communicative event shaped by shared purposes and conventions within a community, such as a research article, a job application letter, or a sermon. Different traditions (English for Specific Purposes, systemic functional linguistics, and Rhetorical Genre Studies) define and study genre in somewhat different ways.
e: A research article introduction typically establishes a research territory, identifies a gap, and then presents the current study.
p: In applied linguistics, closely associated with John Swales (1990), who linked genres to discourse communities and communicative purpose.
s: Swales, J. M. (1990). Genre analysis: English in academic and research settings. Cambridge University Press.

d: An approach to teaching writing (and reading) that makes the purposes, structure, and typical language of specific text types explicit to students. Major traditions include the Sydney School based on systemic functional linguistics, English for specific purposes genre analysis, and Rhetorical Genre Studies in North American writing studies.
e: Before writing research article introductions, graduate students analyze several published introductions and identify common moves, such as establishing a territory and indicating a gap.
p: The Sydney School tradition developed from work begun around 1979–1980 by J. R. Martin, Joan Rothery, and colleagues; the ESP tradition is associated especially with John Swales (1990), whose model of research article introductions underlies the example.
s: Swales, J. M. (1990). Genre analysis: English in academic and research settings. Cambridge University Press.

d: The distinction between information the speaker treats as already known or recoverable for the listener (given) and information presented as not yet known (new). In English, given information tends to come earlier in the clause and new information later, where it often receives the main stress.
e: A: Who broke the vase? B: The vase was broken by the cat. (the vase is given; the cat is new.)
p: Builds on Prague School work; developed for English especially by M. A. K. Halliday (1967) and Wallace Chafe (1976).

d: A vowel-like consonant produced with a quick movement of the tongue or lips. A glide is made much like a high vowel but functions at the edge of a syllable rather than as its nucleus.
e: /j/ in yet is similar to the vowel [i], and /w/ in wet is similar to [u].

d: Describing a sound produced at the glottis, the opening between the vocal folds in the larynx.
e: /h/ in hat is glottal, as is the glottal stop [ʔ] heard in uh-oh (American [ˈʔʌʔoʊ]) and in many British pronunciations of butter [ˈbʌʔə].

d: A version of generative grammar organized into interacting modules such as X-bar theory, Case theory, theta theory, and binding theory, which constrain possible sentences. It was the main framework of the Principles and Parameters approach in the 1980s.
e: Binding theory in GB accounts for why Mary admires herself is grammatical but *Herself admires Mary is not.
p: Introduced by Noam Chomsky in Lectures on Government and Binding (1981).
s: Chomsky, N. (1981). Lectures on government and binding. Foris.

d: Pairs of opposites that sit at two ends of a scale with intermediate points, so both can be denied at the same time. They allow comparison and degree modifiers, and their interpretation depends on a standard set by context.
e: Hot/cold: the soup can be neither hot nor cold (it is warm), and we can say hotter or very cold.
s: Lyons, J. (1977). Semantics (Vols. 1–2). Cambridge University Press.

d: A book written or adapted for language learners, with vocabulary and grammar controlled to suit a particular level, so that learners can read with ease and enjoyment.
e: A 1,000-headword version of Pride and Prejudice in a publisher's graded series for intermediate learners.
r: Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR)

d: A traditional method, derived from the teaching of Latin and Greek, in which learners study explicit grammar rules and vocabulary lists and then translate sentences and texts between the first language and the target language. It emphasizes reading, writing, and accuracy, and gives little attention to speaking or listening.
e: Students memorize the endings of German adjectives, then translate a paragraph from a German novel into English, with the class conducted mostly in English.

d: A morpheme that mainly expresses grammatical relations or categories rather than rich lexical meaning. These include inflectional affixes and function words, and they form a relatively closed class.
e: Past-tense -ed, plural -s, and the words the, of, and and.

d: The property of a sentence being well formed according to the rules of a speaker's mental grammar, usually judged by native or expert speakers' intuitions. Grammaticality is distinct from meaningfulness and from acceptability, which can also be affected by processing difficulty, style, or context.
e: Colorless green ideas sleep furiously is grammatical but semantically odd, whereas *Furiously sleep ideas green colorless is ungrammatical.
p: Noam Chomsky's well-known example sentence Colorless green ideas sleep furiously (1957) was used to show that grammaticality is independent of meaning.
s: Chomsky, N. (1957). Syntactic structures. Mouton.

d: The historical process by which a word with concrete lexical meaning becomes a grammatical marker, or a grammatical marker becomes more grammatical. It typically involves loss of concrete meaning (bleaching), phonetic reduction, and more fixed usage; how strictly the process is one-directional is debated.
e: The motion expression be going to developed into a future marker and is often reduced in speech to gonna, as in It's gonna rain.
p: The term is generally credited to Antoine Meillet in L'évolution des formes grammaticales (1912).
s: Hopper, P. J., & Traugott, E. C. (2003). Grammaticalization (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.

d: A series of changes to the long vowels of English, taking place mainly between about 1400 and 1700, in which long vowels were raised and the highest ones became diphthongs. It explains many mismatches between English spelling, which was becoming fixed during this period, and modern pronunciation; its exact dates, order of steps, and causes are still debated.
e: Middle English mous [muːs] became Modern English mouse /maʊs/, and bite [biːt(ə)] became /baɪt/.
p: Term coined by Otto Jespersen in Part I of A Modern English Grammar on Historical Principles (1909).
s: Jespersen, O. (1909). A modern English grammar on historical principles: Part I. Sounds and spellings. Carl Winter.

d: Four conversational guidelines that, according to Grice, follow from the cooperative principle: quantity (be as informative as needed), quality (be truthful), relation (be relevant), and manner (be clear and orderly). Speakers often do not follow them literally; the point is that hearers interpret utterances as if speakers were trying to.
e: If asked How was the party? and you answer only The food was nice, the listener may infer that the rest was not so good.
p: Proposed by H. Paul Grice (1975).
s: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and conversation. In P. Cole & J. L. Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and semantics: Vol. 3. Speech acts. Academic Press.

d: A set of regular consonant changes that set Proto-Germanic apart from the other Indo-European branches. In this chain shift, voiceless stops became fricatives, plain voiced stops became voiceless stops, and voiced aspirated stops became plain voiced stops (or fricatives). Some apparent exceptions were later explained by Verner's law.
e: Indo-European *p became Germanic *f, so Latin pater and piscis correspond to English father and fish.
p: The correspondences were first described by Rasmus Rask (1818). Jacob Grimm stated them systematically in the second edition of Deutsche Grammatik (vol. 1, 1822), and the law is named after him.

d: The central word of a phrase, which determines the category of the whole phrase and often which other elements may appear with it. For example, a phrase headed by a noun is a noun phrase.
e: In the students in my class, the head is students; the phrase behaves as a plural noun phrase (The students in my class are/*is here).

d: The use of words or expressions that make a statement less absolute, signaling caution, uncertainty, or politeness. In academic writing, hedges let writers present claims carefully and leave room for other views.
e: These results may suggest that…; It seems likely that…; sort of, perhaps, I think.
p: The term 'hedge' was introduced into linguistics by George Lakoff (first presented in 1972, published 1973) for words that make category membership fuzzier, such as sort of; Ken Hyland's (1998) work is a standard reference on hedging in academic writing.
s: Lakoff, G. (1973). Hedges: A study in meaning criteria and the logic of fuzzy concepts. Journal of Philosophical Logic, 2(4).

d: A language connected to a person's family or cultural background, usually acquired at home in a setting where another language dominates society. Definitions vary: some focus on whether a person learned the language at home, others on a person's cultural connection to it regardless of proficiency.
e: A US-born student understands Korean from her parents but feels more comfortable reading and writing in English.

d: The branch of linguistics that studies how languages change over time, why those changes happen, and how languages are related to one another. It takes a diachronic (across-time) view, in contrast with synchronic study of a language at a single moment.
e: Tracing how Old English hlāf 'bread' developed into Modern English loaf is a typical historical-linguistic task.

d: A scoring method in which raters give one overall score based on their general impression of a performance, guided by level descriptions. It is efficient but gives less detailed feedback and can hide uneven profiles.
e: Raters read each placement essay once and assign a single band from 1 to 6.

d: A single word used by a young child to express what an adult would say with a whole phrase or sentence. The term is associated with the one-word stage, roughly from about 12 to 18 months, though researchers debate how much sentence-like meaning children actually intend.
e: A toddler saying Milk! while reaching for a cup may mean 'I want milk' or 'Give me the milk.'

d: A word that is spelled the same as another word but differs in meaning and sometimes in pronunciation.
e: Lead /lid/ 'to guide' and lead /lɛd/ 'a metal' are homographs.

d: The situation in which two or more distinct words happen to have the same form but unrelated meanings, usually by historical accident. Homonyms in the full sense share both pronunciation and spelling; homophones and homographs share only one of these.
e: Bank 'financial institution' and bank 'side of a river' are homonyms.
s: Lyons, J. (1977). Semantics (Vols. 1–2). Cambridge University Press.

d: A word that is pronounced the same as another word but differs in meaning and often in spelling.
e: Right, write and rite are all pronounced /raɪt/ in English.

d: The overuse or misapplication of a form that a speaker believes to be prestigious or correct, often because of linguistic insecurity. In variationist research, it also refers to a group using a prestige variant in careful speech even more than the highest-status group does.
e: Saying between you and I instead of between you and me, because the speaker has been taught that you and me is often “wrong.”

d: A word whose meaning is more general and includes the meanings of more specific words (its hyponyms). The relation from the general term's side is sometimes called hypernymy.
e: Vehicle is a hypernym of car, bus and bicycle.

d: The relation of inclusion between a more specific term (the hyponym) and a more general term (the hypernym), such that the specific one is "a kind of" the general one. Hyponymy creates hierarchical taxonomies and supports entailments from specific to general.
e: Tulip is a hyponym of flower: She bought tulips entails She bought flowers. Tulip and rose are co-hyponyms.
s: Cruse, D. A. (1986). Lexical semantics. Cambridge University Press.

d: In the L2 Motivational Self System, the image of the L2 user a learner would like to become. A vivid and plausible ideal L2 self is argued to motivate effort, because learners want to reduce the gap between their current and desired selves.
e: A nursing student imagines herself confidently comforting Spanish-speaking patients in their language, and this image keeps her studying.

d: In sociolinguistics, a person's sense of who they are and how others position them, seen as constructed and negotiated through language in interaction rather than fixed in advance. People have multiple identities (such as ethnic, gender, professional, and local) that they foreground in different contexts.
e: A university student uses local slang and pronunciations when visiting her hometown to show she still belongs there, and more standard forms in class.
p: An influential framework was proposed by Mary Bucholtz and Kira Hall (2005).
s: Bucholtz, M., & Hall, K. (2005). Identity and interaction: A sociocultural linguistic approach. Discourse Studies, 7(4–5), 585–614.

d: The unique way of speaking of a single individual, shaped by their personal history, the communities they belong to, and their personal habits. No two people's idiolects are exactly alike.
e: One person habitually answers thanks with no worries, pronounces data as [ˈdætə], and uses a favorite filler basically, while her coworkers do not.

d: A fixed or semi-fixed expression whose overall meaning cannot be fully worked out from the literal meanings of its parts. Idioms vary in how transparent and how flexible they are.
e: Kick the bucket means 'die', which does not follow from the meanings of kick and bucket.

d: The proposal that speakers have access to a large number of semi-preconstructed phrases that act as single choices, so that much text is produced from prefabricated units rather than word by word. It is contrasted with the open-choice principle, in which each slot is filled freely by any grammatically possible word; Sinclair argued that the idiom principle is the default in normal text.
e: set eyes on typically occurs with a personal pronoun subject, a perfect verb form, and an expression like never or the moment (I've never set eyes on him), so speakers seem to choose the phrase as a whole rather than combine set + eyes + on freely.
p: Proposed by John Sinclair and set out most fully in Corpus, Concordance, Collocation (1991).
s: Sinclair, J. (1991). Corpus, concordance, collocation. Oxford University Press.

d: The action a speaker intends to perform by making an utterance, such as asking, promising, ordering, or warning. The type of action is called the utterance's illocutionary force, and it is the central level of analysis in speech act theory.
e: I'll be there at six can have the illocutionary force of a promise.
p: Distinguished by J. L. Austin (1962); John Searle (1969, 1976) later proposed a classification of illocutionary acts into representatives (later called assertives), directives, commissives, expressives, and declarations.
s: Austin, J. L. (1962). How to do things with words. Clarendon Press.

d: A universal of the form 'if a language has feature X, it also (always or usually) has feature Y.' Instead of claiming that one feature is found everywhere, it limits which combinations of features occur.
e: Greenberg's Universal 3: languages whose dominant order is VSO are prepositional (they use prepositions, not postpositions).
p: Associated especially with Joseph H. Greenberg's (1963) word order universals.

d: Meaning that a speaker communicates or suggests without saying it explicitly. Grice divided it into conversational implicature, which is inferred from context and the cooperative principle, and conventional implicature, which is attached to particular words.
e: A: Do you want to go to the movies? B: I have an exam tomorrow. B implicates 'no'.
p: Term introduced by H. Paul Grice (1975).
s: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and conversation. In P. Cole & J. L. Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and semantics: Vol. 3. Speech acts. Academic Press.

d: Knowledge of a language that is intuitive and unconscious, and can be accessed quickly and automatically during real-time communication. Learners usually cannot explain it in words; many researchers see it as the main goal of L2 development.
e: A fluent learner instantly judges *She enjoys to swim as wrong (ungrammatical; target: She enjoys swimming) but cannot say why.
s: Ellis, R. (2005). Measuring implicit and explicit knowledge of a second language: A psychometric study. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 27(2).

d: Learning new words as a by-product of activities focused on meaning, such as extensive reading or watching TV, rather than through deliberate study. Gains from a single encounter are usually small, so repeated exposure is important; most researchers recommend combining incidental and intentional learning.
e: After reading several graded readers, a learner understands glimpse without ever having looked it up, because it appeared repeatedly in context.

d: The finding that people interpret language piece by piece as it arrives, integrating each new word into a developing interpretation rather than waiting for the sentence to finish. It allows rapid comprehension but can produce temporary misinterpretations.
e: On hearing The boy will eat the… while viewing a picture with a cake and a toy car, listeners tend to look at the cake before cake is said.

d: The way linguistic forms come to point to (index) social meanings, such as a place, group, stance, or personal quality, through repeated association with particular speakers and situations. Such meanings can build on each other in layers, so a feature that first signals a region may later signal a personality type.
e: In Pittsburgh, pronouncing downtown with a monophthong (spelled “dahntahn”) first signaled working-class local speech and later came to signal local pride.
p: Builds on the semiotics of Charles S. Peirce; developed for language especially by Michael Silverstein, whose notion of “indexical order” (2003) is widely used in sociolinguistics.
s: Silverstein, M. (2003). Indexical order and the dialectics of sociolinguistic life. Language & Communication, 23(3–4), 193–229.

d: A speech act in which the speaker performs one act by means of another, so the sentence form does not match its main function. Indirect requests are common in many languages because they can sound more polite, though how often and how they are used varies across cultures.
e: Can you pass the salt? is formally a question about ability but normally functions as a request.
p: Analyzed in detail by John Searle (1975).
s: Searle, J. R. (1975). Indirect speech acts. In P. Cole & J. L. Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and semantics: Vol. 3. Speech acts. Academic Press.

d: Characteristics that vary from learner to learner and help explain why people learn L2s at different rates and to different levels, such as aptitude, motivation, anxiety, working memory, personality, and learning strategies. Recent work increasingly treats these factors as changing over time and interacting with context, rather than as fixed traits.
e: Two classmates with the same teacher and textbook make very different progress; researchers look at their aptitude, motivation, and anxiety to explain the gap.

d: An affix inserted inside a root or base rather than at its edge. True infixation is rare in English but common in some languages, such as Tagalog.
e: Tagalog -um-: sulat ‘writing; letter’ → sumulat ‘to write; wrote’. English expletive insertion (abso-bloody-lutely) is often called infixation, but some linguists argue it is not a true infix, because the inserted element is a whole word rather than an affix.

d: Morphological marking that creates different grammatical forms of the same word (lexeme) to express categories such as tense, number, person, case, or comparison, without creating a new word or usually changing word class. The boundary between inflection and derivation is not always sharp and is debated.
e: walk → walks, walked, walking; tall → taller, tallest.

d: A communicative activity in which each participant has information the others lack, so they must exchange it through the target language to complete the activity.
e: Student A has a train timetable with some times missing, and Student B has the missing times; they ask and answer questions to complete both timetables.

d: An abbreviation formed from the initial letters of a phrase and pronounced as a sequence of letter names rather than as a word.
e: FBI, BBC, ESL.

d: Techniques that make a target feature in input more noticeable to learners, such as bolding, underlining, or color-coding it in a text (textual enhancement) or giving the input many examples of it (input flood). Sharwood Smith used the term to stress that the teacher can make input more salient but cannot guarantee that learners notice or acquire it.
e: In a reading passage about last weekend, every past-tense ending -ed is printed in bold.
p: Term introduced by Michael Sharwood Smith as a replacement for his earlier term consciousness-raising.
s: Sharwood Smith, M. (1993). Input enhancement in instructed SLA: Theoretical bases. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 15(2), 165–179.

d: The claim that learners acquire language by understanding messages that are slightly beyond their current level (often written “i + 1”), and that comprehensible input is the main or only cause of acquisition. Critics argue that input alone is not sufficient and point to roles for interaction, output, and attention.
e: An intermediate learner reads a graded reader that contains mostly familiar language plus a few new structures she can work out from context and pictures.
p: Proposed by Stephen Krashen; set out at length in his 1985 book.
s: Krashen, S. D. (1985). The input hypothesis: Issues and implications. Longman.

d: A model of how learners connect forms with meanings during comprehension, especially under limited processing capacity. It proposes principles such as a tendency to process content words before grammatical endings and to interpret the first noun in a sentence as the subject, which can lead to misinterpretation.
e: An English-speaking learner of Spanish hears Lo ve María (‘María sees him’) and wrongly interprets it as ‘He sees María,’ treating the first element as the subject.
p: Model developed by Bill VanPatten (1990s).
s: VanPatten, B. (1996). Input processing and grammar instruction in second language acquisition. Ablex.

d: Motivation to learn a language for practical benefits, such as passing an exam, getting a job, or earning more money. It is often contrasted with integrative motivation, though in practice learners usually have a mix of both.
e: An engineer studies English to raise her TOEFL score so that she can be admitted to a graduate program in the United States.
p: Distinction introduced by Robert Gardner and Wallace Lambert (1959, 1972).
s: Gardner, R. C., & Lambert, W. E. (1972). Attitudes and motivation in second-language learning. Newbury House.

d: The part of the input that a learner actually takes in and processes, as opposed to everything the learner is exposed to. Definitions vary: some treat intake as input that has been noticed, others as input that has entered the developing language system.
e: A learner hears hundreds of past-tense verbs in a lecture but, focused on content, processes only the irregular taught because it was repeated and stressed; that form becomes intake.
p: Distinguished from input by S. Pit Corder (1967).
s: Corder, S. P. (1967). The significance of learner’s errors. International Review of Applied Linguistics in Language Teaching, 5, 161–170.

d: Motivation to learn a language that stems from interest in, or a wish to identify with or connect to, the people and culture of the language community. It was long considered especially predictive of success, but later research questioned it, particularly for global languages like English that are not tied to one community.
e: A Canadian English speaker learns French because she wants to take part in Quebec’s cultural life and make Francophone friends.
p: Distinction introduced by Robert Gardner and Wallace Lambert (1959, 1972).
s: Gardner, R. C., & Lambert, W. E. (1972). Attitudes and motivation in second-language learning. Newbury House.

d: The conceptual content of an expression: the set of properties or conditions something must meet for the expression to apply to it. In formal semantics, an intension is often modeled as a function that gives an expression's extension in each possible situation or world.
e: The intension of bachelor includes properties like 'adult', 'male' and 'unmarried'.
p: The intension/extension pair was developed in modern semantics by Rudolf Carnap in Meaning and Necessity (1947), building on Frege's sense/reference distinction.
s: Carnap, R. (1947). Meaning and necessity: A study in semantics and modal logic. University of Chicago Press.

d: The degree of agreement between different raters who score the same performances. Training, clear rubrics, and benchmark samples are commonly used to improve it.
e: Two teachers independently score 30 essays on a six-point scale; if they give the same or adjacent scores to nearly all essays, inter-rater reliability is high.

d: The proposal that conversational interaction, especially when speakers work to resolve communication problems, helps acquisition by making input more comprehensible, drawing learners’ attention to gaps, and giving them feedback. Later versions emphasize that interaction links input, learner attention, and output.
e: Learner: *I go to doctor yesterday. Native speaker: Oh, you went to the doctor yesterday? The reformulation (ungrammatical original) gives the learner a model of the target form during real communication.
p: Developed by Michael Long (1981; updated version 1996).
s: Long, M. H. (1996). The role of the linguistic environment in second language acquisition. In W. C. Ritchie & T. K. Bhatia (Eds.), Handbook of second language acquisition. Academic Press.

d: Competing views on whether explicit knowledge can become implicit knowledge. The non-interface position holds that the two are separate and do not convert; the strong-interface position holds that explicit knowledge can become implicit through practice; weak-interface positions hold that explicit knowledge helps indirectly, for example by promoting noticing.
e: A teacher who believes in a weak interface teaches the rule for English articles briefly, then gives students reading tasks so that they notice articles in context.

d: The developing language system that an L2 learner builds, which has its own rules and is neither the learner’s L1 nor the target language. The concept treats learner language as systematic and worth studying in its own right rather than as a set of failed attempts at the target.
e: A learner who consistently says *He no like coffee (ungrammatical in standard English) is following an interlanguage rule of placing no before the verb to form negatives.
p: Coined by Larry Selinker (1972).
s: Selinker, L. (1972). Interlanguage. International Review of Applied Linguistics in Language Teaching, 10(1–4).

d: The study of how second language learners use, understand, and acquire the pragmatic aspects of a new language. It overlaps with second language acquisition research and with cross-cultural pragmatics.
e: Investigating how Japanese learners of English develop their ability to refuse invitations over time spent abroad.
s: Kasper, G., & Blum-Kulka, S. (Eds.). (1993). Interlanguage pragmatics. Oxford University Press.

d: A standardized system of symbols in which, ideally, each symbol stands for one speech sound, so that the pronunciation of any language can be written down consistently. It is maintained and periodically revised by the International Phonetic Association.
e: English thing is transcribed /θɪŋ/; the symbols θ and ŋ have no single-letter equivalent in ordinary English spelling.
p: Developed by the International Phonetic Association, founded in 1886 (with Paul Passy as a leading figure); the first version of the alphabet appeared in 1888.
s: International Phonetic Association. (1999). Handbook of the International Phonetic Association: A guide to the use of the International Phonetic Alphabet. Cambridge University Press.

d: The idea that every text is shaped by and connected to other texts, through quotation, allusion, borrowing of conventions, or responses to earlier texts. In discourse analysis, it is used to trace how texts draw on and transform other voices.
e: A political speech that echoes I have a dream, or a student essay that cites and responds to published sources.
p: Coined by Julia Kristeva in the late 1960s, drawing on Mikhail Bakhtin's ideas of dialogism.

d: The use of pitch patterns across phrases and utterances to convey meanings that are not part of individual words, such as sentence type, which information is new or important, and the speaker's attitude. Unlike tone, intonation does not distinguish word meanings.
e: You're leaving. said with falling pitch is a statement, while You're leaving? said with rising pitch functions as a question.
s: Ladd, D. R. (2008). Intonational phonology (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.

d: A sociological concept describing learners’ commitment to learning a language as linked to their identities and their hopes for social and material resources; Norton argued that learners invest when they expect a return that will increase their cultural capital and social power. Unlike motivation, often treated as a property of the individual, investment highlights how power relations in a setting can enable or block participation.
e: A highly motivated immigrant learner speaks little English at her workplace because co-workers treat her as an outsider, yet she invests heavily in English in a class where she is respected.
p: Introduced by Bonny Norton (publishing as Norton Peirce, 1995).
s: Norton Peirce, B. (1995). Social identity, investment, and language learning. TESOL Quarterly, 29(1).

d: In generative grammar, a structure out of which a constituent cannot be moved (extracted), so that, for example, a question word cannot be linked to a gap inside it; relative clauses and coordinated phrases are classic examples. Whether islands reflect grammatical constraints or processing limitations is debated.
e: From You met the man who wrote a book, the question *What did you meet the man who wrote __? is ungrammatical because the relative clause is an island.
p: Island constraints were identified and named by John Robert (Haj) Ross in his 1967 MIT dissertation.
s: Ross, J. R. (1967). Constraints on variables in syntax [Doctoral dissertation, Massachusetts Institute of Technology].

d: A language in which most words consist of a single morpheme, with grammatical meanings expressed mainly by separate words and word order rather than by affixes.
e: Mandarin wǒ mǎi le sān běn shū ‘I bought three books’: shū ‘book(s)’ has no plural ending, and completion is shown by the separate particle le.

d: A cooperative activity in which different group members receive different parts of a text or task, and the group must combine all the parts to complete the whole. In language classes it creates a need for every learner to speak.
e: Each of four students reads a different paragraph of a news story; they then retell their parts to one another and work out the full sequence of events.
p: Developed by social psychologist Elliot Aronson and his students in Austin, Texas, in 1971, to reduce hostility in newly desegregated classrooms.

d: A display format in which every occurrence of a search term is lined up in a central column with a fixed amount of text on either side. It is the standard way concordance results are presented.
e: “she made a decision to leave” and “the committee's final decision was announced” are shown as aligned lines with decision in the center column; sorting by the word to the left reveals its typical modifiers and verbs (make a, final).
p: The term was introduced by Hans Peter Luhn of IBM (1960) for automatic indexing of technical literature.
s: Luhn, H. P. (1960). Key word-in-context index for technical literature (KWIC index). American Documentation, 11(4), 288–295.

d: The degree to which a word is unusually frequent (positive keyness) or unusually infrequent (negative keyness) in a target corpus compared with a reference corpus, as measured by a statistic such as log-likelihood or an effect-size measure. Keyword analysis uses keyness to identify words that characterize the “aboutness” or style of a text or genre.
e: Comparing a corpus of biology research articles with a general reference corpus would likely show subject words such as cell and protein as positive key words, and conversational words such as yeah as negative key words.

d: The reasons and drive that lead a person to start learning a language, to keep going, and to invest effort over time. Theories of L2 motivation have shifted from stable orientations toward more dynamic, self-related, and context-sensitive models.
e: A student studies Korean for two hours daily because she wants to work in Seoul and enjoys K-dramas; her persistence reflects strong L2 motivation.

d: A model of language learning motivation built on three components: the ideal L2 self, the ought-to L2 self, and the L2 learning experience. It reframes motivation in terms of learners’ visions of their future selves and partly replaced integrativeness as the leading framework in the field.
e: A learner pictures herself giving presentations in English at an international company (ideal L2 self), feels her parents expect her to pass English exams (ought-to L2 self), and enjoys her current class (learning experience).
p: Proposed by Zoltán Dörnyei (2005, 2009).
s: Dörnyei, Z. (2009). The L2 motivational self system. In Z. Dörnyei & E. Ushioda (Eds.), Motivation, language identity and the L2 self. Multilingual Matters.

d: Describing a consonant produced with the lower lip against or near the upper front teeth.
e: /f/ in fan and /v/ in van are labiodental fricatives; learners whose first language lacks /v/ may replace it with [b] or [w].

d: A hypothesized innate mental capacity that enables children to acquire the grammar of any human language from the input they receive. Later generative work largely reframed it as Universal Grammar; the idea remains contested by usage-based and emergentist researchers.
e: On this view, a child raised in Tokyo and one raised in Lagos use the same innate device to arrive at Japanese and Yoruba grammars, respectively.
p: Proposed by Noam Chomsky in the 1960s, notably in Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (1965).
s: Chomsky, N. (1965). Aspects of the theory of syntax. MIT Press.

d: A specific talent for learning foreign languages, often described as a set of abilities such as sound discrimination and memory for sounds, sensitivity to grammar, ability to infer rules from examples, and rote memory. Aptitude is usually measured by tests and predicts classroom learning rate, though its relationship to naturalistic learning is debated.
e: A learner who quickly figures out the plural rule of an invented language from a few examples on an aptitude test scores high on inductive language-learning ability.
p: Classic model by John B. Carroll, who created the Modern Language Aptitude Test (MLAT) with Stanley Sapon (1959).

d: The evaluations, feelings, and beliefs that people have about languages, varieties, accents, and their speakers. Attitudes are often shaped by stereotypes about the speakers rather than by the language itself, and they can affect education, hiring, and housing decisions.
e: Listeners rate a speaker with a rural accent as friendly and honest but less intelligent than a speaker with a standard accent.

d: The gradual modification of a language's sounds, words, grammar, and meanings across generations of speakers. All living languages change; linguists treat change as normal and systematic rather than as decay, even though the public often perceives new forms as 'corruption'.
e: Old English marked grammatical roles with case forms, as in se cyning 'the king' (subject) vs. þone cyning 'the king' (object), whereas Modern English mostly relies on word order.

d: Any situation in which speakers of different languages interact regularly, together with the linguistic effects of that interaction, such as borrowing, code-switching, convergence of grammatical structures, or the creation of new languages such as pidgins and creoles.
e: Long contact between Spanish and English in the US Southwest has given English words like rodeo and local Spanish words like troca 'truck.'
p: Foundational work by Uriel Weinreich (1953).
s: Weinreich, U. (1953). Languages in contact: Findings and problems. Linguistic Circle of New York.

d: The use of a language or variety that is not generally thought to belong to the speaker, which can raise questions of legitimacy and ethnic boundaries. Crossing can express solidarity, humor, or challenge, but can also reproduce stereotypes.
e: In Ben Rampton's study of adolescents in an English town, young people of Anglo, African Caribbean, and Panjabi backgrounds used Panjabi, Jamaican Creole, and stylized Asian English with one another, including languages not associated with their own background.
p: Developed by Ben Rampton (1995).
s: Rampton, B. (1995). Crossing: Language and ethnicity among adolescents. Longman.

d: The creation of a lasting, multipurpose record of a language, especially audio and video recordings of varied everyday speech together with transcriptions, translations, and annotations, stored in archives for communities and future researchers. It is often distinguished from language description (writing grammars and dictionaries), though the two support each other, and ethical collaboration with speaker communities is central.
e: A team records elders telling traditional stories in their endangered language, transcribes and translates the recordings with community members, and deposits them in a digital archive such as PARADISEC.
p: Its emergence as a distinct field is often traced to Nikolaus P. Himmelmann's (1998) proposal to separate documentation from description.
s: Himmelmann, N. P. (1998). Documentary and descriptive linguistics. Linguistics, 36(1), 161–195.

d: A group of languages that can be shown to descend from one common ancestor, called a proto-language. Relatedness is demonstrated through systematic sound correspondences in basic vocabulary and grammar, not through occasional resemblances; some proposed very large groupings (e.g., Nostratic) remain controversial.
e: English, Russian, Persian, and Hindi belong to the Indo-European family, whereas Finnish and Hungarian belong to the Uralic family.

d: Beliefs and feelings about language and its users, such as which languages are “proper,” who speaks well, or how languages relate to nations, that are shaped by and serve social and political interests. Language ideologies are often taken for granted as common sense.
e: The belief that a nation should have only one language is used to argue for English-only laws.
p: Developed in linguistic anthropology by Michael Silverstein, Judith Irvine, Susan Gal, and others.
s: Irvine, J. T., & Gal, S. (2000). Language ideology and linguistic differentiation. In P. V. Kroskrity (Ed.), Regimes of language: Ideologies, polities, and identities. School of American Research Press.

d: Actions, techniques, or thought processes that learners choose to use to make language learning easier, more effective, or more self-directed. Researchers have classified them in different ways (such as cognitive, metacognitive, memory, and social strategies), and debate continues about how to define and measure them.
e: A learner keeps a notebook of new words with example sentences (cognitive), plans weekly study goals (metacognitive), and joins a conversation club (social).

d: The continued use of a language by a community across generations, especially when it is under pressure from a more dominant language. Maintenance depends on factors such as use in the home, community institutions, and positive attitudes.
e: Many Old Order Amish communities in Pennsylvania have kept Pennsylvania Dutch as their everyday home language for generations while also using English.

d: The state of relative activation of a bilingual's languages at a given moment, ranging from a monolingual mode, where one language is mostly deactivated, to a bilingual mode, where both are highly active and code-switching is likely. The mode depends on factors such as the conversation partner, topic, and setting.
e: A French–English bilingual talking with a monolingual English speaker stays near the monolingual end, but switches freely between languages when chatting with another French–English bilingual.
p: Developed by François Grosjean (see, e.g., Grosjean, 2001).
s: Grosjean, F. (2001). The bilingual's language modes. In J. L. Nicol (Ed.), One mind, two languages: Bilingual language processing. Blackwell.

d: Deliberate efforts, usually by governments or institutions, to influence the functions, forms, or learning of languages in a community. It is commonly divided into status planning, corpus planning, and acquisition planning.
e: Norway developed two official written standards for Norwegian, Bokmål and Nynorsk, through planned reforms.
p: The term was first used by Uriel Weinreich in a 1957 seminar and first discussed in print by Einar Haugen (1959) in a study of Norwegian standardization.
s: Haugen, E. (1959). Planning for a standard language in modern Norway. Anthropological Linguistics, 1(3), 8–21.

d: The decisions, rules, and practices that shape which languages are used, taught, and valued in a society, institution, or family. Spolsky describes it as having three parts: actual language practices, beliefs about language, and deliberate efforts to manage language use.
e: France's 1994 Toubon Law requires French to be used in areas such as advertising and workplace documents.
p: The three-part model is from Bernard Spolsky (2004).
s: Spolsky, B. (2004). Language policy. Cambridge University Press.

d: Efforts, usually led by communities and often supported by linguists and educators, to increase the use of an endangered or no-longer-spoken language, especially by creating new speakers. Approaches include immersion schools, master–apprentice programs, and teaching materials built from documentation; success is often judged by renewed use in daily and community life, not only by learners' proficiency.
e: Māori 'language nest' preschools (kōhanga reo) in New Zealand, begun in the early 1980s, immerse young children in the Māori language.

d: The process by which a community gradually stops using one language and adopts another for most or all purposes. In many immigrant families shift happens over about three generations, and in some cases it leads to the loss of the original language.
e: During the 19th century, most of Ireland shifted from Irish to English as the main everyday language.
p: Major framework by Joshua Fishman (1991), including his Graded Intergenerational Disruption Scale.
s: Fishman, J. A. (1991). Reversing language shift: Theoretical and empirical foundations of assistance to threatened languages. Multilingual Matters.

d: The influence of a learner’s previously known language(s) on the learning and use of a new language. Transfer can affect pronunciation, grammar, vocabulary, and pragmatics, and it can help or hinder learning.
e: A Spanish speaker who says *I have 20 years (ungrammatical in English) is transferring the Spanish pattern tengo 20 años for expressing age.

d: A property claimed to hold for all human languages (an absolute universal) or for far more languages than chance would predict (a statistical universal or tendency). Generative linguists often link universals to an innate Universal Grammar, functional-typological linguists explain them through communicative and processing pressures, and some researchers argue that many proposed universals have exceptions.
e: Absolute: all known spoken languages have both consonants and vowels. Statistical: subject-before-object orders (SOV, SVO) are far more common than object-before-subject orders.
p: Modern typological work on universals is closely associated with Joseph H. Greenberg (1963).
s: Greenberg, J. H. (1963). Some universals of grammar with particular reference to the order of meaningful elements. In J. H. Greenberg (Ed.), Universals of language. MIT Press.

d: The fact that every language exists in many forms, differing across regions, social groups, situations, and individual speakers, in pronunciation, vocabulary, grammar, and discourse. Sociolinguists treat this variation as normal and structured, not as error.
e: In different parts of the United States, people call a sweet carbonated drink soda, pop, or coke.

d: The specialization of the two brain hemispheres for different functions. In most people (about 95% of right-handers and most left-handers), core language functions depend mainly on the left hemisphere, while the right hemisphere is thought to contribute to aspects such as intonation, emotional tone, and figurative or discourse-level meaning.
e: In most right-handed adults, a stroke in the left hemisphere is far more likely to cause aphasia than an equivalent stroke in the right hemisphere.

d: The ideas and assumptions learners hold about language, language learning, and their own abilities, for example about the role of grammar, how long learning takes, or whether some people have a special gift. Beliefs can influence strategy use, motivation, and reactions to teaching methods, and they may change with experience.
e: A learner who believes that learning a language mainly means memorizing vocabulary lists may resist communicative pair-work activities.

d: An electronic collection of texts produced by language learners, usually with information about the learners (first language, proficiency, task). Learner corpora are used to describe interlanguage features, such as overuse, underuse, and errors, often by comparing them with native-speaker or expert-user corpora.
e: The International Corpus of Learner English (ICLE) contains essays, mainly argumentative, written by advanced learners of English from many first-language backgrounds.
p: Sylviane Granger (Université catholique de Louvain), who launched the International Corpus of Learner English, is a founding figure of learner corpus research.
s: Granger, S. (Ed.). (1998). Learner English on computer. Longman.

d: A monolingual dictionary designed for people learning a language, using a restricted defining vocabulary, many corpus-based examples, and information on grammar, collocation, and frequency. It contrasts with other dictionary types such as native-speaker monolingual dictionaries, bilingual dictionaries, and specialized dictionaries (e.g., collocation or academic dictionaries).
e: The Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary, Longman Dictionary of Contemporary English, and Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary are well-known English learner's dictionaries.

d: A clear statement of what learners should be able to do at the end of a lesson or course, ideally in observable and assessable terms. Sheltered instruction models often require both content objectives and language objectives.
e: By the end of the lesson, students will be able to write three sentences comparing two cities using comparative adjectives.

d: In corpus work and lexicography, a headword together with its inflected forms that belong to the same word class. Counting by lemma groups forms such as walk, walks, walked, walking as one unit, but does not include derived forms such as walker.
e: The lemma be includes am, is, are, was, were, been, and being; the noun run and the verb run are usually treated as separate lemmas.

d: The process of grouping or converting inflected word forms to their lemma (base form), usually using a dictionary and part-of-speech information. It differs from stemming, which simply cuts off word endings and may produce non-words.
e: A lemmatizer maps better (adjective) to good and studies to study, whereas a simple stemmer might reduce studies to studi.

d: An abstract dictionary word that groups together all its inflected forms under one meaning. Lexemes are often written in small capitals to distinguish them from individual word forms.
e: The lexeme RUN includes the word forms run, runs, ran, and running.

d: The process of retrieving a word and its information from the mental lexicon, either when recognizing a word in listening or reading or when selecting a word to say. It is influenced by factors such as word frequency, recency of use, and context.
e: High-frequency words like house are typically recognized faster than low-frequency words like hovel, showing a frequency effect on lexical access.

d: Ambiguity that arises because a word in a sentence has more than one meaning, due to homonymy or polysemy. Context usually selects one reading.
e: She went to the bank can mean a financial institution or a riverside.

d: A sequence of three or more words that recurs very frequently in a register and across many different texts, identified purely by frequency and dispersion criteria. Lexical bundles are usually not complete grammatical units or idioms, but they serve discourse functions such as framing, hedging, or organizing text.
e: In academic writing, on the other hand, as a result of, and in the case of are common four-word lexical bundles.
p: The term was introduced in the Longman Grammar of Spoken and Written English (Biber, Johansson, Leech, Conrad, & Finegan, 1999).
s: Biber, D., Johansson, S., Leech, G., Conrad, S., & Finegan, E. (1999). Longman grammar of spoken and written English. Longman.

d: The percentage of running words (tokens) in a text that a reader or listener knows, or that a given word list accounts for. Research suggests comprehension improves as coverage rises, with figures around 95% often cited as a minimum and about 98% as needed for comfortable unassisted reading, though the relationship is gradual rather than a sharp threshold.
e: At 98% coverage, a reader meets about one unknown word in every 50 running words, or roughly six on a page of 300 words.
p: The 98% figure is most closely associated with Hu and Nation's (2000) study of unknown vocabulary density and reading comprehension.

d: An experimental task in which participants see or hear a string of letters or sounds and decide, as quickly as possible, whether it is a real word. Response times and accuracy are used to infer how words are stored and accessed.
e: A participant presses "yes" for table and "no" for the made-up string blick; faster "yes" responses suggest easier lexical access.
s: Meyer, D. E., & Schvaneveldt, R. W. (1971). Facilitation in recognizing pairs of words: Evidence of a dependence between retrieval operations. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 90(2).

d: A unit of vocabulary that carries a single meaning and is stored as a whole in the lexicon, whether it is one word or several. The notion is used to recognize that many meaningful units in language are larger than single orthographic words.
e: dog, look up (in a dictionary), and by and large are each one lexical item, even though the last two are written as several words.

d: A morpheme that carries substantial dictionary (content) meaning, typically the root of a noun, verb, adjective, or adverb. Lexical morphemes form an open class to which new members are easily added.
e: tree, jump, green, and quick in quickly.

d: The part of semantics concerned with the meanings of individual words and other lexical items, including how word meanings are structured and how words relate to one another in meaning.
e: Asking how run in run a race relates to run in run a company is a question in lexical semantics.
s: Cruse, D. A. (1986). Lexical semantics. Cambridge University Press.

d: The theory and practice of compiling dictionaries, including selecting headwords, writing definitions, choosing examples, and organizing senses. Since the 1980s, much lexicography has been corpus-based, using real usage data to decide on senses, frequency information, and examples.
e: Corpus evidence led modern learner's dictionaries to list the most frequent sense of a word first and to flag the most frequent few thousand words (e.g., the Oxford 3000).

d: A language used for communication between people who do not share a first language. It may be someone's native language, a second language for everyone involved, or a pidgin.
e: Swahili is widely used as a lingua franca in East Africa among speakers of many different first languages.

d: Discrimination on the basis of language: ideologies, structures, and practices that create unequal access to power and resources for groups defined by the language or variety they speak. It is often compared to racism and sexism.
e: A school forbids children from speaking their home language even during breaks and punishes them when they do.
p: Coined by Tove Skutnabb-Kangas in the 1980s; see her contributions to Phillipson and Skutnabb-Kangas (1986), Linguicism rules in education.

d: The argument that the dominance of English (or another powerful language) is maintained through structural and cultural inequalities that favor it over other languages, often continuing colonial patterns. Critics argue that it underestimates the choices and agency of people who adopt English for their own purposes.
e: A former colony continues to fund English-medium education and imported textbooks while local languages receive few resources in schools.
p: Proposed by Robert Phillipson (1992).
s: Phillipson, R. (1992). Linguistic imperialism. Oxford University Press.

d: Speakers' feeling that their own way of speaking is inferior or incorrect compared with a prestige norm. It can lead to anxiety about speaking, self-correction, and hypercorrection.
e: A speaker who says she “doesn't speak proper English” and judges her own regional pronunciations as wrong, even though she uses them every day.
p: Measured by William Labov (1966) in his New York City study.
s: Labov, W. (1966). The social stratification of English in New York City. Center for Applied Linguistics.

d: The visibility of languages on public and commercial signs in a given area, such as street names, shop signs, advertisements, and official notices. Studying it reveals which languages are given power and status and which are ignored.
e: In Brussels, street signs show names in both French and Dutch.
p: Influentially defined by Rodrigue Landry and Richard Bourhis (1997).
s: Landry, R., & Bourhis, R. Y. (1997). Linguistic landscape and ethnolinguistic vitality: An empirical study. Journal of Language and Social Psychology, 16(1), 23–49.

d: The idea that the language a person speaks influences how they perceive and think about the world.
