It is associated with Edward Sapir and his student Benjamin Lee Whorf, but neither stated it as a formal hypothesis, and the label 'Sapir–Whorf hypothesis' was applied by other scholars after their deaths. The strong version (linguistic determinism, that language determines thought) is widely rejected, while weaker versions, that language can influence some areas of cognition such as color, space, or time, have some experimental support and remain debated.
e: Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr (Australia) describe locations with cardinal directions ('the cup is north of you') rather than 'left' and 'right', and researchers have argued that this also shapes how they remember spatial arrangements in non-verbal tasks.

d: The full set of linguistic resources (languages, varieties, registers, styles, and ways of speaking) available to a person or a community. Recent work stresses that repertoires reflect life histories and can include partial knowledge of many languages.
e: A Filipino nurse in the United States uses Tagalog, Ilocano, everyday English, and specialized medical English, each in different situations.
p: The notion of a “verbal repertoire” was introduced by John Gumperz (1964).
s: Gumperz, J. J. (1964). Linguistic and social interaction in two communities. American Anthropologist, 66(6), 137–153.

d: The study and classification of languages by their structural features, such as sound inventories, word structure, and word order, regardless of whether they are historically related. Typologists compare broad samples of languages to discover recurring patterns and limits on how languages can vary.
e: Classifying languages by basic clause order groups Japanese (SOV), English (SVO), and Welsh (VSO) into different types.

d: A linguistic feature that can be realized in two or more ways (its variants) that mean the same thing, where the choice of variant correlates with social or stylistic factors. It is the basic unit of analysis in variationist sociolinguistics.
e: The variable (ing) has the variants [ɪŋ] and [ɪn], as in walking versus walkin'; the [ɪn] variant tends to be more frequent in casual speech.
p: Developed as an analytic unit by William Labov (1966).

d: The smooth joining of words in connected speech without a pause. Linking includes joining a final consonant to a following vowel, pronouncing a linking /r/ or adding an intrusive /r/ between vowels in non-rhotic accents, and inserting a glide [j] or [w] between vowels.
e: far away has a linking [r] in non-rhotic British English; law and order may have an intrusive [r]; go on is often [ɡoʊ wɑn] in American English and [ɡəʊ wɒn] in British English.

d: A cover term for l-type (lateral) and r-type (rhotic) consonants, which are grouped together because they often behave alike, for example as the second consonant in an onset cluster.
e: /l/ and /r/ in play and pray are liquids; Japanese has a single liquid phoneme, which is one reason English /l/–/r/ contrasts can be hard for Japanese-speaking learners.

d: The basic act of producing a meaningful utterance: saying particular words with a particular sense and reference. It is the first of Austin's three levels of a speech act.
e: Uttering the words The door is open as a well-formed English sentence about a specific door is the locutionary act.
p: Distinguished by J. L. Austin (1962).
s: Austin, J. L. (1962). How to do things with words. Clarendon Press.

d: A clause that is not part of another clause and can, in principle, stand on its own as a complete sentence. It carries the main assertion, question, or command of the sentence.
e: In I left early because I was tired, I left early is the main clause.

d: The way the airflow is shaped or obstructed when a consonant is produced: for example, by complete closure, by a narrow channel that creates friction, or by lowering the soft palate so that air passes through the nose.
e: /t/ (stop), /s/ (fricative) and /n/ (nasal) are all made at the alveolar ridge but differ in manner of articulation.

d: A method for studying language attitudes in which listeners hear the same speaker recorded in two or more languages or accents (“guises”) without knowing it is the same person, and rate each recording on traits such as intelligence or friendliness. Differences in ratings are taken to reflect attitudes toward the varieties. A related method, the verbal-guise technique, uses different speakers.
e: In a Montreal study, both English- and French-speaking listeners rated the English guises more favorably on several traits, even though the same bilingual speakers produced both guises.
p: Introduced by Wallace Lambert and colleagues in a 1960 study in Montreal.
s: Lambert, W. E., Hodgson, R. C., Gardner, R. C., & Fillenbaum, S. (1960). Evaluational reactions to spoken languages. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 60, 44–51.

d: The Gricean maxim that speakers should be clear: avoid obscurity and ambiguity, be brief, and be orderly.
e: She got married and had a baby is usually understood to describe events in that order, because of the expectation to be orderly.
p: Proposed by H. Paul Grice (1975).
s: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and conversation. In P. Cole & J. L. Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and semantics: Vol. 3. Speech acts. Academic Press.

d: The Gricean maxim that speakers should try to say only what they believe to be true and for which they have adequate evidence.
e: Saying He's a real genius about someone who just made an obvious mistake openly breaks this maxim and is understood as irony.
p: Proposed by H. Paul Grice (1975).
s: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and conversation. In P. Cole & J. L. Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and semantics: Vol. 3. Speech acts. Academic Press.

d: The Gricean maxim that a contribution should be as informative as the purpose of the exchange requires, and not more informative than needed.
e: Saying I ate some of the cookies suggests you did not eat all of them, because all would have been more informative.
p: Proposed by H. Paul Grice (1975).
s: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and conversation. In P. Cole & J. L. Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and semantics: Vol. 3. Speech acts. Academic Press.

d: The Gricean maxim that a contribution should be relevant to the ongoing talk. Grice stated it simply as 'be relevant'; later work, especially relevance theory, tried to define relevance more precisely.
e: A: Where's Sam? B: There's a yellow car outside Lee's house. A infers that Sam may be at Lee's house.
p: Proposed by H. Paul Grice (1975).
s: Grice, H. P. (1975). Logic and conversation. In P. Cole & J. L. Morgan (Eds.), Syntax and semantics: Vol. 3. Speech acts. Academic Press.

d: A perceptual illusion in which seeing a speaker's lip movements changes the speech sound a person hears. It shows that speech perception integrates visual and auditory information.
e: When the audio of [ba] is dubbed onto a video of a face saying [ga], many viewers report hearing [da].
p: Reported by Harry McGurk and John MacDonald (1976).
s: McGurk, H., & MacDonald, J. (1976). Hearing lips and seeing voices. Nature, 264.

d: In sociocultural theory, the idea that humans do not act on the world directly but through tools, both physical (such as dictionaries or computers) and symbolic (especially language). Learning is seen as gaining control over these mediating tools, including through help from other people.
e: A learner talks herself through a hard sentence (OK, “if” plus past, then “would”…), using language as a tool to guide her own thinking.
p: Central concept in Lev Vygotsky’s theory of mind.

d: The store of word knowledge in a speaker's long-term memory, including each word's form (sound and spelling), meaning, grammatical properties, and links to other words. Researchers debate how it is organized, for example whether complex words are stored whole or built from morphemes.
e: Knowing that cat is pronounced /kæt/, is a countable noun, refers to a small feline, and is linked to dog and kitten is part of an English speaker's mental lexicon.

d: The part–whole relation between words, where one word names a part of what another word names. The word for the part is the meronym and the word for the whole is the holonym. Unlike hyponymy, it does not express "a kind of".
e: Wheel is a meronym of car, and finger is a meronym of hand.
s: Cruse, D. A. (1986). Lexical semantics. Cambridge University Press.

d: Language in a text that comments on the text itself or on the writer's relationship with the reader, rather than on the subject matter. Hyland divides it into interactive resources that guide the reader through the text and interactional resources that express stance and engage the reader. Researchers differ on how broadly to define it.
e: In this section, I will argue that…; First…, second…; As noted above…; Note that…
p: The term is usually traced to Zellig Harris (1959); the most widely used model in applied linguistics is Ken Hyland's (2005).
s: Hyland, K. (2005). Metadiscourse: Exploring interaction in writing. Continuum.

d: Corrective feedback in which the teacher gives comments, information, or questions about the form of the learner's utterance, often using grammatical terminology, without giving the correct form.
e: Student: I see her yesterday. Teacher: Yesterday is in the past. What tense do we need?
p: One of the six feedback types in Roy Lyster and Leila Ranta's (1997) classification, based on teacher–student interaction in primary-level French immersion classrooms in Montreal.

d: A figure of speech and cognitive process in which one entity is used to refer to another closely associated with it within the same domain, such as a place for an institution or a part for a whole. Unlike metaphor, it is based on association (contiguity) rather than similarity.
e: The White House announced new rules (place for institution); We need more hands (part for whole, i.e. workers).
p: Treated as a conceptual phenomenon by George Lakoff and Mark Johnson (1980) and developed further by Günter Radden and Zoltán Kövecses (1999).
s: Radden, G., & Kövecses, Z. (1999). Towards a theory of metonymy. In K.-U. Panther & G. Radden (Eds.), Metonymy in language and thought (pp. 17–59). John Benjamins.

d: Creative everyday language practices in cities in which people of different backgrounds mix resources from many languages and use language to play with, adopt, or resist identities. The concept stresses that urban language use combines fixed ideas about languages with fluid practice.
e: Workers at a city produce market chat and joke in a mix of English, Arabic, and Cantonese while selling vegetables.
p: Introduced by Emi Otsuji and Alastair Pennycook (2010).
s: Otsuji, E., & Pennycook, A. (2010). Metrolingualism: Fixity, fluidity and language in flux. International Journal of Multilingualism, 7(3), 240–254.

d: The stage of English from about 1100 to 1500 (dates vary by source), following the Norman Conquest of 1066. It saw the loss of most inflectional endings, large-scale borrowing from French, and strong regional variation in spelling and grammar.
e: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales opens Whan that Aprill with his shoures soote 'When April with its sweet showers'.

d: Two words that differ in only one sound, in the same position, and have different meanings. Minimal pairs are the standard evidence that two sounds belong to different phonemes, and they are widely used in pronunciation teaching.
e: light /laɪt/ and right /raɪt/ show that /l/ and /r/ are separate phonemes in English, although they are not separate phonemes in Japanese.

d: A research program in generative grammar that seeks to explain syntax using as few theoretical mechanisms as possible, centrally the operation Merge, which combines two elements into a larger unit. It is described by its proponents as a program of inquiry rather than a fully specified theory.
e: Merge combines the and book into {the, book}, which can then merge with read to form {read, {the, book}}.
p: Introduced by Noam Chomsky in the early 1990s and set out in The Minimalist Program (1995).
s: Chomsky, N. (1995). The minimalist program. MIT Press.

d: An auxiliary verb that expresses modality such as possibility, necessity, permission, obligation, or ability. English central modals are not inflected for person, are followed by a bare infinitive, and have no nonfinite forms.
e: can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would: She must leave, not *She musts leave (ungrammatical).

d: The semantic domain concerned with possibility, necessity, obligation, permission and the speaker's degree of commitment to what is said. In English it is expressed by modal verbs (may, must), adverbs (perhaps) and other forms; grammatical mood is one way languages mark it.
e: You must leave, It might rain and Perhaps she's right all express modality.
s: Palmer, F. R. (2001). Mood and modality (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.

d: The claim that consciously learned rules serve only as an editor (the “monitor”) that checks and corrects output produced by the acquired system. The monitor is said to work only when the learner has enough time, is focused on form, and knows the rule.
e: When writing an essay, a learner rereads *He walk to school (ungrammatical), remembers the third-person -s rule, and corrects it to He walks to school; in fast speech she may not catch the same slip.
p: Proposed by Stephen Krashen as part of the Monitor Model.
s: Krashen, S. D. (1982). Principles and practice in second language acquisition. Pergamon.

d: An influential but controversial theory of SLA made up of five hypotheses: the acquisition–learning distinction, the Natural Order Hypothesis, the Monitor Hypothesis, the Input Hypothesis, and the Affective Filter Hypothesis. It shaped communicative teaching but has been criticized because several of its claims are difficult to test empirically.
e: A teacher influenced by the Monitor Model spends most class time on understandable stories and conversation rather than grammar drills, and keeps the atmosphere relaxed.
p: Developed by Stephen Krashen in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
s: Krashen, S. D. (1982). Principles and practice in second language acquisition. Pergamon.

d: A vowel whose quality stays roughly the same from beginning to end.
e: The vowel /ɛ/ in bed is a monophthong.

d: A grammatical category, marked on the verb, that expresses the speaker's attitude toward a proposition, such as whether it is presented as fact, command, wish, or hypothetical. Common moods include indicative, imperative, and subjunctive; the term is sometimes used broadly to overlap with modality.
e: Indicative: She is here. Imperative: Be here. Subjunctive: I insist that she be here.

d: The actual spoken or written form (a sequence of sounds or letters) that represents a morpheme in a particular word. A morpheme is the abstract unit; a morph is one concrete realization of it.
e: The plural morpheme appears as the morph -s in cats and as the morph -en in oxen.

d: The smallest unit of language that carries meaning or grammatical function and cannot be split into smaller meaningful parts. Some theories treat morphemes as concrete pieces of words, while others (e.g., word-and-paradigm approaches) question whether words are really built from discrete morphemes at all.
e: unhelpful contains three morphemes: un- + help + -ful.
p: The term was coined by Jan Baudouin de Courtenay in the late 19th century.

d: The classification of languages according to how they build words, especially how many morphemes a word typically contains and how clearly morpheme boundaries can be seen. The classic types are ideal points on a continuum: most languages mix features of several types.
e: Mandarin is often described as isolating, Turkish as agglutinative, Spanish as fusional, and Inuktitut as polysynthetic.
p: Grew out of 19th-century work by Friedrich Schlegel (1808), August Wilhelm Schlegel (1818), and Wilhelm von Humboldt (1836). Edward Sapir (1921) reworked it by separating the degree of synthesis from the technique (for example, agglutination versus fusion).
s: Sapir, E. (1921). Language: An introduction to the study of speech. Harcourt, Brace.

d: The study of how the sound shape of morphemes changes when they combine, that is, the interaction between morphology and phonology. It explains why one morpheme can have several pronunciations.
e: The final /k/ of electric corresponds to /s/ in electricity; the plural ending varies between /s/, /z/, and /ɪz/.

d: In generative syntax, the analysis in which a constituent appears in one position but is also interpreted in another, as if it had been displaced. Types include wh-movement (question words), head movement (e.g., subject–auxiliary inversion), and NP-movement (e.g., passives); nontransformational theories describe these patterns without movement.
e: In Which book did you read __?, which book is interpreted as the object of read (the gap marks its original position).

d: The idea that a person who knows more than one language has a distinct overall language capacity, not simply a native-like L1 plus an incomplete L2. It challenges the practice of judging L2 users only against monolingual native speakers.
e: A bilingual whose L1 vocabulary or speech-sound perception has shifted slightly because of her L2 is seen, from a multicompetence view, as having a different but complete language system.
p: Introduced by Vivian Cook (1991).
s: Cook, V. J. (1991). The poverty-of-the-stimulus argument and multicompetence. Second Language Research, 7(2), 103–117.

d: A student who is developing proficiency in an additional language (often English) while already using one or more other languages. The term is promoted as an asset-based alternative to labels such as English language learner (ELL) or limited English proficient (LEP), which define students mainly by what they have not yet acquired.
e: A fifth grader who speaks Haitian Creole at home, reads some French, and is learning academic English at school is a multilingual learner.

d: The use of more than two languages by an individual or within a community or country. It is the normal situation for a large part of the world's population, and sociolinguists study both individual multilingual practices and societal arrangements among languages.
e: Many people in India use a home language such as Tamil, Hindi as a wider language, and English for higher education and work.

d: A combination of two or more words that behaves as a single lexical unit in some respect, for example in meaning, grammar, or conventional use. The term is used especially in computational linguistics and lexicography and includes idioms, compounds, phrasal verbs, and fixed phrases.
e: kick the bucket (‘die’), take place, as well as, and hot dog are all multiword expressions.

d: An association measure from information theory used to show how strongly two words are attracted to each other, by comparing how often they actually co-occur with how often they would co-occur by chance. MI favors rare, exclusive combinations, so it is often reported alongside measures such as the t-score that favor frequent collocations; an MI of 3 or more is a commonly used cut-off.
e: foregone conclusion receives a very high MI score because foregone rarely occurs with any other noun, whereas of the is very frequent but has a low MI score.
p: Brought into corpus-based lexicography and collocation research by Kenneth Church and Patrick Hanks (1990).
s: Church, K. W., & Hanks, P. (1990). Word association norms, mutual information, and lexicography. Computational Linguistics, 16(1), 22–29.

d: Any continuous sequence of n items (usually words) extracted automatically from a text, regardless of whether the sequence is meaningful. N-grams are a basic unit in corpus analysis and natural language processing; a 2-gram is called a bigram and a 3-gram a trigram.
e: The sentence I want to go contains the bigrams I want, want to, and to go, and the trigrams I want to and want to go.

d: A type of semantic change in which a word's meaning becomes more specific, so that it covers a smaller range of referents than before.
e: Old English mete meant 'food' in general, but Modern English meat refers only to animal flesh eaten as food.

d: A consonant produced with a complete closure in the mouth while the soft palate is lowered, so that air escapes through the nose. The term also describes vowels produced with nasal airflow (nasalized vowels).
e: sum /sʌm/, sun /sʌn/ and sung /sʌŋ/ differ only in their final nasal consonant.

d: An ideology in English language teaching holding that “native speakers” represent the ideal of the language and of teaching methods, which disadvantages teachers and users who are labeled “non-native.” It is criticized for linking language expertise to birthplace and often to race.
e: A job advertisement for English teachers states “native speakers only,” regardless of applicants' qualifications.
p: Term introduced by Adrian Holliday (2006).
s: Holliday, A. (2006). Native-speakerism. ELT Journal, 60(4), 385–387.

d: A group of sounds that share one or more phonetic features and tend to behave alike in phonological patterns. A natural class can be described with fewer features than are needed to describe any single member.
e: English /p/, /t/ and /k/ form the natural class of voiceless stops, and all three are aspirated in the same position (pin, tin, kin).

d: The hypothesis that grammatical features of a language are acquired in a predictable order that does not depend on how simple a rule seems or the order in which it is taught. It drew on morpheme-order studies of English; critics questioned their methods and noted that L1 background and other factors also affect order.
e: Morpheme studies reported that learners of English tend to master progressive -ing (She is running) before third-person -s (She runs), even though -s is taught early.
p: Proposed by Stephen Krashen as one of the five hypotheses of the Monitor Model, building on morpheme-order studies of the 1970s.
s: Krashen, S. D. (1982). Principles and practice in second language acquisition. Pergamon.

d: The systematic collection of information about what learners need to do with the language, what they already know, and what they want, as a basis for designing a course. Sources can include interviews, questionnaires, observation, and analysis of target texts.
e: Before designing a course for hospital nurses, a teacher shadows nurses on the ward, records handover conversations, and surveys staff about their most difficult communication tasks.
p: An influential early, detailed model was proposed by John Munby (1978).
s: Munby, J. (1978). Communicative syllabus design. Cambridge University Press.

d: Politeness strategies that attend to the hearer's negative face by respecting their freedom and minimizing imposition, for example through indirectness, hedging, apologizing, and deference.
e: I'm sorry to bother you, but I was wondering if you could possibly look at my draft.
p: Term from Penelope Brown and Stephen Levinson (1978, 1987).
s: Brown, P., & Levinson, S. C. (1987). Politeness: Some universals in language usage. Cambridge University Press.

d: Transfer that leads to non-target forms because a feature of the previously known language differs from the new language. It is sometimes called interference, a term now often avoided because it suggests the L1 is only an obstacle.
e: A Japanese speaker who omits articles in English (*I bought book yesterday, ungrammatical) may be influenced by Japanese, which has no articles.

d: The adjustments speakers make when a breakdown in understanding occurs, such as asking for clarification, checking comprehension, or confirming what was said. These exchanges are thought to make input more understandable and to push learners to modify their output.
e: Learner A: I saw a … a cow with long hair. Learner B: A cow? You mean a horse? Learner A: No, a goat — with a beard. The clarification request leads to a more precise word.

d: A compound built from combining forms borrowed from Greek or Latin, many of which do not occur as independent English words. Such compounds are common in scientific and academic vocabulary.
e: telephone (tele- ‘far’ + -phone ‘sound’), biology (bio- ‘life’ + -logy ‘study’).

d: The study of how language is represented and processed in the brain, drawing on evidence from brain damage (such as aphasia) and from brain-imaging and electrophysiological methods such as fMRI and EEG. The classic model linking production to Broca's area and comprehension to Wernicke's area is now considered an oversimplification; current models describe language as relying on distributed networks spanning several regions of both hemispheres, though mainly the left.
e: In EEG studies, a sentence ending unexpectedly, as in I take my coffee with cream and socks, produces a larger negative brain response about 400 milliseconds after the final word (the N400) than an expected ending like …cream and sugar.

d: The loss of a phonemic contrast in a particular environment, so that two phonemes that are distinct elsewhere are pronounced the same there. Some experimental studies report that such contrasts are not always completely lost (incomplete neutralization).
e: In German, final devoicing makes Rad 'wheel' and Rat 'advice' both sound like [ʁaːt].
p: Theorized by Nikolai Trubetzkoy in Grundzüge der Phonologie (1939), who linked it to the notion of the archiphoneme.

d: The process or result of turning a verb, adjective, or whole clause into a noun or noun phrase. In Systemic Functional Linguistics it is a key type of grammatical metaphor and is characteristic of academic and scientific writing.
e: The government decided to invest becomes the government's decision to invest; They analyzed the data becomes their analysis of the data.

d: Word formation that does not simply line up morphemes one after another, but changes the internal structure of the base, for example by interleaving consonants and vowels, changing vowels, or reduplicating. The root-and-pattern system of Semitic languages is the best-known case.
e: Arabic root k-t-b ‘writing’: kataba ‘he wrote’, kitāb ‘book’, kātib ‘writer’; also English sing → sang.

d: A test that interprets a person's score by comparing it with the scores of other test takers, often reported as a percentile or rank.
e: A student whose score is reported as the 85th percentile did better than 85% of the comparison group.

d: The claim that learners must consciously register (notice) a language feature in the input for it to become intake and be learned. The strong version—that nothing is learned without noticing—is debated, since some research suggests learning can occur without awareness.
e: A learner reading a story notices for the first time that English says depend on, not *depend of (ungrammatical), and starts using on in her own writing.
p: Proposed by Richard Schmidt (1990).
s: Schmidt, R. W. (1990). The role of consciousness in second language learning. Applied Linguistics, 11(2).

d: A word class whose members typically name people, things, places, or ideas and can head noun phrases. In English, most nouns inflect for number, can take the possessive marker 's, and can follow determiners.
e: idea, teacher, Boston, and happiness are nouns; ideas shows plural inflection.

d: A phrase whose head is a noun or pronoun, which can serve as subject, object, or complement in a clause. Some theories instead treat the determiner as the head, calling the unit a determiner phrase (DP).
e: the three tall buildings on Main Street is a noun phrase headed by buildings.

d: The central and obligatory part of a syllable, usually a vowel but sometimes a sonorant consonant. In intonation analysis, the same word (or nuclear syllable) refers to the most prominent syllable of an intonation phrase.
e: The nucleus of sit is /ɪ/; in button [ˈbʌtn̩], the second syllable's nucleus is the syllabic [n̩].

d: A grammatical function, typically a noun phrase, that is a complement of a verb (or preposition). A direct object is usually the entity directly affected by the action, while an indirect object usually denotes a recipient or beneficiary.
e: In She sent her friend a postcard, a postcard is the direct object and her friend the indirect object.

d: The methodological problem that researchers want to study how people speak when they are not being observed, but they can only collect such data by observing them. Sociolinguists try to reduce its effects through techniques such as long-term fieldwork and engaging topics.
e: An interviewer asks a participant whether they were ever in danger of dying, hoping that emotional involvement will lead to more natural, less self-monitored speech.
p: Term coined by William Labov in Sociolinguistic patterns (1972).
s: Labov, W. (1972). Sociolinguistic patterns. University of Pennsylvania Press.

d: A consonant produced with enough obstruction to build up air pressure behind the constriction; the class includes stops, fricatives and affricates. Obstruents may be voiced or voiceless, and many languages contrast the two.
e: /p/, /z/ and /tʃ/ are obstruents; in German, obstruents become voiceless at the end of a word, so Rad 'wheel' is pronounced [ʁaːt].

d: The earliest recorded stage of English, used in England from about the mid-5th century until roughly 1100 (dates vary by source). Brought by Germanic settlers, it had extensive inflection, fairly flexible word order, and a largely Germanic vocabulary, and modern speakers cannot read it without study.
e: The opening of Beowulf: Hwæt! Wē Gār-Dena in geār-dagum… 'Listen! We [have heard] of the Spear-Danes in days of old…'

d: The consonant or consonants that come before the nucleus within a syllable. Some syllables have no onset.
e: The onset of street is /str/; eat has no onset.

d: In the L2 Motivational Self System, the attributes a learner believes they should have in order to meet others’ expectations or avoid negative outcomes. It reflects more external pressures than the ideal L2 self and has often been found to be a weaker predictor of effort.
e: A student studies English mainly because his family and teachers say he must, and he wants to avoid disappointing them.

d: The proposal that producing language, not only understanding it, contributes to acquisition because it makes learners notice gaps in their knowledge, test hypotheses about how the language works, and reflect on language. It was developed partly from findings that French immersion students in Canada understood French well but produced less accurate grammar.
e: While trying to write If I had known, I would have come, a learner realizes she does not know how to form the past conditional and later pays attention to it in reading.
p: Proposed by Merrill Swain (1985); she later described its noticing, hypothesis-testing, and reflective (metalinguistic) functions (1995).
s: Swain, M. (1985). Communicative competence: Some roles of comprehensible input and comprehensible output in its development. In S. M. Gass & C. G. Madden (Eds.), Input in second language acquisition. Newbury House.

d: A child's use of a word for a wider range of things than adults would include, usually based on shared features like shape, size, or function. The opposite error, underextension, is using a word for too narrow a range.
e: Overextension: a child calls every four-legged animal doggie. Underextension: a child uses cat only for the family's own pet cat.

d: Applying a rule or pattern more widely than the target language allows, so that it is used where exceptions should apply. It is usually treated as evidence that the learner has formed a rule, and it is seen in both child L1 and adult L2 development.
e: Producing *childs or *mouses (ungrammatical) by extending the regular English plural -s to irregular nouns.

d: Openly recognized prestige attached to standard or socially dominant varieties, which most people in a community agree are “correct” or “educated.” Speakers often aim for overtly prestigious forms in formal or careful speech.
e: Many British listeners describe Received Pronunciation as sounding “educated” and use more of its features when reading aloud.

d: Describing a consonant produced with the front (body) of the tongue raised toward the hard palate.
e: /j/ in English yes, [ɲ] in Spanish año 'year', and [ç] in German ich 'I' are palatal.

d: The full set of inflected forms of a lexeme, organized by grammatical categories such as person, number, tense, or case.
e: Spanish present tense of hablar: hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan.

d: In psycholinguistics, the mental process of assigning grammatical structure to a sentence as it is heard or read, so that its meaning can be worked out. Models disagree about whether the parser first uses only syntactic information or uses meaning, context, and frequency from the start.
e: In Put the apple on the towel in the box, listeners must decide whether on the towel describes where to put the apple or which apple is meant.

d: The automatic or manual labeling of each token in a text with its word class (such as noun, verb, or adjective), often with finer distinctions like tense or number. Modern taggers are statistical or machine-learning based and are highly accurate on standard written English but less so on speech, learner texts, or less-resourced languages.
e: In They can fish, a tagger must decide whether can is a modal verb and fish a verb (‘they are able to fish’) or can a lexical verb and fish a noun (‘they put fish in cans’).

d: A construction in which the object of a corresponding active clause becomes the subject and the original subject is omitted or expressed in a by-phrase. In English the passive is formed with be (or get) and a past participle.
e: The window was broken (by the children).

d: The thematic role of the participant that is affected by an action, usually undergoing a change of state. Many authors merge patient with theme or use the terms inconsistently.
e: In The storm destroyed the bridge, the bridge is the patient.

d: In writing instruction, an activity in which students read and comment on each other's drafts, usually guided by questions or criteria, to help the writer revise.
e: Using a guide sheet, partners identify each other's thesis statement, mark one paragraph that needs more evidence, and suggest one improvement.

d: A type of semantic change in which a word acquires a more negative or less respectable meaning over time.
e: Old English gesǣlig meant 'happy, blessed', but its descendant silly now means 'foolish'.

d: The study of what non-linguists believe about dialects: where they think dialect boundaries are, which varieties they consider correct or pleasant, and how they describe differences. It treats these folk beliefs as important data.
e: Participants draw on a blank map of the United States where they think “Southern” speech begins and label regions as “correct,” “twangy,” or “fast.”
p: Developed especially by Dennis Preston (1989).
s: Preston, D. R. (1989). Perceptual dialectology: Nonlinguists' views of areal linguistics. Foris.

d: An utterance that does not describe an action but performs it in the act of being said; it cannot be true or false, only successful or unsuccessful. Explicit performatives often contain a performative verb in the first person present tense, sometimes with hereby.
e: I hereby name this ship the Queen Elizabeth; I promise to call you.
p: Introduced by J. L. Austin, who contrasted performatives with 'constatives' (statements) before arguing that the distinction breaks down (Austin, 1962).
s: Austin, J. L. (1962). How to do things with words. Clarendon Press.

d: The effect that an utterance actually has on the listener's thoughts, feelings, or actions, whether intended or not. Unlike the illocutionary act, it depends on how the hearer responds.
e: A warning such as There's a car coming! has the perlocutionary effect of making the listener step back.
p: Distinguished by J. L. Austin (1962).
s: Austin, J. L. (1962). How to do things with words. Clarendon Press.

d: Deictic reference to the participants in the speech event: the speaker (first person), the addressee (second person), and others (third person). It is mostly expressed through pronouns and verb agreement.
e: In I told you about her, I, you, and her point to different people depending on who is talking to whom.

d: The smallest unit of sound in a particular language that can distinguish one word from another. A phoneme is an abstract category that is pronounced through one or more concrete sounds (its allophones); some researchers question whether phonemes are psychologically real units or mainly a descriptive tool.
e: English /p/ and /b/ are separate phonemes because pat /pæt/ and bat /bæt/ are different words.
p: The French term phonème was introduced by A. Dufriche-Desgenettes in the early 1870s simply to mean a speech sound; its modern, more abstract sense developed mainly in the work of Jan Baudouin de Courtenay and Mikołaj Kruszewski of the Kazan school.

d: A way of writing pronunciation that records only the phonemes of a language and leaves out predictable phonetic detail. It is written between slashes and is often equated with broad transcription, although broad transcription can also simply mean a transcription with little detail.
e: pin written phonemically is /pɪn/, without showing that the /p/ is aspirated.

d: A way of writing pronunciation that records the actual sounds produced, including details that are predictable in the language, such as aspiration or nasalization. It is written in square brackets; a very detailed version that uses many diacritics is called narrow transcription.
e: pin written phonetically is [pʰɪ̃n], showing the aspirated [pʰ] and the nasalized vowel before [n].

d: The branch of linguistics that studies speech sounds as physical events: how they are made by the speech organs (articulatory phonetics), how they travel as sound waves (acoustic phonetics), and how listeners hear and identify them (auditory phonetics).
e: Measuring that the vowel in bead is noticeably longer than the vowel in beat in English is a phonetic observation.
s: Ladefoged, P., & Johnson, K. (2015). A course in phonetics (7th ed.). Cengage Learning.

d: In Baddeley and Hitch's model of working memory, the component that briefly holds speech-based information and keeps it active through silent rehearsal. It is thought to play a role in learning new word forms, including vocabulary in a second language.
e: Repeating an unfamiliar phone number or a new foreign word like Schmetterling silently to yourself until you can write it down relies on the phonological loop.
p: Part of the working memory model proposed by Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch (1974), where it was originally called the articulatory loop.
s: Baddeley, A. D., & Hitch, G. (1974). Working memory. In G. H. Bower (Ed.), The psychology of learning and motivation (Vol. 8). Academic Press.

d: A formal statement describing a systematic change in sounds in a particular environment, mapping an underlying form onto its pronunciation; it is often written A → B / C __ D (“A becomes B between C and D”). Constraint-based approaches such as Optimality Theory model the same patterns without ordered rules.
e: A simplified English aspiration rule: a voiceless stop becomes aspirated at the beginning of a stressed syllable (/p/ → [pʰ] in pin).
p: Ordered phonological rules are central to generative phonology as set out by Noam Chomsky and Morris Halle (1968).
s: Chomsky, N., & Halle, M. (1968). The sound pattern of English. Harper & Row.

d: The study of how speech sounds are organized into systems and patterns, in one language or across languages: which sound differences signal meaning, how sounds may combine, and how they change in context. Phonetics looks at sounds as physical events, while phonology treats them as units of a linguistic system, though where exactly the boundary lies is debated.
e: English speakers hear [pʰ] and [p] as “the same sound” /p/, whereas in Thai the two sounds distinguish different words; this difference is a phonological fact about each language.

d: The set of restrictions in a language on which sounds may occur in which positions and which sequences of sounds are allowed. Phonotactic knowledge lets speakers judge whether an invented word sounds like a possible word of their language.
e: English allows /bl/ at the start of a word, so blick is a possible nonword, but not /bn/, so *bnick is not a possible English word (* marks an impossible form).

d: A verb combined with one or more particles (adverbs or prepositions) to form a unit whose meaning is often not predictable from its parts. Some grammars reserve the term for verb + adverb particle and call combinations like look after “prepositional verbs”; phrasal verbs are frequent in informal English and a well-known difficulty for learners.
e: give up (‘stop trying’), look after (‘take care of’), and put up with (‘tolerate’); in turn the light off the particle can move after the object.

d: A constituent built around a head word, which determines the phrase's category and main properties. A phrase may consist of the head alone or the head together with complements, modifiers, and specifiers.
e: very proud of her students is an adjective phrase headed by the adjective proud.

d: A rule that specifies how a category can be expanded into its immediate constituents, such as S → NP VP. A set of such rules generates the possible tree structures of a language.
e: The rules S → NP VP, NP → Det N, and VP → V NP, together with a lexicon supplying the words, generate the dog chased the cat.
p: Phrase structure grammar was formalized for linguistics by Noam Chomsky in Syntactic Structures (1957).
s: Chomsky, N. (1957). Syntactic structures. Mouton.

d: A contact language that develops when groups without a common language need to communicate for limited purposes such as trade, typically with a reduced vocabulary and grammar drawn from the languages involved. A pidgin has no native speakers, but it has its own rules and is not simply “broken” language.
e: Russenorsk, a pidgin combining Russian and Norwegian elements, was used by Russian and Norwegian traders in the Arctic during the 18th and 19th centuries.

d: The perceived highness or lowness of the voice. Its main physical correlate is fundamental frequency (F0), the rate at which the vocal folds vibrate.
e: A rise in pitch at the end of Coffee? marks it as an offer or question rather than a statement.

d: Deictic reference to locations relative to the speaker or other participants. Languages differ in how many distance contrasts they make; English mainly contrasts near and far.
e: this vs. that, here vs. there, and come vs. go in English.

d: The location in the vocal tract where the main constriction for a consonant is made, usually described by which articulators come together (for example, the lips, or the tongue and the roof of the mouth).
e: /p/ (bilabial), /t/ (alveolar) and /k/ (velar) are all voiceless stops; they differ only in place of articulation.

d: A test used to assign learners to the course or level most suitable for them.
e: New students at a language school take a grammar, reading, and listening test, and their scores decide whether they start in Level 2 or Level 4.

d: An individual's integrated and usually uneven competence in several languages and varieties, which are drawn on together rather than kept in separate compartments. In European language policy it is contrasted with multilingualism, which then refers to the presence of several languages in a society.
e: A traveler uses her Spanish to understand Italian signs, asks a question in English, and thanks the shopkeeper in a few words of Italian.
p: Promoted by the Council of Europe, especially in the Common European Framework of Reference (2001).
s: Council of Europe. (2001). Common European Framework of Reference for Languages: Learning, teaching, assessment. Cambridge University Press.

d: An approach that explains linguistic politeness as strategies speakers use to manage face, especially when performing acts that might threaten it. Brown and Levinson's model claimed broad cross-cultural validity, but it has been criticized for reflecting Western, individualist assumptions and has been challenged by later 'discursive' approaches that treat politeness as something participants judge in interaction.
e: Choosing Would you mind lending me your notes? rather than Give me your notes to reduce the imposition on a classmate.
p: Most closely associated with Penelope Brown and Stephen Levinson (1978; reissued 1987); other influential models include those of Robin Lakoff (1973) and Geoffrey Leech (1983).
s: Brown, P., & Levinson, S. C. (1987). Politeness: Some universals in language usage. Cambridge University Press.

d: The situation in which one word has several related meanings that are felt to belong together, often linked through extension such as metaphor or metonymy. Dictionaries usually list polysemous senses under a single entry, but the line between polysemy and homonymy is not always clear.
e: Head can mean a body part, the leader of a group (head of department) or the top of something (head of the table).
s: Lyons, J. (1977). Semantics (Vols. 1–2). Cambridge University Press.

d: A language in which a single word can contain many morphemes, often including several roots, so that one word can express what other languages need a whole sentence for. Definitions vary, and some linguists require features such as noun incorporation.
e: Inuktitut words can express what English needs a whole clause for: tukisinngittunga ‘I don't understand’ = tukisi- ‘understand’ + -nngit- ‘not’ + -tunga ‘I’. Longer Inuktitut words can stack many more suffixes.
p: The term polysynthesis was first used by Peter Stephen Du Ponceau (1819) to describe Indigenous languages of the Americas.

d: Assessment based on a purposeful collection of a learner's work over time, often including drafts, final products, and reflections. It documents growth and process rather than performance on a single occasion, though scoring consistency can be a challenge.
e: At the end of a semester, a writing student submits a portfolio of three revised essays with earlier drafts and a reflective cover letter explaining her revisions.

d: A word that packs the forms and meanings of two words into one; in everyday use it is largely a synonym of "blend." In morphological theory, "portmanteau morph" also refers to a single indivisible morph that expresses two or more morphemes at once.
e: slithy (lithe + slimy) from “Jabberwocky”; French au ‘to the’ (before a masculine singular noun), which fuses à ‘to’ + le ‘the’, is a portmanteau morph.
p: Lewis Carroll first used "portmanteau" for this kind of word in Through the Looking-Glass (1871), where Humpty Dumpty explains words in “Jabberwocky.”

d: Politeness strategies that attend to the hearer's positive face by showing friendliness, approval, solidarity, or common ground.
e: Hey buddy, you're great at this. Could you help me out with my code? (compliments and in-group address).
p: Term from Penelope Brown and Stephen Levinson (1978, 1987).
s: Brown, P., & Levinson, S. C. (1987). Politeness: Some universals in language usage. Cambridge University Press.

d: Transfer that makes learning easier because a feature of the previously known language matches the new language. It often goes unnoticed because it produces correct forms.
e: A German speaker learning English benefits from cognates such as Haus/house and from similar adjective–noun order (das rote Auto / the red car).

d: Describing a consonant produced with the tongue blade against or near the area just behind the alveolar ridge. The English sounds of this type are traditionally called palato-alveolar.
e: /ʃ/ in ship, /ʒ/ in measure, /tʃ/ in chip and /dʒ/ in jam are postalveolar.

d: The argument that the language children hear is too limited, and lacks enough explicit evidence of what is ungrammatical, to explain the complex grammatical knowledge they end up with, so some knowledge must be innate. Critics, especially in usage-based approaches, argue that input is richer and statistical learning more powerful than this argument assumes.
e: Chomsky's classic case: children form questions like Is the man who is tall happy? and do not produce *Is the man who tall is happy? (ungrammatical), even though, he argued, they rarely hear examples that would rule out the second pattern. Critics dispute how rare such evidence actually is.
a: Argument from poverty of the stimulus
p: Associated with Noam Chomsky, who used the phrase "poverty of the stimulus" in Rules and Representations (1980).

d: The linguistic side of pragmatics: the particular forms and strategies a language offers for performing communicative acts, such as the different ways of making a request or softening a refusal.
e: Knowing that English requests can be made with Can you…?, Would you mind…?, or I was wondering if…, and that these differ in politeness.
p: Distinction drawn by Geoffrey Leech (1983) and applied to learners by Jenny Thomas (1983).
s: Leech, G. N. (1983). Principles of pragmatics. Longman.

d: The ability to use language appropriately in social contexts and to understand speakers' intended meanings, including knowing which forms to use for an act like requesting and when they are socially suitable. It is usually treated as one component of communicative competence and is often described as having pragmalinguistic and sociopragmatic sides.
e: A learner who knows that Give me the pen is grammatical but chooses Could I borrow your pen? with a stranger is showing pragmatic competence.
s: Kasper, G., & Rose, K. R. (2002). Pragmatic development in a second language. Blackwell.

d: A failure to understand or convey intended meaning that results from pragmatic rather than grammatical problems. Thomas distinguished pragmalinguistic failure (using the wrong form for an act) from sociopragmatic failure (misjudging social norms).
e: A student who writes to a professor I want you to read my essay by Friday may be seen as rude, even though the sentence is grammatical.
p: Classic account by Jenny Thomas (1983).
s: Thomas, J. (1983). Cross-cultural pragmatic failure. Applied Linguistics, 4(2).

d: The influence of a speaker's knowledge of pragmatics in one language and culture on how they use and understand another. Transfer that leads to appropriate use is called positive transfer; transfer that leads to misunderstanding is negative transfer.
e: A learner translating a polite request form directly from their first language into English, where it may sound too blunt or too formal.
s: Kasper, G. (1992). Pragmatic transfer. Second Language Research, 8(3).

d: The study of how people use language in context and how listeners work out what a speaker means, which is often more than the literal meaning of the words. It covers topics such as speech acts, implicature, deixis, and politeness. Where exactly the boundary between pragmatics and semantics lies is still debated.
e: Literally, It's cold in here describes the temperature, but in context it can work as a request to close the window.
p: The term in its modern sense goes back to Charles Morris (1938), who divided the study of signs into syntactics, semantics, and pragmatics.
s: Levinson, S. C. (1983). Pragmatics. Cambridge University Press.

d: In traditional grammar, the part of a clause that says something about the subject, consisting of the verb and its complements and modifiers. In logic and semantics the term is used more narrowly for an expression such as a verb that takes arguments.
e: In The children played in the park, the predicate is played in the park.

d: In conversation analysis, the observation that some responses to a first pair part are 'preferred' (usually produced quickly and simply, such as accepting an invitation) while others are 'dispreferred' (often delayed, hedged, and accompanied by reasons, such as refusing). 'Preference' here describes structural patterns, not speakers' personal wishes.
e: A: Can you come Saturday? B: Oh, um, well, I'd love to, but I've got to work. (a dispreferred refusal with delay and an account).
p: Developed in conversation analysis by Harvey Sacks and others; Anita Pomerantz's (1984) study of agreement and disagreement is a classic account.
s: Pomerantz, A. (1984). Agreeing and disagreeing with assessments: Some features of preferred/dispreferred turn shapes. In J. M. Atkinson & J. Heritage (Eds.), Structures of social action: Studies in conversation analysis. Cambridge University Press.

d: An affix attached before the base.
e: re- in rewrite, un- in unkind, pre- in preview.

d: A closed-class word that typically expresses relations of space, time, or other connections and takes a noun phrase as its complement. Languages in which these words follow their complement have postpositions instead.
e: in, on, under, during, with; compare Japanese Tōkyō ni 'in/to Tokyo', where ni is a postposition.

d: A phrase headed by a preposition, normally followed by a noun phrase as its complement. Prepositional phrases often function as adjuncts or as complements of verbs, nouns, and adjectives.
e: under the table is a prepositional phrase headed by under.

d: A common lesson structure in which the teacher first presents a language form, learners then practice it in controlled exercises, and finally use it in freer communicative activities. Critics argue that it assumes learners acquire forms in the order and at the pace they are taught.
e: The teacher explains the present perfect with a timeline, students complete gap-fill sentences, and then they interview classmates using Have you ever…?

d: The social value or respect attached to a language, variety, or linguistic feature, which usually reflects the social status of the people who use it rather than any linguistic quality. Sociolinguists distinguish overt prestige from covert prestige.
e: In many countries, a variety associated with educated urban speakers is seen as the “best” way to speak and is used by newsreaders.

d: Background information that a sentence takes for granted as already true or shared. A key test is that presuppositions usually survive when the sentence is negated or turned into a question, which ordinary entailments do not. Whether presupposition is best treated as semantic or pragmatic is debated.
e: Jen stopped smoking and Jen didn't stop smoking both presuppose that Jen used to smoke.
p: Discussed by Gottlob Frege (1892) and brought to prominence by P. F. Strawson (1950) in his critique of Bertrand Russell's theory of descriptions.
s: Strawson, P. F. (1950). On referring. Mind, 59(235), 320–344.

d: A word or construction that typically gives rise to a presupposition. Common triggers include definite descriptions, factive verbs, change-of-state verbs, iteratives like again, and cleft sentences.
e: In Lia regrets leaving, the factive verb regret triggers the presupposition that Lia left.

d: An effect in which earlier exposure to one stimulus (the prime) changes how a later stimulus (the target) is processed, usually making it faster or more accurate. Priming can be based on repetition, form, meaning, or sentence structure, and is widely used to study mental representations.
e: After reading The boy gave the teacher an apple, a speaker becomes more likely to describe a new picture with the same double-object structure (The girl handed the man a book), an instance of structural priming.

d: A generative framework proposing that all languages share universal principles, while variation results from a limited set of parameters with fixed options that learners set on the basis of input. Proposed parameters include head direction (head-initial versus head-final) and whether subjects can be omitted (pro-drop).
e: Under the head-direction parameter, English verbs precede their objects (eat apples), while Japanese verbs follow them (ringo o taberu, 'apples eat').
p: Developed by Noam Chomsky and colleagues, most influentially in Lectures on Government and Binding (1981).
s: Chomsky, N. (1981). Lectures on government and binding. Foris.

d: Speech directed to oneself rather than to others, often quiet and abbreviated, used to plan, guide, or regulate one’s own thinking and actions. In SLA, learners’ private speech, such as repeating or practicing new forms under their breath, is studied as evidence of how they internalize language.
e: After the teacher says We went to the museum, a student quietly repeats went… went… we went to herself before raising her hand.
p: Concept derived from Lev Vygotsky’s work on the relation between thought and language.

d: An approach to teaching writing that treats it as a recursive process of planning, drafting, revising, and editing, with feedback between drafts, rather than focusing only on the final product. Critics such as genre theorists argue that it can neglect the expectations of particular text types.
e: Students brainstorm ideas, write a first draft, get comments in a writing conference and from peers, revise the content, and only then edit for grammar.
p: Grew out of research on how writers compose, notably Janet Emig's The Composing Processes of Twelfth Graders (1971); Vivian Zamel (1982) was an early advocate of the process approach for ESL writing.
s: Zamel, V. (1982). Writing: The process of discovering meaning. TESOL Quarterly, 16(2), 195–209.

d: A theory that seeks to explain developmental sequences by the processing procedures learners can handle: learners are claimed to produce only structures whose grammatical information they are able to process, and to develop these procedures in a fixed hierarchy. It predicts, for example, that agreement within a phrase emerges before agreement across phrases.
e: Learners of English typically mark plural within a phrase (two cats) before they reliably mark subject–verb agreement across the clause (The cat sleeps).
p: Developed by Manfred Pienemann (1998).
s: Pienemann, M. (1998). Language processing and second language development: Processability theory. John Benjamins.

d: Words a person can retrieve and use appropriately when speaking or writing. Producing a word demands more knowledge (spelling, pronunciation, grammar, collocation) than recognizing it, so productive vocabulary usually lags behind receptive vocabulary.
e: A learner who writes The results were reluctantly accepted by the committee shows productive knowledge of reluctantly.

d: The degree to which a morphological process can be used by speakers to create new words. Productivity is a matter of degree, and researchers measure it in different ways, for example by counting new formations in a corpus.
e: English -ness is highly productive and attaches freely to new adjectives, while -th (warmth, growth) is rarely, if ever, used to form new words today.
s: Bauer, L. (2001). Morphological productivity. Cambridge University Press.

d: A test that measures a person's general ability in a language, regardless of any particular course of study, often for admission, employment, or certification.
e: A university uses scores from the TOEFL iBT or IELTS to decide whether international applicants have enough English for academic study.
r: Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR)

d: A word that stands in for a noun phrase or refers to an entity already known from context. English pronouns include personal, possessive, reflexive, demonstrative, interrogative, and relative types, and personal pronouns are marked for case.
e: Maria said she would call me; herself is a reflexive pronoun.

d: The meaning content of a declarative sentence that can be true or false, independent of the particular words or language used to express it. Different sentences can express the same proposition.
e: Snow is white and French La neige est blanche express the same proposition.

d: An umbrella term for the properties of speech that extend beyond individual segments, such as stress, rhythm, intonation, tempo and pausing, and for the way speech is grouped into units such as phrases. Prosody helps signal structure, emphasis and attitude.
e: Stress placement distinguishes a BLACKbird (a species of bird) from a black BIRD (any bird that is black).

d: The reconstructed ancestor of the Indo-European language family, whose branches include Germanic, Romance (Italic), Celtic, Slavic, Greek, and Indo-Iranian. It is thought to have been spoken several thousand years ago, but its homeland and date are still debated (e.g., the Pontic–Caspian steppe hypothesis vs. the Anatolian hypothesis).
e: PIE *ph₂tḗr 'father' is reconstructed from cognates such as Sanskrit pitár-, Greek patḗr, Latin pater, and Gothic fadar.
p: Sir William Jones's 1786 presidential address (the “Third Anniversary Discourse”) to the Asiatic Society in Calcutta, which proposed that Sanskrit, Greek, and Latin, and probably Gothic, Celtic, and Persian, came from a common source that may no longer exist, is often cited as a starting point for Indo-European comparative linguistics.

d: The hypothetical common ancestor of a language family, reconstructed by systematically comparing its descendants. Because most proto-languages were never written down, reconstructed forms are marked with an asterisk (*) to show they are not directly attested.
e: Proto-Germanic *fōts 'foot' is reconstructed as the source of English foot, German Fuß, and Swedish fot.

d: A theory of categorization holding that categories are organized around best or most typical examples (prototypes), with membership a matter of degree rather than a strict set of necessary and sufficient conditions. It challenged the classical view of categories and became central in cognitive semantics.
e: For many English speakers, a robin is judged a better example of bird than a penguin or an ostrich.
p: Developed by psychologist Eleanor Rosch in the 1970s.
s: Rosch, E. (1975). Cognitive representations of semantic categories. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 104(3), 192–233.

d: The study of the mental processes and representations involved in understanding, producing, and acquiring language. It combines methods from linguistics and cognitive psychology, typically using experiments that measure reaction times, errors, or eye movements.
e: A psycholinguist might time how quickly people recognize the word doctor after seeing nurse versus after seeing table.

d: Language production in which learners are required to express themselves more precisely, coherently, or accurately than they normally would. It is argued to stretch learners’ interlanguage by moving them from meaning-based to more grammar-based processing.
e: After a learner says *Yesterday I go park (ungrammatical), the teacher responds Sorry, when?, and the learner reformulates: Yesterday I went to the park.
p: Concept introduced by Merrill Swain in her work on comprehensible output (1985).

d: A field that examines how ideas about race and ideas about language shape each other, for example how speakers from racialized groups may be heard as using deficient language even when they use forms that would count as standard from other speakers. It shifts attention from speakers' supposed language deficits to the perceptions and ideologies of listeners and institutions.
e: A Latinx student's bilingual practices are described as a problem to fix, while a white student's similar use of Spanish is praised as an asset.
p: The notion of raciolinguistic ideologies was introduced by Nelson Flores and Jonathan Rosa (2015); the field was further shaped by H. Samy Alim, John R. Rickford, and Arnetha F. Ball's edited volume Raciolinguistics (2016).
s: Flores, N., & Rosa, J. (2015). Undoing appropriateness: Raciolinguistic ideologies and language diversity in education. Harvard Educational Review, 85(2), 149–171.

d: The mental processes readers use to build meaning from text. Bottom-up processing works from smaller units upward (letters, words, sentences), while top-down processing uses prior knowledge, context, and expectations; most current models are interactive, assuming both operate together.
e: A reader decodes the letters of an unfamiliar word like sextant (bottom-up) but also guesses its meaning from a passage about sailing (top-down).

d: Implicit corrective feedback in which the teacher reformulates all or part of a learner's incorrect utterance in correct form, without saying that an error occurred. Because recasts do not interrupt communication, learners sometimes fail to notice them as corrections.
e: Student: He goed to the store. Teacher: Oh, he went to the store. What did he buy?
p: One of the six feedback types in Roy Lyster and Leila Ranta's (1997) classification, based on teacher–student interaction in primary-level French immersion classrooms in Montreal.

d: Words a person can recognize and understand when listening or reading. Receptive vocabulary is generally larger than productive vocabulary, and many researchers see the two as points on a continuum rather than separate stores.
e: A learner understands reluctant when reading it in a novel but would not think to use it in their own writing.

d: The process of working out unrecorded earlier forms of a language. Comparative reconstruction draws on cognates across related languages, while internal reconstruction uses irregular patterns within a single language; scholars disagree about whether reconstructed forms represent real past speech or are formulas summarizing correspondences.
e: From Sanskrit bhrā́tar-, Latin frāter, and English brother, linguists reconstruct PIE *bʰréh₂tēr 'brother'.

d: The property by which a structure can contain another structure of the same type, allowing, in principle, sentences of unlimited length. It has been proposed as a core feature of the human language faculty, although the claim that all languages show recursion has been challenged (e.g., in debates over the Amazonian language Pirahã).
e: Sam thinks [that Lee knows [that Kim left]] embeds clauses within clauses.
p: Proposed as the core of the narrow language faculty by Marc Hauser, Noam Chomsky, and W. Tecumseh Fitch (2002).
s: Hauser, M. D., Chomsky, N., & Fitch, W. T. (2002). The faculty of language: What is it, who has it, and how did it evolve? Science, 298(5598).

d: A morphological process in which all or part of a base is repeated to express a grammatical or semantic change, such as plurality, intensity, or aspect. It may be full (whole word) or partial (part of the word).
e: Indonesian rumah ‘house’ → rumah-rumah ‘houses’ (full); Tagalog sumulat ‘to write’ → susulat ‘will write’, where the first syllable of the root sulat is copied (partial).

d: The relation between a linguistic expression and the entity, event or situation in the world that it is used to pick out. Many linguists treat reference as something speakers do with expressions in context, rather than a fixed property of words.
e: In My sister lives in Boston, the phrase my sister refers to one particular person, who changes depending on who is speaking.
p: Classic accounts include Gottlob Frege (1892), Bertrand Russell (1905) and P. F. Strawson (1950).

d: A large, usually general corpus used as a benchmark against which a smaller or more specialized corpus is compared. Choosing the reference corpus affects results, because the key words found depend on what the target is compared with.
e: A researcher compares a corpus of student essays with the Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA) to find which words students overuse or underuse.

d: A variety of language defined by its situation of use, such as its purpose, topic, or setting, rather than by who is speaking. Different traditions define register somewhat differently (for example, in terms of field, tenor, and mode in systemic functional linguistics), but all link recurring linguistic features to recurring situations.
e: A doctor writes myocardial infarction in a medical report but says heart attack when talking to a patient.

d: A subordinate clause that modifies a noun, typically introduced by a relative pronoun (who, which) or that, or with no introducing word at all. Restrictive relative clauses identify which referent is meant, while nonrestrictive ones add extra information.
e: In The book that I borrowed is overdue, that I borrowed is a restrictive relative clause modifying book.

d: A cognitive theory of communication which proposes that human cognition tends to seek relevance, and that hearers interpret an utterance by looking for the meaning that gives enough useful effects for the least processing effort. It replaces Grice's set of maxims with principles of relevance (in the 1995 edition, a cognitive and a communicative principle) and remains in debate with neo-Gricean approaches.
e: A: Would you like some coffee? B: Coffee would keep me awake. A must decide, using context, whether B wants to stay awake (yes) or sleep (no).
p: Developed by Dan Sperber and Deirdre Wilson (1986; 2nd ed. 1995).
s: Sperber, D., & Wilson, D. (1986). Relevance: Communication and cognition. Blackwell.

d: The consistency of test scores across occasions, test forms, items, or raters. A test cannot support valid interpretations if its results are not reasonably consistent, but a reliable test is not necessarily valid.
e: If a student takes the same vocabulary test twice in one week with no studying and scores 82 and then 51, the test has low reliability.

d: The ways speakers deal with problems in speaking, hearing, or understanding during conversation. Repair can be started by the speaker of the trouble (self-initiated) or by someone else (other-initiated), and conversation analysts have found a general preference for self-repair.
e: Self-repair: I saw him on Tuesday, I mean Wednesday. Other-initiated: A: She's at the clinic. B: The what?
p: Classic account by Emanuel Schegloff, Gail Jefferson, and Harvey Sacks (1977).
s: Schegloff, E. A., Jefferson, G., & Sacks, H. (1977). The preference for self-correction in the organization of repair in conversation. Language, 53(2).

d: Corrective feedback in which the teacher repeats the learner's incorrect utterance, usually with rising intonation or stress on the error, to draw attention to it.
e: Student: I am agree. Teacher: I am agree? (with rising intonation)
p: One of the six feedback types in Roy Lyster and Leila Ranta's (1997) classification, based on teacher–student interaction in primary-level French immersion classrooms in Montreal.

d: The part of a syllable made up of the nucleus and the coda. The rhyme matters for stress and syllable weight, and it is also the part of words that rhymes in poetry.
e: In cat /kæt/ the rhyme is /æt/, which it shares with hat and mat.

d: The core morpheme of a word that carries its main lexical meaning and cannot be analyzed further into smaller morphemes. A root remains after all affixes have been removed.
e: act is the root of reactivation (re- + act + -iv(e) + -ate + -ion).

d: A scoring guide that lists the criteria for evaluating a performance and describes what different levels of quality look like for each criterion.
e: An essay rubric with four criteria (content, organization, language use, mechanics), each scored from 1 to 4 with a description for each level.

d: Temporary, adjustable support that a more skilled person (or peer) gives a learner so that the learner can complete a task they could not yet manage alone; the support is gradually withdrawn as the learner becomes more capable. The term is widely used but sometimes criticized when applied to any kind of help, regardless of whether it adapts to the learner.
e: A teacher first gives a sentence frame (I think ___ because ___), then just the word because, and finally no prompt as students learn to justify opinions.
p: Term introduced by David Wood, Jerome Bruner, and Gail Ross (1976).
s: Wood, D., Bruner, J. S., & Ross, G. (1976). The role of tutoring in problem solving. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 17(2).

d: A conversational implicature that arises when a speaker uses a weaker term from a scale of informativeness (for example the scale some, most, all, ordered from weaker to stronger), leading the listener to infer that the stronger terms do not apply. Such ordered sets are often called Horn scales.
e: The movie was good often implies 'not excellent'; Sam or Kim will come often implies 'not both'.
p: Such scales are named after Laurence Horn, whose highly influential work on scalar implicature began with his 1972 UCLA dissertation, On the semantic properties of logical operators in English.
s: Horn, L. R. (1989). A natural history of negation. University of Chicago Press.

d: The mid central vowel [ə], produced with the tongue in a relaxed, neutral position. In English it is the most frequent vowel and occurs almost only in unstressed syllables; its name comes from a vowel sign in Hebrew grammar.
e: The first and last vowels of banana (American /bəˈnænə/, British /bəˈnɑːnə/) and the first vowel of about /əˈbaʊt/ are schwa.

d: Ambiguity that arises when a sentence contains two or more logical operators, such as quantifiers or negation, and it is unclear which one takes wider scope.
e: Every student read a book can mean each student read some book (possibly different ones) or there is one particular book that every student read.

d: Any language learned after the first language has begun to be established. Some writers distinguish a second language (used in the surrounding community) from a foreign language (learned mainly in class where it is not widely spoken), but in SLA research “L2” often covers both.
e: English is an L2 for a Brazilian engineer who started learning it at age 12; for a Korean student learning French in Seoul, French is often called a foreign language but is still an L2 in research terms.

d: The process by which people learn any language after their first, whether in a classroom or through everyday exposure, and also the academic field that studies this process. In this field, “second” usually covers any additional language (third, fourth, and so on), not only the second one learned.
e: A Vietnamese-speaking adult who moves to Boston and gradually becomes able to follow English conversations at work is undergoing SLA; a researcher who records and analyzes her developing English is doing SLA research.

d: A single consonant or vowel treated as a discrete unit in the analysis of speech. Because speech is physically continuous and neighboring sounds overlap, dividing it into segments is an analytical simplification.
e: cat /kæt/ consists of three segments: /k/, /æ/ and /t/.

d: Self-assessment asks learners to judge their own work or ability, and peer assessment asks them to judge classmates' work, usually against shared criteria. Both are used to develop learner autonomy and awareness of quality, although their accuracy as scores varies.
e: Students rate their own oral presentation with a checklist, then a partner rates it with the same checklist, and they compare their judgments.

d: A general theory of human motivation, applied to L2 learning, which distinguishes intrinsic motivation (doing something for its own enjoyment) from several kinds of extrinsic motivation that range from externally controlled to self-endorsed. It proposes that motivation thrives when people’s needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness are met.
e: A learner who reads Japanese manga for fun is intrinsically motivated; one who studies only to avoid a parent’s criticism shows externally regulated motivation.
p: Developed by psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan; applied to L2 learning notably by Kimberly Noels and colleagues (2000).
s: Deci, E. L., & Ryan, R. M. (1985). Intrinsic motivation and self-determination in human behavior. Plenum.

d: The oddness of an expression that is grammatically well-formed but whose word meanings clash, so it cannot be interpreted literally. Such expressions may still be understood figuratively or in fiction.
e: Colorless green ideas sleep furiously is grammatical but semantically anomalous: ideas cannot literally be green or sleep.

d: Change in the meaning of a word over time. Common types include broadening, narrowing, amelioration, and pejoration, along with shifts based on metaphor and metonymy.
e: Nice goes back (via French) to Latin nescius 'ignorant'; in Middle English it often meant 'foolish', and only later came to mean 'pleasant'.

d: A basic component of meaning, usually written in small capitals or brackets with a plus or minus value, used to describe and compare the meanings of words. Some theories go further and treat a small set of such components as universal semantic primitives, a stronger and more contested claim.
e: [±ANIMATE] distinguishes dog (+ANIMATE) from rock (−ANIMATE).

d: A set of words that share a general area of meaning and divide that area up among themselves, so the meaning of each word depends partly on the others in the set. Languages can divide the same field in different ways.
e: Color terms form a semantic field: some languages have one basic term covering both green and blue, while English has two.
p: Field theory is most closely associated with Jost Trier (1931), building on earlier German work.

d: A type of priming in which a word is processed faster when it follows a word related in meaning. It is often taken as evidence that words in the mental lexicon are linked by meaning, with activation spreading between related entries.
e: People decide that butter is a real word faster when it follows bread than when it follows nurse.
p: Demonstrated in an early, influential lexical decision experiment by David E. Meyer and Roger W. Schvaneveldt (1971).
s: Meyer, D. E., & Schvaneveldt, R. W. (1971). Facilitation in recognizing pairs of words: Evidence of a dependence between retrieval operations. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 90(2).

d: A positive or negative evaluative meaning that a word picks up from the words it habitually occurs with, often without being part of its dictionary definition. The concept is debated: some scholars treat it as a feature of a whole extended unit of meaning, others argue “semantic preference” or “evaluative prosody” are clearer labels.
e: The phrasal verb set in mostly occurs with unpleasant subjects (rot, decay, bad weather), so Happiness set in sounds odd or ironic.
p: Popularized by Bill Louw (1993), who credited the idea to John Sinclair; Sinclair's corpus work on units of meaning (e.g., set in) supplied the classic examples.
s: Louw, B. (1993). Irony in the text or insincerity in the writer? The diagnostic potential of semantic prosodies. In M. Baker, G. Francis, & E. Tognini-Bonelli (Eds.), Text and technology: In honour of John Sinclair (pp. 157–176). John Benjamins.

d: The branch of linguistics that studies meaning: what words, phrases and sentences mean, and how those meanings relate to each other and to the world. It is usually distinguished from pragmatics, which deals with meaning that depends on context and speaker intention, although where the boundary lies is debated.
e: Semantics explains why The cat is on the mat and The mat is under the cat describe the same situation.
s: Lyons, J. (1977). Semantics (Vols. 1–2). Cambridge University Press.

d: A diagram showing meaning as a three-way relation between a linguistic form (a word or symbol), a concept or thought, and a referent in the world. Its main point is that words connect to things only indirectly, through the minds of language users.
