e: The word tree evokes the concept TREE, which in turn relates to actual trees; the word itself has no direct link to them.
p: Popularized by C. K. Ogden and I. A. Richards (1923); similar three-way models go back much earlier, as far as Aristotle.
s: Ogden, C. K., & Richards, I. A. (1923). The meaning of meaning. Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner.

d: The meaning an expression has as part of the language system, independent of any particular situation: the concept or mode of presentation it expresses, and its place in the network of meaning relations with other expressions. Sense is contrasted with reference, the thing in the world an expression picks out on a given occasion.
e: The morning star and the evening star have different senses but refer to the same object, the planet Venus.
p: The sense–reference distinction was introduced by Gottlob Frege (1892) as Sinn and Bedeutung.
s: Frege, G. (1892). Über Sinn und Bedeutung. Zeitschrift für Philosophie und philosophische Kritik, 100(1), 25–50.

d: The meaning relations that hold between words or expressions within a language, such as synonymy, antonymy, hyponymy and meronymy. On a structuralist view, part of a word's sense is its position in this network.
e: Rose is a hyponym of flower, an antonym-like contrast holds between hot and cold, and petal is a meronym of flower.
s: Cruse, D. A. (1986). Lexical semantics. Cambridge University Press.

d: A classification of sentences by their grammatical form, usually declarative, interrogative, imperative, and exclamative. Form and function do not always match: an interrogative such as Can you pass the salt? is often used as a request.
e: Declarative: You are ready. Interrogative: Are you ready? Imperative: Get ready. Exclamative: How ready you are!

d: An approach to teaching grade-level content to students who are still learning the language of instruction, making the content comprehensible through visuals, adapted speech, hands-on activities, and explicit language support. The best-known model is the Sheltered Instruction Observation Protocol (SIOP), which organizes lesson planning and observation around eight components.
e: A middle-school science teacher posts both content and language objectives, pre-teaches the words evaporate and condense, and uses a diagram and demonstration of the water cycle.
p: The SIOP Model was developed by Jana Echevarría, MaryEllen Vogt, and Deborah J. Short (2000).
s: Echevarría, J., Vogt, M., & Short, D. J. (2000). Making content comprehensible for English language learners: The SIOP model. Allyn & Bacon.
a: Specially designed academic instruction in English (SDAIE)

d: An initial stage in which some L2 learners, especially young children in a new language environment, say little or nothing in the new language while they listen and build comprehension. Its length varies widely, and not all learners go through one; researchers debate whether it reflects learning, anxiety, or social factors.
e: A five-year-old newly arrived from Syria sits quietly in an English-medium kindergarten for several weeks, following routines and pointing, before producing first phrases like my turn.

d: An approach that treats L2 learning like learning other complex skills: knowledge begins as declarative (knowing that) and, through practice, becomes procedural (knowing how) and then automatic. It is associated with the strong-interface view and with research on practice in language learning.
e: A learner first consciously recalls the rule for forming English questions with do, then, after much practice, produces Do you live here? quickly without thinking about it.

d: An unintended error in spontaneous speech, such as swapping, anticipating, or substituting sounds, morphemes, or words. Because these errors follow regular patterns, they are used as evidence about the units and stages of speech production.
e: Saying a lack of pies instead of a pack of lies swaps the initial consonants /p/ and /l/; such swaps are sometimes called spoonerisms.
p: Victoria Fromkin (1971) influentially argued that speech errors provide evidence for linguistic units.
s: Fromkin, V. A. (1971). The non-anomalous nature of anomalous utterances. Language, 47(1).

d: The encoding in language of social relationships between speakers, addressees, or people referred to, such as relative status or intimacy. It is often seen in honorifics and in choices between pronouns or forms of address.
e: French tu (familiar) vs. vous (formal) for 'you'; English Dr. Smith vs. Jane.

d: The web of relationships a person has with others. Dense networks (where everyone knows everyone) and multiplex networks (where people are linked in several ways, such as kin, neighbors, and coworkers) tend to reinforce local linguistic norms, while loose networks make change easier.
e: In working-class Belfast, speakers whose friends, relatives, and coworkers all lived in the same neighborhood used more local vernacular forms than speakers with looser ties.
p: Introduced into sociolinguistics by Lesley Milroy (1980) through her Belfast research.
s: Milroy, L. (1980). Language and social networks. Basil Blackwell.

d: A model of L2 learning that links attitudes toward the language community and learning situation, integrativeness, and motivation to achievement, while also including aptitude and anxiety. It dominated L2 motivation research for decades and was tested with questionnaires such as the Attitude/Motivation Test Battery (AMTB).
e: A researcher gives secondary-school French learners in Ontario a questionnaire on attitudes toward French Canadians and correlates the scores with course grades.
p: Developed by Robert Gardner, building on his work with Wallace Lambert.
s: Gardner, R. C. (1985). Social psychology and second language learning: The role of attitudes and motivation. Edward Arnold.

d: An approach rooted in the work of the Soviet psychologist Lev Vygotsky which holds that human thinking, including language learning, develops through social interaction and is mediated by cultural tools, especially language. In SLA it treats learning as something that happens first between people and is later internalized by the individual.
e: Two learners jointly reconstruct a text, discussing which verb tense to use; a sociocultural researcher studies how their talk enables each learner to do what neither could do alone.
p: Based on the work of Lev Vygotsky; developed for SLA especially by James Lantolf and colleagues.
s: Lantolf, J. P., & Thorne, S. L. (2006). Sociocultural theory and the genesis of second language development. Oxford University Press.

d: A variety associated with a particular social group, most often a social class, rather than with a region. Sociolects show that people from the same place may speak differently depending on their social position.
e: In New York City in the 1960s, r-less pronunciations such as fourth floor [fɔːθ flɔː] were more common among working-class speakers than among upper-middle-class speakers.

d: The study of the relationship between language and society: how language use varies with social factors such as region, class, ethnicity, gender, age, and situation, and how people use language to express identity, build relationships, and negotiate power. Some scholars separate sociolinguistics (which focuses on language) from the sociology of language (which focuses on society), but the two overlap heavily.
e: A researcher records speakers of different ages in one city to see whether younger people say walkin' instead of walking more often than older people.

d: The social side of pragmatics: the cultural norms and social judgments that shape what is appropriate to say, to whom, and when, such as views about status, distance, and what counts as an imposition.
e: Knowing whether it is acceptable in a given culture to ask a new acquaintance about their salary.
p: Distinction drawn by Geoffrey Leech (1983) and applied to learners by Jenny Thomas (1983).
s: Leech, G. N. (1983). Principles of pragmatics. Longman.

d: A sound produced with relatively free airflow and no build-up of air pressure; the class includes vowels, nasals, liquids and glides. Sonorants are typically voiced.
e: /m/, /l/, /w/ and all vowels are sonorants; English sonorant consonants can even form a syllable on their own, as in button [ˈbʌtn̩].

d: The relative loudness or resonance of a sound compared with others. Sounds are often ranked on a sonority scale from most to least sonorous: vowels, glides, liquids, nasals, fricatives, stops; the exact ranking and its physical basis are debated.
e: In plant /plænt/, sonority rises from /p/ to /l/ to the vowel /æ/ and then falls through /n/ to /t/.

d: The proposal that within a syllable, sonority rises from the onset to the nucleus and falls from the nucleus to the coda. It captures a strong cross-linguistic tendency but has well-known exceptions, such as clusters of /s/ followed by a stop.
e: blink fits the principle (rising /b/–/l/–vowel, falling /ŋ/–/k/), whereas stay /steɪ/ is an exception, since /s/ is more sonorous than the following /t/.
p: The idea goes back to Eduard Sievers and Otto Jespersen (late 19th and early 20th centuries) and was developed in modern phonology by, among others, Elisabeth Selkirk (1984) and G. N. Clements (1990).
s: Clements, G. N. (1990). The role of the sonority cycle in core syllabification. In J. Kingston & M. E. Beckman (Eds.), Papers in laboratory phonology I: Between the grammar and physics of speech. Cambridge University Press.

d: A change in how the sounds of a language are pronounced over time, for example when a sound is lost, merges with another, or changes in a particular environment. The 19th-century Neogrammarians argued that sound changes apply regularly, without exceptions, wherever their conditions are met; later work on lexical diffusion showed that some changes spread gradually from word to word.
e: Word-initial /k/ before /n/ was lost in English, so knee and knight, once pronounced with [kn-], now begin with /n/.

d: A regular, repeated match between sounds in the same positions in words of related languages. Systematic correspondences, rather than random similarities, are the main evidence that languages share an ancestor, and they guide reconstruction.
e: Word-initial Latin /p/ regularly matches English /f/: pater–father, pēs (stem ped-)–foot, piscis–fish.

d: In X-bar theory, the position at the edge of a phrase that combines with the intermediate projection (X′) to form the full phrase (XP). What occupies this position depends on the phrase and the version of the theory, e.g., determiners or possessors in older analyses of noun phrases, and subjects in analyses of clauses.
e: In older X-bar analyses of the picture of Mary, the occupies the specifier of the noun phrase headed by picture.

d: An utterance seen as an action that the speaker performs, such as promising, requesting, apologizing, or warning. Speech act theory holds that saying something is often also doing something.
e: Saying I'm sorry I was late performs the act of apologizing.
p: Introduced by the philosopher J. L. Austin (lectures of 1955, published 1962) and systematized by John Searle (1969).
s: Austin, J. L. (1962). How to do things with words. Clarendon Press.

d: A group of people who share ways of using language and norms for interpreting and evaluating it. Definitions differ: some stress regular interaction among members, while Labov stressed shared evaluations of variation, even when actual usage differs.
e: New Yorkers in Labov's study used different amounts of /r/ but agreed that pronouncing /r/ sounded more prestigious, so they formed one speech community in his sense.

d: The processes by which listeners turn a continuous, highly variable acoustic signal into recognizable speech sounds, words, and meanings. A central puzzle is how listeners cope with variation across speakers, speaking rates, and surrounding sounds.
e: Listeners hear the /d/ in dee and doo as the same sound even though its acoustic form differs depending on the following vowel.

d: The processes by which a speaker turns an intended message into spoken words, typically modeled as stages of conceptualizing the message, formulating it (choosing words and grammar, then sound forms), and articulating it. Evidence comes from speech errors, pauses, and picture-naming experiments.
e: To describe a picture, a speaker must select the concept DOG, retrieve the word dog, assemble its sounds (/dɒɡ/ in British or /dɔɡ/ in many American accents), and move the articulators.
p: The best-known stage model is Willem Levelt's (1989).
s: Levelt, W. J. M. (1989). Speaking: From intention to articulation. MIT Press.

d: The pattern of timing of stressed and unstressed syllables in speech. Languages were traditionally classified as stress-timed (stresses at roughly equal intervals, as claimed for English) or syllable-timed (syllables of roughly equal length, as claimed for French or Spanish), but measurements have not confirmed strict equal timing, and many researchers now treat rhythm as a continuum.
e: In English, CATS chase MICE and the CATS have been CHAsing the MICE are often said to take a similar amount of time because unstressed syllables are compressed, though acoustic studies show this is only a tendency.
p: The stress-timed / syllable-timed distinction was first set out in this form by Kenneth Pike (1945) and generalized as a claim about all languages by David Abercrombie (1967).
s: Abercrombie, D. (1967). Elements of general phonetics. Edinburgh University Press.

d: The ways speakers and writers express their attitudes, feelings, judgments, or degree of certainty about what they say, and position themselves in relation to others. Stance can be expressed through words (unfortunately, clearly), grammar (modal verbs), and other choices.
e: This argument is clearly flawed (strong certainty) vs. This argument might be flawed (tentative).
p: Influential early corpus study by Douglas Biber and Edward Finegan (1989); later developed for academic writing by Ken Hyland (2005), among others. John Du Bois’s (2007) “stance triangle” models stancetaking as an interactional act of evaluating an object, positioning oneself, and aligning with others.
s: Biber, D., & Finegan, E. (1989). Styles of stance in English: Lexical and grammatical marking of evidentiality and affect. Text, 9(1).

d: A variety that has been codified in dictionaries, grammars, and style guides and is used in education, government, publishing, and the media, where it is widely seen as “correct.” Linguists stress that a standard gains its status through social and historical processes, not because it is linguistically superior to other varieties.
e: Standard Written English as used in academic journals, with spellings and usage set out in reference works such as dictionaries and style manuals.

d: The belief that there is a single, uniform, correct form of a language, usually based on the speech of powerful groups, and that other varieties are deficient. This belief can be used to justify discrimination against speakers of nonstandard varieties and accents.
e: A qualified job applicant is rejected because the interviewer feels her accent “doesn't sound professional.”
p: The term was defined influentially by Rosina Lippi-Green (1997) in her analysis of accent discrimination in the United States, building on James and Lesley Milroy's earlier work on the ideology of standardization.
s: Lippi-Green, R. (1997). English with an accent: Language, ideology, and discrimination in the United States. Routledge.

d: Language planning that concerns the social functions and official standing of a language, such as choosing national or official languages or deciding which languages are used in courts, schools, and government.
e: South Africa's 1996 Constitution originally recognized eleven official languages.
p: The distinction between status and corpus planning is credited to Heinz Kloss (1969).
s: Kloss, H. (1969). Research possibilities on group bilingualism: A report. International Center for Research on Bilingualism.

d: The part of a word to which inflectional affixes are attached; it may be a bare root or a root with derivational affixes. Usage varies between authors, and some use "stem" and "base" almost interchangeably.
e: In teachers, the stem is teacher (root teach + derivational -er), to which the plural -s is added.

d: A consonant produced by completely blocking the airflow in the mouth, letting pressure build up, and then releasing it. Plosive usually refers specifically to oral stops released with a burst; some phoneticians also count nasals as stops because the mouth is closed.
e: /p/, /b/, /t/, /d/, /k/ and /ɡ/ in pea, bee, tea, D, key and ghee are English stops.

d: The relative prominence of a syllable compared with neighboring syllables, signaled by combinations of greater length, loudness, pitch movement and full vowel quality. Linguists distinguish word (lexical) stress, which belongs to individual words, from sentence stress, which highlights words within an utterance.
e: In American English, record as a noun is stressed on the first syllable, /ˈrɛkɚd/, but as a verb on the second, /rɪˈkɔrd/ (British /ˈrekɔːd/ and /rɪˈkɔːd/).

d: Ambiguity that arises because a sentence or phrase can be assigned more than one syntactic structure, even though each word has one meaning. Each reading corresponds to a different tree or grouping of constituents.
e: I saw the man with the telescope: either I used the telescope, or the man had it, depending on whether with the telescope attaches to the verb phrase or the noun phrase.

d: Variation within one speaker's language as they move between situations, audiences, or identities, often described on a scale from casual to formal. Researchers disagree on what drives style: attention paid to speech (Labov), the audience being addressed (Bell), or speakers' active self-presentation.
e: A student says I'm gonna grab food to friends but I am going to get something to eat in a job interview.

d: A grammatical function, typically a noun phrase, that in English usually comes before the verb, agrees with the finite verb, and takes nominative case if it is a pronoun. The subject is often, but not always, the doer of the action; in passives and with some verbs it is not.
e: In The letters were delivered, the letters is the subject even though it does not perform the action.

d: A clause that is embedded within another clause and depends on it, often introduced by a subordinating conjunction, a complementizer, or a relative pronoun. Subordinate clauses can function as complements, modifiers of nouns, or adverbials.
e: In She said that she was busy, that she was busy is a subordinate clause functioning as the object of said.

d: A situation in which learning a second language (usually a socially dominant one) leads to the gradual loss or replacement of the first language. It often occurs among minority-language speakers whose L1 receives little support at school or in society.
e: A child of Haitian Creole-speaking parents attends English-only schools in Boston and, by adolescence, understands but no longer speaks Haitian Creole.
p: Terms commonly attributed to Wallace Lambert (1975).

d: An affix attached after the base. English uses suffixes for all of its inflection and for much of its derivation.
e: -ed in walked (inflectional) and -ment in government (derivational).

d: Assessment at the end of a unit, course, or program to judge and report how much learners have achieved, often for grades or certification. The same test can serve formative and summative purposes depending on how the results are used.
e: A final exam that determines whether students pass an intermediate Spanish course is summative.

d: A term for the complex diversity created by recent migration, where people differ not only in national origin and language but also in migration status, length of stay, religion, and social networks. Sociolinguists use it to study mobile and mixed language practices, though some critics argue that such diversity is not entirely new.
e: A London neighborhood where residents from dozens of countries, with different legal statuses and languages, share schools, shops, and social media groups.
p: Coined by the social scientist Steven Vertovec, who developed it in a 2007 article.
s: Vertovec, S. (2007). Super-diversity and its implications. Ethnic and Racial Studies, 30(6), 1024–1054.

d: The use of a completely different, unrelated form to fill a cell in a word's paradigm instead of the expected regular form.
e: go → went; good → better → best.

d: A feature of speech that spreads over more than one segment, such as stress, tone, intonation or length. The term overlaps heavily with prosody, and many writers use the two interchangeably.
e: The noun INsult and the verb inSULT contain the same segments; they differ only in the suprasegmental feature of stress.

d: In transformational grammar, the level of syntactic representation that results after transformations have applied to the deep structure, closer to the sentence as actually pronounced. Later generative models replaced it or reconceived it (e.g., as S-structure, then eliminated in Minimalism).
e: What did you buy? has what at the front in surface structure, though it is interpreted as the object of buy.
p: Introduced in this form by Noam Chomsky in Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (1965).
s: Chomsky, N. (1965). Aspects of the theory of syntax. MIT Press.
a: S-structure (later term in Government and Binding theory)

d: A consonant, usually a sonorant, that forms the nucleus of a syllable without a vowel. In IPA it is marked with a small vertical line under the symbol.
e: In British English, button [ˈbʌtn̩] and bottle [ˈbɒtl̩] end in syllabic consonants; Czech vlk 'wolf' has syllabic [l] as its only nucleus.

d: A unit of sound organization that is usually built around a vowel (the nucleus), with optional consonants before and after it. Speakers count syllables easily, but there is no generally agreed phonetic definition, and where syllable boundaries fall is sometimes debated.
e: banana has three syllables (ba.na.na), while strengths has only one.

d: A plan that specifies what will be taught in a language course and in what order. Common types include structural (grammar-based), notional-functional (based on meanings and functions such as requesting or apologizing), situational, topic-based, skills-based, and task-based syllabuses. Wilkins distinguished synthetic syllabuses, which present language piece by piece, from analytic ones, which present whole chunks of language use.
e: A notional-functional syllabus might have units titled Making requests, Giving advice, and Expressing agreement, whereas a structural one would have units such as Present simple and Modal verbs.
p: The synthetic/analytic distinction comes from David Wilkins (1976).
s: Wilkins, D. A. (1976). Notional syllabuses. Oxford University Press.

d: The relation between words or expressions that have the same or nearly the same meaning. Most linguists argue that complete synonymy (identical in every context, register and connotation) is very rare, so most synonyms are near-synonyms.
e: Big and large are near-synonyms, but my big sister cannot be replaced by my large sister with the same meaning.
s: Cruse, D. A. (1986). Lexical semantics. Cambridge University Press.

d: The study of how words combine into phrases, clauses, and sentences, and of the rules or principles that govern those combinations in a language. The term also refers to that system of sentence structure itself.
e: English syntax allows The dog chased the cat but not *Dog the cat the chased (ungrammatical).

d: A language that expresses grammatical relations largely through morphology within words (affixes, stem changes) rather than through separate words and word order. Agglutinative, fusional, and polysynthetic languages are all synthetic to different degrees.
e: Latin amābō ‘I will love’ expresses in one word what English expresses with three.

d: A theory of language that treats grammar as a set of choices for making meaning in social contexts, organized around three metafunctions: ideational (representing experience), interpersonal (enacting relationships), and textual (organizing the message). It is widely used in education, discourse analysis, and genre-based writing pedagogy.
e: SFL analyzes The committee rejected the proposal as an Actor (the committee) + material Process (rejected) + Goal (the proposal).
p: Developed by M. A. K. Halliday from the 1960s onward.
s: Halliday, M. A. K. (1985). An introduction to functional grammar. Edward Arnold.

d: A consonant produced by a single, very brief contact of the tongue against the roof of the mouth. Some phoneticians distinguish taps from flaps by the direction of the tongue movement, but the two terms are often used interchangeably.
e: The middle consonant of American English water [ˈwɑɾɚ] is a tap; Spanish contrasts the tap in pero 'but' [ˈpeɾo] with the trill in perro 'dog' [ˈpero].

d: In language teaching, an activity in which learners use language mainly to achieve a non-linguistic outcome, with meaning as the primary focus. Definitions vary, but most require a gap of some kind, learners' own linguistic resources, and a result that can be checked. Some writers separate real-world tasks from pedagogical tasks.
e: Pairs compare two nearly identical pictures without showing them to each other and must find six differences. Success is judged by the differences found, not by grammatical accuracy.

d: An approach in which the main unit of teaching is the task: a meaning-focused activity with a clear communicative outcome. Language forms are addressed mainly as they arise while learners carry out tasks. Supporters see it as consistent with SLA research, while critics question its fit with exam-driven and low-proficiency contexts.
e: A class first watches a teacher plan a party (pre-task), then groups plan their own party within a budget (task), and finally report their plans and look at useful language (post-task).
p: Early proposals include N. S. Prabhu's Bangalore Project in South India (1979–1984), reported in Prabhu (1987), and Michael H. Long's (1985) case for task-based teaching.
s: Prabhu, N. S. (1987). Second language pedagogy. Oxford University Press.

d: The proposal that instruction can help learners only with structures they are developmentally ready for, that is, structures at or just beyond their current stage. Teaching a structure too far ahead of the learner’s stage is predicted to have little effect on spontaneous use.
e: A learner who already fronts question words but does not yet invert (*Where you are going?, ungrammatical) may benefit from instruction on inversion (Where are you going?), the next stage, but is predicted to gain little from instruction on later-stage structures such as indirect questions (I wonder where you are going).
p: Proposed by Manfred Pienemann (1984); later grounded in his Processability Theory.
s: Pienemann, M. (1984). Psychological constraints on the teachability of languages. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 6(2), 186–214.

d: Early child speech, typically from around age two, in which content words are combined while function words and grammatical endings are mostly left out, resembling the compressed style of old telegrams. The pattern is clearest in children learning languages like English; children learning richly inflected languages often use some inflections quite early.
e: A child says Daddy go work for 'Daddy is going to work' or Mommy shoe for 'That is Mommy's shoe.'
s: Brown, R. (1973). A first language: The early stages. Harvard University Press.

d: A grammatical category that locates a situation in time, usually relative to the moment of speaking, and is marked on the verb. Many linguists argue that English has only two inflectional tenses, past and present, with future time expressed by modals and other constructions.
e: walks (present) versus walked (past); will walk expresses future time with a modal.

d: A distinction between two sets of vowels in English and related languages: tense vowels are typically longer and more peripheral in the vowel space, and lax vowels shorter and more central. The idea that tense vowels involve more muscular tension is disputed, so the classes are often defined by their distribution instead, for example, lax vowels do not end a stressed word-final syllable.
e: Tense /i/ in beat contrasts with lax /ɪ/ in bit; a pronunciation such as *[bɪ] is not a possible English word.

d: The professional field of teaching English to people whose first language is not English, together with the research and teacher education that support it. The acronym also names TESOL International Association, the main professional organization for the field.
e: A graduate student taking courses in second language acquisition, materials design, and assessment to work as an English teacher for adult immigrants is preparing for a career in TESOL.
a: Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages

d: The semantic role that a participant plays in the event or state described by a verb, such as the one who acts, the one affected, or the one who perceives. There is no agreed-upon list of roles, and some researchers argue that roles are clusters of properties rather than fixed categories.
e: In Ana opened the door with a key, Ana is the agent, the door the patient/theme and a key the instrument.
p: Developed in generative linguistics by Jeffrey Gruber (1965) as "thematic relations" and by Charles Fillmore (1968) as "deep cases"; David Dowty (1991) later proposed proto-roles.
s: Fillmore, C. J. (1968). The case for case. In E. Bach & R. T. Harms (Eds.), Universals in linguistic theory (pp. 1–88). Holt, Rinehart and Winston.

d: The thematic role of the participant that is moved, located, or whose state or location is described, without necessarily being changed by the action. Some frameworks do not distinguish theme from patient.
e: In Tom passed the salt to Kim, the salt is the theme (with Kim as the goal or recipient).
p: The notion of theme as a thematic relation is associated with Jeffrey Gruber (1965).

d: A way of analyzing the clause as a message: the theme is the starting point of the clause (what it is about, or where it begins), and the rheme is the rest, which develops it. Definitions differ between the Prague School, which links theme to given information, and Halliday's systemic functional linguistics, which defines theme by first position in the clause.
e: In Yesterday, my brother bought a car, Yesterday is the theme in Halliday's analysis and my brother bought a car is the rheme.
p: Associated with the Prague School, especially Vilém Mathesius, and later with M. A. K. Halliday in systemic functional linguistics.

d: A model that describes the spread of English in three concentric circles: the Inner Circle, where English is the main native language; the Outer Circle, where English has official or institutional roles after colonial history; and the Expanding Circle, where English is learned mainly as a foreign language. Critics note that it classifies by nation and overlooks variation within countries and the growth of English as a lingua franca.
e: The United States and the United Kingdom (Inner Circle); India, Nigeria, and Singapore (Outer Circle); China, Brazil, and Japan (Expanding Circle).
p: Proposed by Braj B. Kachru (1985).
s: Kachru, B. B. (1985). Standards, codification and sociolinguistic realism: The English language in the outer circle. In R. Quirk & H. G. Widdowson (Eds.), English in the world: Teaching and learning the language and literatures. Cambridge University Press.

d: Deictic reference to time measured from the moment of speaking (or sometimes another reference point). It is expressed through adverbs and, in many languages, through tense.
e: now, then, yesterday, next week, ago.

d: A temporary failure to retrieve a known word, accompanied by a strong feeling that it is about to be recalled. Speakers often can report partial information, such as the first sound or number of syllables, suggesting that meaning and sound form are retrieved separately.
e: Someone trying to name a navigation instrument knows it starts with s and has two syllables but cannot quite produce sextant.
p: First studied experimentally by Roger Brown and David McNeill (1966).
s: Brown, R., & McNeill, D. (1966). The "tip of the tongue" phenomenon. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 5(4).

d: A single occurrence of a word form in a text; the number of tokens is the total running word count. Corpus sizes are normally reported in tokens.
e: The cat saw the dog. contains five tokens (punctuation usually excluded): The, cat, saw, the, dog.

d: The process of dividing a text into individual units (tokens), usually words and punctuation marks, as a first step in computer analysis. Decisions about contractions, hyphens, numbers, and languages written without spaces mean that different tools may count the same text differently.
e: One tokenizer splits don't into do + n't, while another keeps don't as a single token, giving different word counts.

d: The use of pitch level or pitch movement on a syllable to distinguish word meanings or grammatical meanings. Languages that use pitch in this way, such as Mandarin, Yoruba and Vietnamese, are called tone languages.
e: In Mandarin, mā (high level tone) means 'mother' and mǎ (low dipping tone) means 'horse'.

d: In transformational-generative grammar, a rule that changes one syntactic structure into another, for example by moving, adding, or deleting elements. Transformations were used to relate sentences such as actives and passives, or statements and questions.
e: A question transformation relates You can swim to Can you swim? by moving the auxiliary before the subject.
p: The notion was developed by Zellig Harris in the 1950s and made central to generative grammar by his student Noam Chomsky in Syntactic Structures (1957).
s: Chomsky, N. (1957). Syntactic structures. Mouton.

d: In conversation analysis, a point in a turn, typically the possible end of a grammatical, intonational, or action unit, where another speaker may legitimately start talking.
e: After A says I finally finished my thesis., the end of the sentence is a point where B can respond: Congratulations!
p: Concept from Harvey Sacks, Emanuel Schegloff, and Gail Jefferson (1974).
s: Sacks, H., Schegloff, E. A., & Jefferson, G. (1974). A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation. Language, 50(4).

d: The property of a verb (or clause) concerning whether it takes objects: intransitive verbs take none, transitive verbs take one, and ditransitive verbs take two. Many verbs can be used in more than one way, and some linguists treat transitivity as a matter of degree rather than a strict category.
e: Intransitive: She slept. Transitive: She wrote a letter. Ditransitive: She gave him a letter.

d: A view of bilingual language use in which speakers draw on one integrated linguistic repertoire rather than switching between two separate language systems; the term also names teaching approaches that let students use all their languages for learning. Scholars debate how far it replaces older concepts like code-switching and whether named languages remain useful categories.
e: Students read an article in English, discuss it in small groups in Spanish and English, and write notes mixing both languages before drafting an English essay.
p: The Welsh term trawsieithu was used by Cen Williams (1994) for a bilingual teaching practice in Welsh secondary schools and rendered in English as “translanguaging” by Colin Baker; the concept was later developed by Ofelia García and Li Wei.
s: García, O., & Li Wei. (2014). Translanguaging: Language, bilingualism and education. Palgrave Macmillan.

d: Teaching that deliberately invites students to use their full linguistic repertoire, including languages other than the language of instruction, for learning, thinking, and making meaning. It treats bilingual students' languages as one integrated resource rather than separate systems to be kept apart. Critics and supporters debate how it should balance full-repertoire use with developing the target language.
e: Students discuss a short story in Spanish and English in small groups, take notes in either language, and then write a final analysis in English.
p: The term translanguaging grew out of Cen Williams's work on Welsh–English bilingual classrooms (Welsh trawsieithu); translanguaging pedagogy for U.S. classrooms has been developed especially by Ofelia García and colleagues.
s: García, O., Johnson, S. I., & Seltzer, K. (2017). The translanguaging classroom: Leveraging student bilingualism for learning. Caslon.

d: A graphic representation of the hierarchical structure of a sentence, in which nodes labeled with categories branch into their constituents. Trees make visible which words group together and how phrases are nested.
e: [S [NP The dog] [VP [V chased] [NP the cat]]] can be drawn as a tree with S at the top branching into NP and VP.

d: The conditions the world would have to meet for a sentence (or proposition) to be true. Knowing a sentence's meaning is often said, in formal semantics, to include knowing its truth conditions.
e: The door is closed is true if and only if the door in question is closed.

d: An approach to meaning that explains the meaning of a sentence in terms of the conditions under which it would be true, and builds sentence meanings from word meanings using logic. It is the core of most formal semantics. Critics note that it says little about non-declarative sentences, connotation or context-dependent meaning.
e: It analyzes Every student passed as true just in case each member of the set of students is in the set of people who passed.
p: Rooted in the work of Gottlob Frege and Alfred Tarski; proposed as a theory of natural-language meaning by Donald Davidson (1967) and developed formally by Richard Montague.
s: Davidson, D. (1967). Truth and meaning. Synthese, 17(1), 304–323.

d: The way participants in a conversation organize who speaks when, usually with one person speaking at a time and with short gaps and overlaps. Conversation analysts describe it in terms of turn construction units and points where a change of speaker becomes possible.
e: A speaker ends a question with …right, Maria?, selecting Maria to take the next turn.
p: Classic model by Harvey Sacks, Emanuel Schegloff, and Gail Jefferson (1974).
s: Sacks, H., Schegloff, E. A., & Jefferson, G. (1974). A simplest systematics for the organization of turn-taking for conversation. Language, 50(4).

d: A distinct word form in a text or corpus, counted only once no matter how many times it occurs. Whether capitalized and lowercase forms (e.g., The and the) count as one type depends on the software settings.
e: The cat saw the dog. has five tokens but four types (the, cat, saw, dog) if case is ignored.

d: The number of types divided by the number of tokens in a text, used as a simple measure of lexical variety. Because the ratio falls as texts get longer, it is unreliable for comparing texts of different lengths, so adjusted measures (e.g., standardized TTR, MATTR, or MTLD) are often preferred.
e: The cat saw the dog. has 4 types and 5 tokens, giving a TTR of 4/5 = 0.80.

d: A developmental pattern in which a learner first uses a form correctly, then begins to use it incorrectly, and later uses it correctly again. The dip is usually interpreted as a sign of restructuring: the learner has moved from memorized items to a general rule that is temporarily overapplied.
e: A learner first says went (memorized), later says *goed (ungrammatical, after learning the regular -ed rule), and eventually returns to went.

d: The final or highest level of proficiency an L2 learner reaches after long exposure, when further development appears to have leveled off. Research on ultimate attainment often asks whether late learners can become indistinguishable from native speakers; some scholars question using native speakers as the benchmark at all.
e: A study compares the grammar judgments of adults who have lived in the country for 20+ years with those of lifelong native speakers to examine their ultimate attainment.

d: An intransitive verb whose single argument behaves in some ways like an object, typically an entity that undergoes change rather than acts deliberately. Unaccusatives are contrasted with unergative verbs, whose subject is more agent-like.
e: The ice melted and The guests arrived contain unaccusative verbs, while The child laughed contains an unergative verb.
p: The Unaccusative Hypothesis was proposed by David Perlmutter (1978) within Relational Grammar.
s: Perlmutter, D. M. (1978). Impersonal passives and the unaccusative hypothesis. In Proceedings of the Fourth Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society. Berkeley Linguistics Society.

d: The abstract form of a word or morpheme assumed to be stored in the mind, from which its actual pronunciations (surface representations) are derived. How abstract underlying representations can be is a long-standing debate in phonology.
e: The English plural suffix is often analyzed as underlying /z/, which surfaces as [z] in dogs, [s] in cats and [əz] in buses; other analyses propose a different underlying form.
p: A core concept of generative phonology, developed especially in Noam Chomsky and Morris Halle (1968).
s: Chomsky, N., & Halle, M. (1968). The sound pattern of English. Harper & Row.

d: A framework for planning lessons and materials that are accessible to all learners from the start, rather than adapting them afterward for particular students. It recommends offering multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression.
e: A teacher provides a lecture as video with captions, a transcript, and an audio file, and lets students show learning through an essay, a podcast, or an annotated slide deck.
p: Developed by David H. Rose, Anne Meyer, and colleagues at CAST (Center for Applied Special Technology).
s: Rose, D. H., & Meyer, A. (2002). Teaching every student in the digital age: Universal design for learning. ASCD.

d: In generative linguistics, the proposed innate set of principles and constraints common to all human languages that guides children's language acquisition. Its existence and content are widely debated; usage-based and other approaches argue that general learning abilities and input can explain much of what UG is meant to explain.
e: Proponents point to the fact that children acquiring any language appear to follow structure-dependent rules, for example forming Is the man who is tall happy? rather than *Is the man who tall is happy?
p: Closely associated with Noam Chomsky, especially Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (1965) and later work.
s: Chomsky, N. (1965). Aspects of the theory of syntax. MIT Press.

d: A learner’s immediate response to a teacher’s or interlocutor’s corrective feedback, which may include repairing the error or simply acknowledging the feedback. Uptake is easy to observe in classroom data, but it is debated how well it predicts long-term learning. (The word is also used more loosely for what learners report having learned from a lesson.)
e: Student: *She have two brothers. Teacher: She has? Student: Oh, she has two brothers. The student’s correction is uptake with repair.
p: Defined in the corrective-feedback sense by Roy Lyster and Leila Ranta (1997).
s: Lyster, R., & Ranta, L. (1997). Corrective feedback and learner uptake: Negotiation of form in communicative classrooms. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 19(1).

d: A family of approaches holding that language is learned from experience with language use through general cognitive abilities, such as pattern detection and memory for frequency, rather than through a language-specific innate faculty. Learners are seen as gradually building a network of form–meaning pairings (constructions) from the input.
e: A learner hears Can I have a…? many times in cafes, first uses it as a fixed chunk, and later varies it creatively: Can I have the bill?, Can I have more time?

d: Lack of precise boundaries in a word's meaning, so that for some cases it is unclear whether the word applies. Vagueness differs from ambiguity: a vague word has one meaning with fuzzy edges, while an ambiguous word has two or more distinct meanings.
e: Tall is vague: there is no exact height at which a person becomes tall.

d: The number and type of arguments a verb (or other head) requires or allows in order to form a complete clause. Verbs can be described as avalent (no arguments), monovalent, divalent, or trivalent.
e: Rain has no true arguments (It rained), sleep has one, see has two, and give has three.
p: Most closely associated with Lucien Tesnière, who borrowed the term from chemistry for his dependency-based syntax, published posthumously in 1959.
s: Tesnière, L. (1959). Éléments de syntaxe structurale. Klincksieck.

d: The degree to which evidence and reasoning support the interpretations and uses made of test scores. Older accounts listed separate kinds of validity, while most current theory, following Messick, treats validity as a single concept built from several kinds of evidence, including consequences of test use.
e: A speaking test that uses only multiple-choice grammar items would have weak validity as a measure of oral communication ability.

d: An approach that uses recordings of everyday speech and statistical analysis to show how the choice between alternative linguistic forms is patterned by social and linguistic factors, and how such patterns reveal language change in progress. It treats variation as systematic rather than random or “sloppy.”
e: Labov counted how often department store employees in New York City pronounced the /r/ in fourth floor, and found that /r/ use rose with the social prestige of the store.
p: Pioneered by William Labov, especially in his New York City research (1966).
s: Labov, W. (1966). The social stratification of English in New York City. Center for Applied Linguistics.

d: A neutral cover term for any identifiable form of a language, such as a dialect, a standard, a register, a pidgin, or a creole. Linguists often prefer it because it avoids the social judgments attached to words like “dialect” or “language.”
e: Nigerian English, Cockney, and the English of legal contracts can all be described as varieties of English.

d: Describing a consonant produced with the back of the tongue against or near the soft palate (velum).
e: /k/ in cat, /ɡ/ in go and /ŋ/ in sing are velar.

d: A word class whose members typically express actions, events, or states and head the predicate of a clause. In English, verbs inflect for tense and, in the present, for agreement with a third-person singular subject.
e: walk, walks, walked; know, knew.

d: A phrase headed by a verb, together with its complements and modifiers. In many analyses the verb phrase corresponds roughly to the predicate of a clause.
e: In Maria gave her brother a book, the verb phrase is gave her brother a book.

d: (1) The everyday local language of a community, as opposed to a classical, official, or standard language. (2) In variationist research, a speaker's most casual and least self-monitored style, which is thought to show their most systematic patterns.
e: In medieval Italy, Latin was used for scholarship, but Dante wrote the Divine Comedy in the Tuscan vernacular.

d: How well a person knows the words they know, including meanings, collocations, grammatical patterns, word parts, and register. Researchers disagree on how to define and measure depth, and on whether it is truly separate from size, since the two correlate strongly.
e: Two learners both know that commit means ‘carry out (a wrong act)’, but only one also knows that it collocates with crime and offense, that it appears in patterns like be committed to helping, and that it has the derived form commitment.

d: The number of words (often counted in word families) a person knows at least at a basic form–meaning level. It is the “breadth” dimension of vocabulary knowledge and is typically estimated with tests that sample words from different frequency bands.
e: A learner whose test result is 6,000 word families is estimated to know about 6,000 families in total; the figure is extrapolated from a sample of tested words, not a count of every word known.

d: A grammatical category that expresses the relation between the participants in an event and the grammatical functions of subject and object. Active and passive are the best-known voices; some languages also have middle or antipassive voices, and some analyses also treat causatives as a type of voice.
e: Active: The committee approved the plan. Passive: The plan was approved by the committee.

d: The time between the release of a stop closure and the start of vocal-fold vibration. Voicing may begin before the release (negative VOT), shortly after it (short lag) or well after it (long lag, heard as aspiration), and languages divide this continuum into categories in different ways.
e: English /p/ in pie has a long-lag VOT, while Spanish /p/ in pan 'bread' has a short-lag VOT, so Spanish /p/ can sound like /b/ to English listeners.
p: Established as a cross-linguistic measure of stop voicing by Leigh Lisker and Arthur Abramson (1964).
s: Lisker, L., & Abramson, A. S. (1964). A cross-language study of voicing in initial stops: Acoustical measurements. Word, 20(3), 384–422.

d: Vibration of the vocal folds during the production of a sound. Sounds produced with this vibration are voiced, and sounds produced without it are voiceless; in many languages this difference distinguishes phonemes.
e: /s/ in sip is voiceless and /z/ in zip is voiced; placing a hand on the throat lets learners feel the vibration during /z/.

d: A speech sound produced with a relatively open vocal tract, so that air flows without significant obstruction. Vowels normally form the nucleus of a syllable and are described by tongue height, tongue backness and lip rounding.
e: /i/ in see is a high front unrounded vowel; /u/ in blue is a high back rounded vowel.

d: The weakening of vowels in unstressed syllables, which become shorter and more central in quality, often schwa. Vowel reduction is a strong feature of English and contributes to its rhythm.
e: The first vowel is full in photograph (American /ˈfoʊtəɡræf/) but reduced to schwa in photography (American /fəˈtɑɡrəfi/), where stress has shifted; British English shows the same pattern (/ˈfəʊtəɡrɑːf/, /fəˈtɒɡrəfi/).

d: The effect that a test has on teaching and learning before and around it. Washback can be positive, as when a test encourages useful practice, or negative, as when teachers narrow the curriculum to test-preparation drills.
e: When a national exam added a speaking section, teachers began to spend more class time on oral practice, a positive washback effect.
s: Alderson, J. C., & Wall, D. (1993). Does washback exist? Applied Linguistics, 14(2), 115–129.

d: The reduced pronunciation of a function word (such as an article, auxiliary, preposition or pronoun) when it is unstressed, as opposed to its strong or citation form. Weak forms are normal in fluent English and are important for listening comprehension.
e: can is usually /kən/ in I can swim but takes its strong form /kæn/ in the reply Yes, I can.
s: Roach, P. (2009). English phonetics and phonology: A practical course (4th ed.). Cambridge University Press.

d: A type of aphasia marked by fluent, normally paced speech that is often empty of meaning or contains wrong or invented words, together with poor comprehension. It is classically linked to damage in the posterior part of the left superior temporal gyrus (Wernicke's area), although the responsible lesions often extend into neighboring temporal and parietal regions.
e: A patient might say I was over at the other one and then the plinter went to the thing, speaking smoothly but conveying little meaning.

d: A region in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus, usually in the left hemisphere, traditionally associated with language comprehension. Its exact boundaries and functions are debated, and current research treats it as one part of a wider temporal–parietal–frontal language network rather than a single comprehension center.
e: Damage here can leave a person speaking fluently but struggling to understand a simple spoken request like Point to the window.
p: Named after the German neurologist Carl Wernicke, who described the associated aphasia in 1874.

d: A U.S.-based organization, housed at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, whose member states and agencies use its English language development standards and assessments, such as WIDA ACCESS (formerly ACCESS for ELLs), to identify and monitor multilingual learners in K–12 schools. Its standards describe language development across six proficiency levels, with level 6 open-ended.
e: A school administers the WIDA ACCESS test each year to decide whether a student still needs English language development services.
s: WIDA. (2020). WIDA English language development standards framework, 2020 edition: Kindergarten–grade 12. Board of Regents of the University of Wisconsin System.

d: A learner’s readiness to start a conversation in the L2 with a particular person at a particular time when given the chance. In L2 research it is treated as influenced by both stable factors (such as personality and confidence) and situational ones (such as the topic, interlocutor, and group size).
e: A student who has high proficiency but stays silent in a large lecture, yet chats freely in English with one classmate over coffee, shows that WTC varies with the situation.
p: Originally a first-language communication construct; developed as an L2 model by Peter MacIntyre, Richard Clément, Zoltán Dörnyei, and Kimberly Noels (1998).
s: MacIntyre, P. D., Clément, R., Dörnyei, Z., & Noels, K. A. (1998). Conceptualizing willingness to communicate in a L2: A situational model of L2 confidence and affiliation. The Modern Language Journal, 82(4).

d: A category of words that share grammatical behavior, such as noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, determiner, pronoun, and conjunction. Classes are best identified by morphological and distributional criteria rather than by meaning alone; open classes accept new members easily, closed classes rarely do.
e: Google was added to the open verb class (to google something), but English rarely gains new prepositions or determiners.

d: A base word together with its inflected forms and its transparent derived forms, treated as one unit for counting vocabulary. Bauer and Nation (1993) proposed a scale of levels for deciding which affixes to include; researchers debate whether learners really know whole families, and some lists (e.g., the AVL) use lemmas instead.
e: The word family of develop includes develops, developed, developing, development, developmental, and undeveloped.
p: The levels for defining word families were set out by Laurie Bauer and Paul Nation (1993).
s: Bauer, L., & Nation, P. (1993). Word families. International Journal of Lexicography, 6(4), 253–279.

d: A particular concrete form of a lexeme as it appears in speech or writing, carrying specific grammatical features.
e: took is the past-tense word form of the lexeme TAKE.

d: The range of different things a person can know about a word. Paul Nation's widely used framework divides it into form (spoken, written, word parts), meaning (form–meaning link, concepts and referents, associations), and use (grammatical functions, collocations, constraints on use), each known receptively and productively.
e: Fully knowing argue includes its pronunciation /ˈɑːrɡjuː/, spelling, the derived form argument, its meanings, patterns like argue that… and argue with someone, and its typical register.
p: The form–meaning–use framework is set out by Paul Nation in Learning Vocabulary in Another Language (2001; 2nd ed. 2013).
s: Nation, I. S. P. (2013). Learning vocabulary in another language (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.

d: The order in which elements such as subject, verb, and object appear in a clause, as well as the order of words within phrases. Languages differ in their basic order (e.g., SVO, SOV, VSO) and in how flexible that order is.
e: English is SVO (Mary eats apples); Japanese is SOV (Mari wa ringo o taberu, literally 'Mary apples eats').

d: The classification of languages by the usual order of subject (S), verb (V), and object (O) in a basic clause, together with related orders such as adposition and noun or noun and genitive. SOV and SVO are by far the most common types: in Matthew Dryer's sample of 1,376 languages in the World Atlas of Language Structures (WALS), 564 are SOV and 488 SVO (about three quarters together), while 189 show no single dominant order. Many correlations can be described in terms of head direction (head-initial vs. head-final), and for languages with flexible order, identifying one 'basic' order is debated.
e: English The dog chased the cat is SVO; Japanese Inu ga neko o oikaketa (dog-SUBJ cat-OBJ chased) is SOV.
p: Modern word order typology is usually traced to Joseph H. Greenberg (1963).

d: A limited-capacity system for temporarily holding and manipulating information while carrying out tasks such as understanding a sentence or doing mental arithmetic. In the widely used multicomponent model, it includes a central executive, a phonological loop, and a visuospatial sketchpad, with an episodic buffer added by Baddeley in 2000.
e: Keeping the subject the reporter in mind until you reach the verb in The reporter that the senator attacked admitted the error places demands on working memory.
p: Multicomponent model proposed by Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch (1974).
s: Baddeley, A. D., & Hitch, G. (1974). Working memory. In G. H. Bower (Ed.), The psychology of learning and motivation (Vol. 8). Academic Press.

d: The many varieties of English used around the world, and the field that studies them as legitimate varieties with their own norms rather than as imperfect versions of British or American English. The plural “Englishes” emphasizes this diversity.
e: Indian English uses prepone to mean 'move to an earlier time,' the opposite of postpone.
p: Associated above all with Braj B. Kachru.
s: Kachru, B. B. (1985). Standards, codification and sociolinguistic realism: The English language in the outer circle. In R. Quirk & H. G. Widdowson (Eds.), English in the world: Teaching and learning the language and literatures. Cambridge University Press.

d: A one-to-one or small-group conversation between a teacher or tutor and a student writer about a draft in progress. Conferences aim to help writers think through revisions, and research has explored how power and talk patterns shape them.
e: In a ten-minute conference, the instructor asks a student what her main argument is, then helps her see that two of her paragraphs support a different point.

d: In generative grammar, a theory of phrase structure proposing that all phrases share the same basic template: a head (X) combines with a complement to form X′ (X-bar), which combines with a specifier to form the full phrase XP. It aims to capture similarities across categories and languages.
e: [NP [Det the] [N′ [N student] [PP of physics]]], where student is the head and of physics its complement.
p: First proposed by Noam Chomsky in "Remarks on Nominalization" (1970) and developed in detail by Ray Jackendoff (1977).
s: Jackendoff, R. (1977). X-bar syntax: A study of phrase structure. MIT Press.

d: A morpheme proposed in an analysis to have no visible or audible form, used to explain a grammatical meaning that is present without any overt marking. Whether zero morphemes are real units or just analytic conveniences is debated.
e: Plural sheep (one sheep, two sheep) is often analyzed as sheep + ∅.

d: An empirical pattern in which a word's frequency is roughly inversely proportional to its rank in a frequency list. As a result, a small number of very frequent words make up a large share of any text, while most word types are rare.
e: In English corpora, the is the most frequent word and occurs roughly twice as often as the second-ranked word (of); at the other end, a large share of the types in a corpus (often close to half) occur only once.
p: Named after George Kingsley Zipf, who popularized it, most fully in his 1949 book; similar patterns had been noticed by earlier researchers.
s: Zipf, G. K. (1949). Human behavior and the principle of least effort. Addison-Wesley.

d: The gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with help from a more capable person or through collaboration. In sociocultural theory, learning is said to be most productive in this zone, and the ZPD is often seen as a way of identifying a learner’s emerging abilities.
e: A learner cannot yet form past-tense questions alone, but succeeds when the teacher prompts: Remember: Did you…? This task lies within her ZPD.
p: Concept developed by Lev Vygotsky.
s: Vygotsky, L. S. (1978). Mind in society: The development of higher psychological processes. Harvard University Press.
